Download the AWS Events mobile app to build your schedule.

Join the conversation on social media using #reInvent.

Note: Session schedule and availability are subject to change. Check the AWS re:Invent Session Catalog for the most up-to-date information.

Stay connected: Join the #reInvent conversation on social media and connect with other attendees!

See you in Las Vegas!

Baqir Naqvi

Baqir is a Product Marketing Manager, Technical, focused on digital sovereignty and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud in AWS Product Marketing. He helps customers across Europe and around the world understand how AWS solutions can help them meet their digital sovereignty requirements so they can build and innovate with confidence.

articles.title: Firefox free VPN drops its 50GB launch cap until January 31
articles.context: Firefox users in supported regions get unlimited browsing on desktop and Android once they sign in with a Mozilla account
articles.full_text:
Mozilla has removed the data limit on the free VPN built into Firefox. Firefox users in supported regions get unlimited browsing on desktop and Android once they sign in with a Mozilla account.

The VPN shipped with Firefox 149 in March with a 50GB monthly cap. That is plenty for reading and ordinary browsing, but someone streaming video through the browser can use it up fast. The VPN protects traffic inside Firefox and nothing else on the device. Mail clients, chat apps and anything else running next to the browser still use the normal connection. Mozilla says iOS support is coming but hasn’t given a date.

Turning it on takes a Mozilla account. On desktop the VPN sits in the toolbar, and on Android it’s under Settings > VPN. At launch it covered the U.S., U.K., Germany and France. To protect apps outside the browser, Mozilla sells Mozilla VPN as a separate paid subscription.

articles.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
articles.context: Get an updated version of Git > The post Git security vulnerabilities announced appeared first on The GitHub Blog
articles.full_text:
Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Vulnerabilities in Git

CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.

An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone.

The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

[Advisory]

Additional hardening

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Protecting GitHub users

We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible.

We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git.

GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git.

Update Git

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Get an updated version of Git >

The post Git security vulnerabilities announced appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

articles.title: Three China-Nexus Espionage Campaigns Linked Through Sparrow Malware Ecosystem
articles.context: Although initially assumed to be independent sets of attacks, each with its own backdoors and post-exploitation tooling, they have all been linked through a malware ecosystem...
articles.full_text:
Three distinct threat activity clusters with shared infrastructure and malware code similarities have been observed targeting telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions, and critical infrastructure across Latin America, Asia, and Europe over the past year.

Check Point Research is tracking the clusters under the names SilentDelivery, OceanGate, and DarkWire. Although initially assumed to be independent sets of attacks, each with its own backdoors and post-exploitation tooling, they have all been linked through a malware ecosystem called Sparrow.

The entity behind the Sparrow framework has been codenamed CopperDragon, and is assessed to be a digital quartermaster developing tools for China-nexus threat actors, including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, Tropic Trooper, UAT-9244, and UAT-8302.

"Each cluster employed a different toolset and different initial access techniques, including compromising internet-facing infrastructure and highly selective watering hole attacks," Check Point said in a technical report published today. "The compromised websites that were used for watering hole attacks were of government, shipping, and IT and research sectors."

Attacks mounted by FamousSparrow are known for deploying backdoors like SparrowDoor (and its variants Crowdoor and TernDoor), SparroWocky, and HemiGate. It's also assessed to share some degree of overlap with Salt Typhoon. However, the precise nature of the relationship remains unclear.

The cyber espionage ecosystem linked to CopperDragon is driven by three prominent clusters -

SilentDelivery (Beginning in early 2026), which conducts highly selective watering hole attacks targeting Europe and Asia that distribute a backdoor called SquadC (aka SquawkDoor) through trojanized MSI installers masquerading as certificate repair utilities

OceanGate (2025-2026), which primarily focuses on Asian organizations with a variant of SparrowDoor after obtaining initial access via internet-facing Linux servers and then moving laterally into Windows environments

DarkWire (Mid 2025), which targets telecommunications providers and government organizations across Latin America using backdoors called CopperDoor (aka SparroWocky) and CopperDNS

SilentDelivery

The SilentDelivery chain begins with the attacker injecting heavily obfuscated JavaScript into legitimate websites frequented by their intended targets. Visitors to the sites are greeted by a Google Chrome SSL certificate warning that instructs users to install a "Certificate Fix" utility to restore access.

The so-called utility, once deployed, delivers either SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant. All the compromised websites have been found to be related to government, shipping, IT, and research sectors in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong, and Indonesia.

According to a report published by Positive Technologies in August 2026, there are indications that the campaign has also targeted entities in Egypt and the Philippines using this method.

"The JavaScript injected into the compromised websites is heavily obfuscated using jsjiami, a publicly available JavaScript obfuscation service," Check Point said. "It first checks whether the user is running Windows and, in some cases, verifies that the website’s domain matches the intended compromised domain."

The script then repeatedly sends status-check requests to a command-and-control (C2) server to fingerprint the user based on IP and geolocation, and ultimately decide whether to continue the attack and serve the fake warning.

Source: Positive Technologies

Written in C/C++, SquadC is a Windows backdoor that enables initial foothold over the infected host. It establishes persistence by means of a Windows Registry Run key that masquerades as a Windows update assistant. Further analysis has uncovered that the malware is also distributed via phishing emails targeting Indonesian organizations.

The phishing email comes with a Windows Shortcut (LNK) disguised as a PDF document, which, when opened, abuses the legitimate "ftp.exe" binary to run a batch script that's responsible for displaying an empty file as a decoy, while launching SquadC via DLL sideloading.

OceanGate

The OceanGate operation, on the other hand, has been observed targeting both Windows and Linux environments, deploying previously undocumented tooling to maintain access, move laterally across the network, and exfiltrate sensitive data.

The Linux phase of the attack involves two new backdoors -

AnnobinDoor, a Go-based backdoor that supports a wide array of features, such as remote access, interactive shell, file management, SOCKS proxying, SSH tunneling, port forwarding, and reverse connections, and enables the infected Linux machine to function as both a remote shell and an internal network pivot

SparrowShell, a modular Linux backdoor that shares overlaps with its Windows counterpart, SparrowDoor

"After harvesting credentials from multiple users and establishing a strong foothold in the Linux environment, the actor moved into the Windows environment," Check Point explained. "The actor attempted to log in to several Windows machines over RDP, trying different passwords until it successfully authenticated with an administrator account."

This step is followed by the deployment of bespoke post-exploitation tools and a variant of SparrowDoor -

CopperAdu, a post-exploitation tool which configures a compromised Windows machine for remote administrative access

CopperList, a Windows reconnaissance tool for collecting host information, disk details, and a recursive file inventory, including file paths, sizes, and timestamps

CopperLogger, a Raw Input-based keylogger to capture keyboard input events, along with monitoring clipboard activity, active window titles, and associated process names and paths

CopperLsa, a utility that collects passwords, hashes, and authentication tokens from NTLM and Kerberos

What's more, the threat actor has been found incorporating kernel rootkits and kernel-level access capabilities into SparrowDoor and SparrowShell to evade defenses through process hiding and to capture and manipulate network packet capture using WinDivert drivers.

"The actor abused the driver to convert SparrowDoor into a passive backdoor that intercepts and manipulates packets at the kernel level, making its traffic less visible," Check Point said. "This allows the backdoor to listen internally on one port while receiving connections through an externally accessible port, such as 443, that is already used by a legitimate service."

"The backdoor applies a strict filter to intercept connections from a specific source IP address to the legitimate service's port. It manipulates the packet and rewrites the destination port to the backdoor’s internal listening port, typically a high port such as 49628. For response traffic, it rewrites the source port back to the external service port, making the responses appear to originate from the legitimate service."

Interestingly, SparrowShell shares code- and infrastructure-level similarities with a malware called Mélofée that was first described by ExaTrack in March 2023 as based on the open-source Reptile rootkit. This has raised the possibility that CopperDragon is also behind the development and supply of Mélofée.

DarkWire

The third and last cluster of activity centers around Latin America, with a particular focus on telecommunications operators and government entities. These attacks led to the deployment of two newly identified backdoors called CopperDoor and CopperDNS as a possible replacement for SparrowDoor.

Also supporting these operations is a set of custom tools -

CopperLoader, a reflective loader typically deployed through DLL sideloading and is used to deliver additional tools, including CopperDoor, CopperDNS, CopperProxy, and CopperLsass

CopperDoor, a memory-resident modular backdoor

CopperDNS, a CopperDoor variant that communicates through DNS tunneling using MX queries

CopperProxy, a SOCKS5 proxy

PyProxy, a lightweight UDP relay written in Python

CopperLsass, a dedicated module for dumping the LSASS process for credential harvesting

"The operation heavily relies on DLL sideloading as a primary execution technique, often abusing executables that are not widely observed among other threat actors in the wild," Check Point said. "To minimize their footprint, the operators deliberately avoided creating new directories on disk, instead placing their tools within existing system paths."

"CopperDoor infrastructure demonstrated a higher level of operational security. Most IP addresses were located in Latin America, often within the same country as the victim organization. This proximity likely helps the malicious traffic blend in with legitimate network activity and reduces the chances of detection."

articles.title: CISA Expands Incident Reporting Form While CIRCIA Mandate Waits
articles.context: More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat
articles.full_text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has rolled out a revamped cyber incident reporting form that asks more granular questions about incident types and frames observed activity in MITRE ATT&CK terms.

CISA outlined the changes in an announcement published November 9 and the updated web-based questionnaire is available through its Incident Reporting Portal.

The agency said better data quality will help it connect related threat activity into broader trends that would otherwise look like separate incidents. The update draws on community feedback CISA has received over the years.

More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms

The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Questions about observed activity now use MITRE ATT&CK, a framework for describing adversary behavior that CISA said is familiar to the cyber community.

The changes are meant to support rapid but thorough threat analysis, according to CISA.

"In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization's detection is another's protection," said Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity. "As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation's collective defense."

For now, only federal civilian agencies are required to report incidents to CISA. The agency encouraged other organizations that experience an incident to report voluntarily, and information they submit can be protected from disclosure under the Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (PCII) Program.

CIRCIA Rule Remains at White House

The update comes as the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) awaits approval. The rule went to the White House for review on October 1 and remains listed as pending.

Read more on CIRCIA: US Critical Infrastructure Braces for Sweeping New Cyber Reporting Rules

Once the rule takes effect, covered critical infrastructure organizations would have to report qualifying cyber incidents within 72 hours of reasonably believing they occurred and ransom payments within 24 hours of making them, according to CISA.

CISA published its proposed CIRCIA rule in April 2024 but missed an October 2025 statutory deadline to finalize it. Many comments on the proposal asked for a narrower scope, less burden and closer alignment with other federal reporting rules, according to CISA's regulatory agenda.

CISA's announcement did not mention CIRCIA or whether the enhanced reporting form would be used under the pending rule.

articles.title: Software Transparency Is Changing: Allan Friedman on SBOM, AI BOMs and What Comes Next
articles.context: That capability becomes critical when organizations face the next Log4j style vulnerability, compromise of a major software package, malicious update, or other widespread supply...
articles.full_text:
Modern software is built on layers of dependencies, open source components, third party libraries and increasingly, artificial intelligence models and external data sources. For security teams, understanding exactly what is running inside an application has become less of a compliance exercise and more of an operational necessity.

That is the foundation behind the Software Bill of Materials, or SBOM.

In a recent episode of the SecurityWeek Podcast, host Brian “SchleiF” Schleifer sat down with cybersecurity policy expert Allan Friedman for a wide-ranging discussion about the origins of SBOM, how organizations should actually use the data, the emergence of AI BOMs, vulnerability management, VEX, and where software transparency may be heading next.

Friedman, who helped drive early government and industry work around SBOM, offered perhaps the simplest explanation for why the concept matters.

“Software isn’t written, it’s assembled,” Friedman said. “What’s it assembled out of? More software.”

In practical terms, an SBOM provides a structured representation of the components and dependencies that allow software to function. But Friedman emphasized throughout the conversation that producing an SBOM is not the end goal. The real value comes from what organizations, and their suppliers can do with the information.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

SBOM Is About Response, Not Just Inventory

Much of the early SBOM conversation focused on whether vendors could generate the documents and whether customers should require them.

The more important question today may be: What happens after you receive one?

Friedman argues that one of the first indicators of software supply chain maturity is simply knowing that a supplier can generate an accurate SBOM.

That capability becomes critical when organizations face the next Log4j style vulnerability, compromise of a major software package, malicious update, or other widespread supply chain event.

A supplier that understands the components within its products can determine its exposure far more quickly than one forced to reconstruct dependencies during an incident. For customers, the same visibility can dramatically shorten response time.

Instead of spending days or weeks contacting vendors and attempting to determine which systems contain a vulnerable component, security teams can analyze their software inventory and dependencies directly.

The objective, however, should ultimately be deeper integration.

Friedman said SBOM information needs to become another source of enterprise security data, feeding vulnerability management, asset management, procurement and continuous risk management processes rather than existing as a static document stored somewhere for future reference.

That distinction matters because attackers are not limited to vulnerabilities associated with the name of the software vendor.

A smaller vendor’s application may contain an outdated framework, library or open source component with a known weakness. Without component level visibility, an organization may never associate that vulnerability with the commercial product deployed in its environment.

Not Every Vulnerability Creates the Same Risk

More visibility can also create another problem: more alerts.

Finding that a vulnerable component exists inside an application does not necessarily mean the vulnerability is exploitable within that specific implementation.

Friedman highlighted the Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange, or VEX, as an important companion to SBOM. VEX provides a machine processable method for communicating whether a vulnerability actually affects a product.

An application, for example, may contain a vulnerable version of a software library but never use the functionality associated with the vulnerability. VEX can provide the context needed to distinguish between the presence of a vulnerable component and an exploitable condition.

That becomes increasingly important as organizations face what Friedman jokingly described as the “vulnerpocalypse”: an environment in which security teams have far more vulnerability information than they have resources to investigate manually.

The combination of SBOM and VEX creates the possibility of better prioritization rather than simply more data.

AI Makes the Transparency Problem More Complicated

The next evolution is already underway.

As organizations embed machine learning, generative AI and autonomous agents into applications, traditional software inventories may no longer capture everything security teams need to understand.

Friedman described the emergence of the AI BOM as inevitable.

At its core, AI is still software, meaning traditional software components remain relevant. But AI systems introduce additional elements that may need to be documented, including the model itself, the data supporting the model, external data sources and the surrounding infrastructure or “harnesses” used to operate the system.

That creates new questions.

Where did the model originate?

What data was used to support it?

What external data is being introduced at runtime?

Who owns the model?

What happens when an agent dynamically creates a tool, executes an action and then disappears?

The last question becomes particularly challenging as AI systems become more dynamic and agentic.

Friedman suggested that the answer may increasingly involve a convergence between traditional BOM concepts, logging, information architecture and third party risk management.

The goal is not necessarily to force every piece of information into an AI BOM. Instead, organizations need enough transparency and supporting evidence to reconstruct what happened, understand dependencies, enforce controls and conduct forensic analysis when necessary.

Transparency Should Favor the Defender

Resistance to SBOM adoption has often centered on concerns about intellectual property and the possibility that providing detailed information about software components could benefit attackers.

Friedman challenged that argument.

Modern reverse engineering capabilities already allow determined attackers to analyze software and identify many of its underlying components. Automated attack frameworks and ransomware operations also frequently do not require an SBOM because they simply test systems against known exploits.

Defenders face a different problem. They need to know where vulnerable components exist across potentially thousands of systems.

“You know who does need visibility into what’s in a piece of software? Blue Team,” Friedman said.

SBOM standards can also support redaction where legitimate proprietary concerns exist, allowing suppliers to disclose the existence of a dependency without necessarily revealing every detail associated with it.

The larger issue, Friedman argued, is determining what information actually needs protection and balancing that concern against the operational value software transparency provides defenders.

From SBOM to an “Omnibomb”

SBOM may ultimately be only one layer of a much larger transparency ecosystem.

AI bills of materials are emerging alongside cryptographic bills of materials designed to identify cryptographic dependencies as organizations prepare for crypto agility and post quantum computing.

Hardware bills of materials can provide similar visibility into physical components such as semiconductors.

Friedman suggested that those different transparency mechanisms could eventually converge into what he jokingly called an “omnibomb.”

Before that happens, however, there is significant work left to do.

Even today’s SBOM ecosystem continues to struggle with interoperability. Two quality SBOM tools analyzing the same software may not necessarily produce identical dependency graphs, making harmonization, minimum requirements and common expectations critical.

Friedman pointed to continuing work among governments, cybersecurity agencies, industry and the open source community to define those expectations and create an ecosystem in which SBOM information can move between suppliers, customers and security tools in a meaningful way.

The ultimate destination is not another compliance document, it is continuous software transparency.

Organizations should be able to understand what their systems depend on, correlate that information with emerging threats and vulnerabilities, determine where actual exposure exists and make risk decisions quickly enough to matter.

Or, as Friedman repeatedly emphasized during the conversation, SBOM is not supposed to solve every cybersecurity problem. It is data. What organizations do with that data is where the security value begins.

Watch or listen to the full SecurityWeek Podcast conversation with Allan Friedman for a deeper discussion on SBOM, AI BOMs, VEX, software supply chain security, continuous monitoring and the future of software transparency.

articles.title: Google Widens Gemini 4 Carbon Access After AI Agents Verify Signal Code
articles.context: Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team used the model to confirm that two bugs in a popular open source project were exploitable, with severity comparable to...
articles.full_text:
Google on Tuesday expanded access to Gemini 4 Carbon and said agents built on the model helped formally verify core security guarantees in the code behind the Signal protocol.

Paying developers and businesses can now use Carbon via the Gemini API and Gemini for business, and Google AI Ultra subscribers are getting access. Introductory rates of $2/$10 per million input/output tokens apply until November 30, then double.

Until now, only select cyber defenders in Google’s Fairwind Program could use Carbon. They still need Fairwind membership for Carbon for cyber, which Google says tops key benchmarks for discovering, exploiting and fixing vulnerabilities.

According to Google, Wiz used Carbon for cyber to find zero-days at two major SaaS providers within two hours. Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team used the model to confirm that two bugs in a popular open source project were exploitable, with severity comparable to PHP2Shell, a pair of PHP flaws that attackers have already exploited.

“By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch,” Google said.

Separately, Google DeepMind introduced AlphaProof Code, which pairs human experts with AI agents to formally verify software, mathematically demonstrating that it meets defined requirements.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The team applied it to libsignal, the Signal protocol’s reference implementation. Versions of the protocol also run in WhatsApp and Google Messages.

Humans worked with agents running on Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 to write the specifications defining what had to be proven. Carbon-based agents then generated all of the roughly 6.5 million lines of Lean proofs, with Lean rejecting any invalid ones.

The proven guarantees, including forward secrecy, post-compromise security, and authentication, hold for the compiled machine code, while most protocol verification examines only the design.

Five researchers did the proof work in four weeks, something Google says has traditionally taken specialists years.

To show the method catches real flaws, the team reinserted two old, already-patched libsignal bugs and proved that those builds break the security guarantees.

The results cover Google’s own build of the code, run through a small command-line wrapper, and “not Signal’s own applications.” Side channels were also excluded from parts of the analysis.

“The results suggest that AI can make formal verification, historically too expensive for most software, practical for real-world systems,” the researchers wrote.

“As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code’s privacy guarantees,” said Signal CTO Ehren Kret.

Google is publicly releasing the specifications and proofs.

articles.title: Critical Xen Orchestra auth bypass flaw exploited to hijack VM servers
articles.context: A critical authentication bypass vulnerability in Xen Orchestra is being actively exploited in attacks that could grant administrator privileges and allow takeover of XCP-ng...
articles.full_text:
A critical authentication bypass vulnerability in Xen Orchestra is being actively exploited in attacks that could grant administrator privileges and allow takeover of XCP-ng virtualization hosts.

Xen Orchestra is a web-based management platform developed by French software company Vates, used to manage XCP-ng virtualization environments, including virtual machines, hosts, and pools.

The vulnerability, tracked as VSA-2026-062, affects Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance (XOA) and allows remote attackers with network access to the management interface to bypass authentication using a specially crafted cookie. A CVE identifier and CVSS score have not been assigned yet.

According to a Vates security advisory, the flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication tokens sent through REST API requests.

The flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication cookies.

By sending a specially crafted cookie (authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D) containing an empty JSON object ({}), attackers can trick the platform into retrieving an existing authentication token and logging them in as its owner, without requiring actual credentials.

Once authenticated, attackers can retrieve "reusable login token IDs" through the /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens REST API endpoint, which can be used for further access.

"An adversary can bypass authentication and perform actions with 'Admin' privilege. Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root," warns Vates.

The company has released Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 (stable) and 6.10.0 (latest), including patched xo-server packages 5.211.2 and 5.213.1 to fix these security vulnerabilities.

Administrators should install the update immediately, and if not possible, restrict Xen Orchestra access to dedicated management networks and block known malicious IP addresses.

Security researchers Filip Magic and Christoffer Olsen of TDC NET Security discovered the vulnerability.

Exploited in attacks

Vates confirmed that the vulnerability is being actively exploited and shared the following indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help administrators identify attacks:

Attacker's infrastructure: Connections to 91.211.251.112:8001 or ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid.onion:3333.

Suspicious authentication cookies: HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}.

Virtual machines: A VM named pivot2.

Modified VM configurations: Virtual machines configured with the hvm_serial: file parameter.

Unusual files: /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6.

Administrators can also run the following commands on XCP-ng hosts to check for unusual VM configurations, virtual machines configured to use a file for its serial port, and malicious files:

xe vm-list params=name-label,platform | grep -B1 'hvm_serial: file' zgrep -- '-serial file:' /var/log/xensource.log* ls -la /etc/ld.so.preload /.ustar* /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar*

However, Vates warns that exploitation will not generate any identifiers in logs, such as the use of specially crafted cookies, and instead must be detected through HTTP monitoring.

The company also says these IOCs are only associated with this known attack campaign and may differ for other threat actors.

Companies that believe they are compromised should rotate passwords and secrets used by their virtualization environments.

articles.title: X.Org patches eight server vulnerabilities a month after fixing 12 others
articles.context: A monitor is the attack tool CVE-2026-109091 sits in the code that reads EDID, the block of data a monitor sends to describe the resolutions and refresh rates it supports
articles.full_text:
X.Org has fixed eight vulnerabilities in the X.Org X server and Xwayland, including one in the Xorg server that lets a malicious monitor corrupt its memory. The fixes ship in xorg-server 21.1.26 and xwayland 24.1.15, and each of the eight affects versions before those two releases.

The X server provides the low-level display layer for graphical desktops on many Linux and Unix systems. Xwayland runs X11 applications on desktops built on Wayland, the newer display protocol, so Wayland users who run X11 applications are exposed too. The flaws can crash the server, corrupt its memory, or make it read or write outside the memory it should touch, and one can leak memory contents.

A monitor is the attack tool

CVE-2026-109091 sits in the code that reads EDID, the block of data a monitor sends to describe the resolutions and refresh rates it supports. The Xorg server copies a monitor’s display-range entries into fixed-size arrays without checking the count against the arrays’ limits. Feed it more entries than the arrays hold, from a rigged monitor or a crafted EDID, and the excess spills into neighboring data, which can crash the server or corrupt memory.

An attacker going after this flaw needs a malicious monitor, or a doctored EDID, in front of the server. The other seven flaws sit in the code that handles X protocol requests, the messages applications send to the X server.

Size checks that wrap around

Four of the seven are in Xv, the X Video extension applications use to pass video frames to the server. In CVE-2026-109092, a negative size from the server’s hardware-specific code plus a crafted offset wraps XvShmPutImage’s bounds check, letting the server read or write outside a shared memory segment. CVE-2026-109095, in the glamor acceleration code, computes image sizes with 32-bit integers that wrap to small values for large images, so the server reads past the data the client sent. CVE-2026-109096 and CVE-2026-109903 both start from a negative image size: one lets a request with no image data pass the length check, and the other reports the bogus size to the client, which may then allocate or use a buffer of the wrong size.

CVE-2026-109093 is an out-of-bounds stack write in XTest, the extension that lets clients inject fake keyboard and mouse events. The server copies input values into a fixed-size stack array before checking that they fit. The last two, CVE-2026-109904 and CVE-2026-109094, are integer overflows in the X-Resource extension. On 32-bit servers, a large count wraps so a short request passes the length check, and the server reads or walks past the end of the request buffer.

No severity ratings

X.Org published no severity ratings or CVSS scores and did not say whether any of the eight could lead to code execution. Admins have to rank the bugs themselves, and the three that can write out of bounds, CVE-2026-109091, -109092 and -109093, are the ones to weigh first.

X.Org released xorg-server 21.1.26 about a month after 21.1.25, which fixed 12 flaws. Anyone who installed that update in October has another one to install now. Distributions usually backport the patches into their own package versions, so look for the CVE numbers in your distribution’s advisory.

articles.title: Trump taps Palantir security chief to run battered US cyber defense agency
articles.context: The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025
articles.full_text: President Donald Trump has nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, putting an executive from the controversial government supplier in line to run America's civilian cyber defense agency. The nomination, announced on Monday, could end CISA's nearly two-year wait for a Senate-confirmed director following Jen Easterly's departure in January 2025. LoSapio has served as Palantir's CISO since September 2024, having previously led the company's infrastructure and network security team. He first joined the data analytics outfit in 2013, later spent a spell at database company SingleStore, and returned to Palantir in 2017. If confirmed, LoSapio would move from securing Palantir's systems to leading the federal government's main civilian cyber defense agency. CISA protects federal civilian networks and works with critical infrastructure operators, including power, water, and telecommunications providers. It's a substantial job, particularly given the state of the agency he would inherit. CISA has shed more than 1,000 staff, roughly a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to the White House, according to reports. It's now trying to plug the gaps, although acting director Nick Andersen said in September that around 250 would-be recruits were still waiting for security clearance before they could get to work. Andersen has been running CISA since February. With fewer people to go around, CISA is also rethinking where to spend its time. A strategy published last month emphasizes infrastructure whose failure would do the most damage, raising questions about what gets less attention as the agency operates with fewer staff. LoSapio would be the second person Trump has put forward for the role. His previous pick, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April after spending more than a year awaiting confirmation, with his nomination becoming caught up in a dispute involving Republican Senator Rick Scott over Coast Guard contracting. The nomination arrives late in the congressional calendar. If the Senate does not confirm LoSapio before the current Congress ends, Trump would have to nominate him again for consideration by the incoming Democratic-controlled Senate. Palantir, co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has become a major supplier of technology to US government agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Its work with immigration authorities has attracted criticism from civil liberties groups and Democratic lawmakers concerned about surveillance and the handling of sensitive personal information. The controversy isn't confined to the US either. In the UK, WhatsApp messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove this week indicate that Palantir privately lobbied a health minister to consider extending its software into GP patient records, despite that data being expressly excluded from its £330 million NHS England contract for the Federated Data Platform. That revelation follows news that NHS England wants greater oversight of Palantir's claims about the benefits of its software, amid questions over the evidence supporting its performance figures. Those controversies could make LoSapio's confirmation hearings particularly interesting, especially as Democrats prepare to scrutinize Palantir's government business more closely. It's unclear whether LoSapio plans to leave Palantir or what would happen to any financial interests he holds in the company if confirmed. Those are questions likely to come up during a confirmation process that CISA, having spent nearly two years without a permanent boss while losing a third of its workforce, could probably do without dragging on any longer. ®

articles.title: Iranian hackers turned up the heat on French supermarket freezers, says France
articles.context: Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire
articles.full_text:
Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire.

According to French authorities, a hacking unit from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) sabotaged food refrigeration systems at approximately 700 retail sites, sparking at least 15 fires and causing tens of millions of euros worth of damage.

On the night of 11 October, the hackers seized remote control of refrigeration controllers and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. As a report published by the French government’s computer emergency response team (CERT-FR) describes, victims of the attack included Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché, as well as butchers, a slaughterhouse, and food-processing plants.

According to French media reports, the targeted refrigeration controllers were made by Danish firm Danfoss, and the attackers targeted older versions of its software.

The finger of blame has been pointed by French authorities in the direction of Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within the IRGC. Evidence which is said to have led them to that conclusion includes that the same infrastructure was used, during the same period, to scan Schneider Electric equipment at energy and water facilities. and traces of Farsi. Perhaps the most telling clue of all, however, was that the attack was being trumpeted by a propaganda outlet linked to the hacking unit barely a day later.

Shahid Kaveh is said to hide behind a variety of different "hacktivist" guises including CyberAv3ngers, Soldiers of Solomon, and Cyber Isnaad Front.

The official French report names three men: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, head of the IRGC's Electronic and Cyber Center, and Shahid Kaveh commanders Mahdi Lashgarian and Reza Salarvand.

The same hackers are also believed to have targeted small hydroelectric facilities, while a second Iranian unit called Shahid Shoostari (also known as Emennet Pasargad), is held responsible for attacks on Charlie Hebdo and an attempt to hijack display screens during the 2024 Paris Olympics.

In early November there was a second wave of attacks on refrigeration units which hit businesses across Europe, including three French blood service sites. These attacks have not yet been officially attributed to Iran.

Regardless of who is behind the attacks, it is clearly important that any organisation properly defends its refrigeration systems to prevent tampering. As such, it remains good advice to ensure that operational technology (OT) interfaces are not exposed to the internet, that controller software is kept up to date, that default passwords are changed, and that OT networks are segmented and monitored for unexpected changes.

With fridge attacks like this continuing to create disruption and cost millions of euros, we can expect relations between Paris and Tehran to remain frosty for some time.

articles.title: Attackers Exploit AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Sandbox-Evading Python Backdoor
articles.context: The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an attack that exploited two now-patched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS to deliver a Python-based implant.

The activity, observed by Huntress in early October 2026, involves the exploitation of a chain comprising CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. Patches for the two vulnerabilities were released by Ahsay Backup in mid-October 2026.

The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach to deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners on compromised systems.

"However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups," Huntress researcher Jonathan Semon said.

Specifically, the unknown threat actor is said to have left five families of Jakarta Server Pages (JSP, formerly JavaServer Pages) web shells -

nsmind.jsp, a signed API with command execution and file transfer capabilities using exec, cd, upload, and download parameters

AhsayCBS.jsp, a loader that hides encrypted payloads in the pixel data of PNG images and runs them from memory

Keyed command shell, which compares a hard-coded key against its own copy and, if it matches, runs the command via "cmd.exe"

Keyed shell with file write, which expands on the keyed command web shell with the ability to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and deploy more tools

status_<six_random_letters>.jsp or st_<six_random_letters>.jsp (e.g., st_jgaejj.jsp), which are used to run commands, recursively delete any path provided as input, and delete themselves using cmd, del, and rm parameters.

"[AhsayCBS.jsp's] disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint," Huntress explained. "The web shell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later."

The attack, besides deploying an XMRig miner masquerading as Microsoft Edge, has been found to deliver a second XMRig miner ("kvm-agent.exe") that restarts every minute through a SYSTEM scheduled task, while using a different wallet and mining pool.

The most notable aspect of the intrusion revolves around the Python backdoor ("main.py"), which is designed to run only on the host it's staged on and prevent it from executing within a sandbox or an analyst's machine.

It achieves this by computing the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file with the same name in the same directory housing the Python implant, and then runs an embedded x64 DLL in memory that contacts a command-and-control (C2) server ("creepexplosiondarknight[.]com").

In an attempt to fly under the radar, the attack chain also configures Microsoft Defender exclusions, while serving tunneling tools (GOST and Chisel) and legitimate remote access software (AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop) to establish persistent access.

Evidence indicates that the threat actor may have targeted servers holding or managing backups.

"On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI," Semon said.

"Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident."

articles.title: Binance warns of iOS flaw that could leak crypto wallet secrets
articles.context: Public exploit available “worse_query” is a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape technique that allows an application to cross security boundaries and access the storage of...
articles.full_text:
Binance is warning about a vulnerability in Apple’s iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 that could allow third-party apps to read private files stored by other apps, including cryptocurrency seed phrases, secret keys, and login credentials.

The crypto exchange clarifies that the issue is at the iOS level and does not impact only the Binance app.

“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem,” Binance says.

At this time, no cryptocurrency losses have been confirmed, but Binance urges users to install the update immediately as a precaution.

The company recommends that users delete any unnecessary and untrusted apps and apply the latest versions for iOS and other apps.

Where compromise is suspected, Binance advises users to transfer funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

Public exploit available

“worse_query” is a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape technique that allows an application to cross security boundaries and access the storage of other applications.

Yesterday, a proof-of-concept exploit has been published that uses a tool called WQ Files to perform attacks relying on the technique. Specifically, WQ Files uses “worse_query” to browse, export, edit, and delete other apps’ data without requiring a jailbreak.

An attacker could

The tool must be installed on an iPhone for the attack to work, but an attacker could distribute it through untrusted sources as a sideloaded app, bypassing Apple's App Store.

WQ Files has been confirmed to work on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2, the same versions that Binance warned about.

Apple on November 9 released iOS security updates (iOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3, and 18.7.12) that address nine flaws. One of the fixed vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-113963, could allow an app to access sensitive user data.

It is unclear if this is the same security issue Binance is warning of, though.

The CVE-2026-113963 problem was reported by László Várady flaw, who found that the access occurred through App Intents, not App Group containers.

BleepingComputer has contacted Apple for clarifications and a request for comment, and we will add an update once we receive more details.
