articles.title: Blind Eagle Uses Fake Court Notices to Deliver Remote Access Trojan Across Latin America
articles.context: Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-...
articles.full_text:
The threat actor known as Blind Eagle has resurfaced with a new campaign targeting organizations in Latin America through judicial and administrative-themed phishing lures to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) that shares its lineage with AsyncRAT and DCRat.

"The campaign uses Portuguese and Spanish lures that resemble court notifications, fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents," Zenox said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Assessed to be a Spanish-speaking group and active since 2018, Blind Eagle (aka APT-C-36) has a track record of using spear-phishing lures to distribute commodity RATs like AsyncRAT, BitRAT, Lime RAT, NjRAT, Quasar RAT, and Remcos RAT.

Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-laced attachment.

One email containing a Colombian judicial-themed XHTML file has been identified as a weaponized Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) image that renders a bogus web page impersonating Colombia's Fiscalía General de la Nación, also referred to as the Office of the Attorney General.

The web page, for its part, employs a technique known as HTML smuggling to assemble the next-stage ZIP archive payload locally in the web browser using ZipCrypto, thereby circumventing email security controls.

Present within the ZIP archive is a JavaScript dropper that masquerades as Network Configuration Auditor version 2.7.298. The JavaScript code conducts environment reconnaissance, and collects details such as system version, network profile, installation date, memory size, computer name, environment variables, and directories localized in Portuguese and Spanish.

Upon execution, it launches a Visual Basic Script that performs Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, while displaying a fake criminal-citation page as a distraction mechanism.

In parallel, the malware also takes steps to delete the original XHTML artifact, clears Mark of the Web (MotW) metadata, and sets up persistence on the host under the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically executed on system startup.

The attack culminates with the use of PowerShell to decode and launch the final RAT payload in memory. The trojan is an AsyncRAT fork with DCRat lineage based on code structure, configuration, build characteristics, and observed behavior.

"The targeting of judicial, fiscal, administrative and educational organizations gives the operation access to highly sensitive legal, financial and institutional information," Zenox said.

"Combined with the Portuguese and Spanish lures, Brazilian infrastructure, operational timezone and regional victimology, these elements establish the campaign as an APT-C-36 operation conducted through a Brazilian operational cluster."

Zenox told The Hacker News that it could not confirm whether any of these attacks had succeeded against real-world targets. However, during the campaign period between late October and early November 2026, it observed a large-scale wave of targeted phishing involving nearly 3,300 malicious emails.

While not all of these messages targeted organizations in Colombia, the country continues to remain a priority target for Blind Eagle for a combination of reasons.

"The repeated targeting of Colombia likely reflects multiple factors, with one of the main enabling factors being the structural vulnerabilities and uneven security maturity across parts of the country's critical, public, financial, and private-sector infrastructure," Zenox security researcher Gabriel Alves said.

"These conditions may increase the likelihood of successful compromises and offer greater opportunities to monetize access, steal sensitive data or funds, or reuse compromised credentials against critical systems. This is further supported by regional actors' familiarity with the Colombian context and is consistent with patterns observed among Latin American threat actors."

(The story was updated after publication to include additional insights from Zenox.)

articles.title: Chat Feels Safer Than Email. Attackers Are Counting on It.
articles.context: KnowBe4 Threat Labs turns real-world attack telemetry and more than 15 years of data into live detection models across the Email & Collaboration Security suite, so defenses...
articles.full_text:
Lead Analysts: Prabhakaran R and Jeewan Singh Jalal

You think twice before clicking a link in an unexpected email. Do you do the same for a message in Microsoft Teams?

A new message arrives in your Teams chat with the familiar notification sound, a participant’s name, and a link. It feels like a colleague, not a stranger. That feeling is the opening attackers look for.

Two things decide whether that message does harm. Can the channel stop it before it reaches your user? And if it gets through, does the user recognize the lure and know what to do? Both matter, and this post covers both.

Modern business depends on external collaboration across sales, finance, and IT. External access and guest participation are standard Teams features, not security oversights, and external access is open to all domains by default. Teams is also no longer where only people talk to people. A message could come from a colleague, an authorized AI agent/chabot, or an attacker, and most people have little to tell them apart.

Attackers exploit this openness by sending external messages that follow the same social engineering patterns as phishing emails and blend into your users' daily routine. They could also aim a message at an agent instead of a person. The question is no longer only whether a phishing message looks real. It is who and what you can trust at work.

KnowBe4 Threat Labs has consistently observed attackers imitating routine messages such as support requests, invoices, and meeting chat posts. Weekly detections grew from five in the week of June 22 to a peak of 301 in the week of September 28 (Figure 1). This post covers what we observed, what the attackers are after, and how the attacks play out.

What makes these messages effective is that a phishing message in chat looks like a routine work message: a link, a support request, a payment follow-up. People may not expect an attack on this channel, so they may take such messages at face value. The words alone rarely settle it. The better question is who is sending, from where and why.

Key Findings

Attackers follow work into Microsoft Teams. Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email has carried for years. Wherever your team works, attackers follow. A small request in chat is usually the first step toward a larger goal, such as device access, stolen money, or leverage for extortion.

Business needs keep the door open. Teams have to stay open to customers, vendors and partners, so blocking outsiders is neither practical nor enough. Attackers blend into that traffic, so judging the words alone is not reliable. Ask who is sending, from where, and why.

Teams have safeguards, but they depend on the user. Teams shows an external label and an Accept/Block prompt at first contact, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 adds Safe Links and zero-hour auto purge where it is licensed. Attackers succeed when a user clicks through those warnings. Email has sender authentication, link analysis, and gateways. Conversations inside Teams sit outside the reach of third-party email gateways, and Teams chat gives fewer sender checks: display names are easy to choose, links can be disguised, and previews can mislead.

Defense has to cover the conversation and the click. Use both Microsoft's own settings and third-party protection as your technical controls. Train your users on this threat vector, so people know what a lure in Teams looks like and how to report it. Be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message.

Why Are Attackers Moving Into Microsoft Teams?

Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email carried for years, and the following factors make Teams an attractive place for them.

Outside contact is normal. Your teams have to talk to customers, vendors, and partners, so external messages and guests are expected. A harmful message blends in with the many legitimate ones.

Impersonation is easy. Email has checks that block direct domain spoofing. Chat gives fewer sender-checking signals, and a sender can often choose the name users see.

Awareness is lower. Phishing awareness training has traditionally focused on email, so users may look harder at an unexpected email than at a chat message.

Email security doesn’t automatically cover Teams. Many security vendors now extend protection to collaboration tools. An organization that has not extended its controls to Teams leaves that channel uncovered.

One target list covers two channels. An attacker who already has a list of email addresses can reach the same people in Teams, where external access allows it, with little added effort. That gives them two channels to attack instead of one.

How Does an Attack in Teams Unfold?

Most attacks in a collaboration tool follow the same path, whatever the lure.

1. The attacker poses as a trusted contact. Display names are easy to choose, so the sender can appear as IT support, a vendor, or a colleague. A request from an individual account may show only the name the sender chose and an “External” label.

2. The attacker sends a lure. Default or permissive external-access settings let the message in, such as open external access, personal accounts that can start chats, or trial-only tenants that an admin has chosen to allow. The app, the notification and the chat context all look familiar, and the attacker can build the conversation slowly, so the request feels like a natural next step.

3. The user acts on the request. One step is enough: a click, a session started or a reply, because the request looks like routine work. Attackers may also call the user in Teams to talk them through the steps.

4. The user lands on a fake page or receives a payload. The user leaves Teams for the attacker’s web page, or a payload is delivered. A link can display one address and open another, and senders can edit a message after sending it, so what the user sees later may differ from the original.

5. The user hands over credentials, grants access, or pays. The fake page, tool, or payment request asks for one more action, and the user completes it.

6. The attacker gains access. The attacker now holds credentials, system access or the requested payment.

The attacker can then send the next lure through the compromised account, and the cycle repeats.

What Do Attackers Send in Teams, and What Do They Want?

The message types below are cases we observed. For each one, we describe what the attacker likely wants and where the activity can lead. The messages look different, but they serve a similar set of goals.

The “IT Support” Message

Why it works: Help desk requests feel routine, and people want their problem fixed. The user opens the session themselves, so the attacker gets access with the user’s approval.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is full control of the endpoint. Standard defenses often miss this because remote administration tools are legitimate software. With that access, an attacker can take saved passwords, active session cookies, and sensitive documents. This allows them to reach corporate email, Teams, and wider enterprise systems. It also gives them a foothold for lateral movement across internal networks and for deploying further remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools or ransomware.

2. The Urgent Invoice

Why it works: Payment requests with a deadline push people to act before they check, and a personal greeting makes the request feel real.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is money, stolen credentials, malware deployment, or all three. Depending on what the target does, that can mean payments sent to an attacker-controlled account, malware that steals credentials or sets up remote access, and the compromised account being used to send similar requests to colleagues or vendors.

3. The Ransom Note in Chat

Why it works: The message reaches the user directly, with no email gateway in its path.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is payment or an immediate response. The first message alone rarely shows whether the claim is real: it could follow a genuine compromise, or it could be a bluff meant to exploit fear and force a quick reply. Responding under pressure risks paying a ransom for nothing, overlooking an active breach if the claim is true, or causing internal panic when nothing was compromised.

What Should Defenders Do?

Protect messages and meetings, and be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message. Start with your people, then your Teams settings.

How can users stop these messages?

1. Treat chat like email. Teach users to question links and requests in Teams, including in meeting chats.

2. Teach the “External” label. Ask users to check it before acting on a message that claims to come from support or leadership. For individual Microsoft accounts it can be one of the few cues available.

3. Preview before accepting. Teach users to read an external message request first and to decline it if it is unexpected, even when curiosity says otherwise.

4. Check the real link. Ask users to hover over a link and read the address before clicking, because the text shown can differ from the destination.

5. Never start a remote session someone sends you. Route support requests through the help desk.

6. Verify payment changes through a second channel. Confirm new payment details by phone with a known contact before paying.

7. Treat a ransom message as an incident. Report it to your security team and do not reply.

8. Stop sharing passwords in chat. Use a password manager or a one-time secret tool.

What if a user already acted?

Plan for the click. Reset the user’s password, revoke their active sessions, check for remote-access tools they installed, and review any payment they made.

How do you narrow the door in Teams?

Attackers can only message your users if your Teams settings allow it. You control those settings, and they are worth a review. Microsoft documents each one in its Teams external access guidance . Your business needs some outside contact, so the goal is not to block everyone. The goal is to allow the contact you need and nothing more. Start by reviewing which external tenants can message your users and who can join your meeting chats.

Settings to review

-AllowFederatedUsers: turns external communication with other organizations on or off.

-AllowedDomains and -BlockedDomains: limit access to trusted partners or block malicious domains.

-AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowTeamsConsumerInbound: manage chat with unmanaged accounts and block uninvited outreach.

-AllowPublicUsers: controls chat with Skype users.

1. Allow only essential partner domains. Prefer allow-lists to block-lists, because block-lists only stop known threats. Blocking a main domain still leaves its subdomains open. To block all subdomains, run:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -BlockAllSubdomains $True

2. Block trial-only tenants. Unlicensed trial tenants are easy tools for attackers. Microsoft blocks them by default, but verify that your setting is still “Blocked”:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked"

When the setting is “Blocked,” users from trial-only tenants cannot search for, chat with, call or meet with your team, and they are removed from existing chats. Setting it to “Allowed” turns these safeguards off.

3. Restrict personal accounts. Personal Microsoft accounts are harder to verify: the sender chooses the display name, and no organization vouches for the account. Disable: AllowTeamsConsumerInbound to stop inbound chats from them, and evaluate AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowPublicUsers against your needs.

4. Block malicious senders. You can block a harmful sender individually without changing global policy:

In the Teams admin center, go to Users > External access.

Turn on “Block specific users from communicating with people in my organization.”

Select “Block a user”, enter the person’s email address or messaging resource identifier (MRI), and select Apply.

The list holds a maximum of 200 users. You can also manage it with Set-CsTeamsExternalAccessConfiguration.

Where Can KnowBe4 Help?

Attackers move between channels, and a single campaign can use several. Reputation checks and sender history say little about a message from someone who has joined a meeting you are in. Protection has to read the message and respond when a user acts on it.

KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security brings together KnowBe4 Defend (inbound email and messaging security, including Microsoft Teams), KnowBe4 Prevent (outbound email security) and PhishER Plus (incident response). Its behavioral AI protects the conversation and coaches your workforce wherever work happens.

Multi-engine detection. KnowBe4 analyzes message text, sender relationships, links, and attachments at the same time, plus email headers when the message is an email. It checks what the message asks the user to do and how the sender relates to the recipient. A domain reputation check sees neither.

Coaching at the point of risk. Contextual coaching, real-time nudges, and localized banners and tags in 13 languages show users why a message looks suspicious at the moment it appears. According to KnowBe4 internal data, 97% of users stop before proceeding with a high-risk action when a teachable moment appears.

Threat intelligence. KnowBe4 Threat Labs turns real-world attack telemetry and more than 15 years of data into live detection models across the Email & Collaboration Security suite, so defenses update as new patterns appear.

Protect the Places Your Team Works

Your people spend their day in email, chat and meetings. Your security should cover all these.

See how KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security helps protect your digital workforce.

articles.title: iOS Sandbox Escape Is Public, and Apple Hasn’t Confirmed a Fix
articles.context: No attacks are reported and no fix is confirmed
articles.full_text:
A public iOS sandbox escape could expose wallet keys, Binance warns. No attacks are reported and no fix is confirmed.

On 10 November, Binance warned users about a public iOS sandbox escape that lets one app read the files of other apps. Seed phrases, private keys and login credentials could be exposed to a malicious app, the exchange said.

“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.” reads the warning.

Binance advises users to remove apps installed from untrusted sources, update iOS and all apps to the latest official versions, and, if a breach is suspected, move funds to a new wallet on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

— Binance (@binance) November 10, 2026

A researcher known as ‘forcequitOS’ published the PoC exploit code, called worse_query, on GitHub. Apple released security updates for both iOS versions the following day, but its release notes mysteriously don’t report a fix for the issue. The good news is that neither Binance nor the researcher has reported any attacks or data theft.

“worse_query is the direct successor to bad_query and essentially replaces it. To use worse_query, you’ll have to set up an App Group container for your app.” forcequitOS wrote.

The proof-of-concept can access the data folders used by all apps and, on iOS 27, some system folders as well. To work, an app must create an App Group container. The researcher says the code is intended for developers and “isn’t useful by itself.” However, other developers have already used it to build apps that can be installed on iPhones.

One example is WQ Files, a file manager developed by Christoph Kolbicz, TheHackerNews reports.

“WQ Files is a file browser, app data manager and cache cleaner for iOS 26 and 27. “WQ” stands for worse_query, the sandbox technique it is built on. It reaches other apps’ and system containers with no jailbreak and no kernel exploit. Tested on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2.” reads the description.

It can access data belonging to other apps without requiring a jailbreak or a kernel exploit. It can also edit, delete and clear that data. Users can install it through sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the required App Group when users sign in with their Apple ID.

I agree (and I wasn't planning on it), but I don't mind the loss of any potential bounty tbh, when Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here.

— forcequit (@forcequitOS) November 8, 2026

The forcequitOS says they have no intention of seeking a bug bounty from Apple and are willing to give up any potential reward because of Apple’s delayed response and the inappropriate behavior of people publicly misusing or exaggerating the exploit.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Apple)

articles.title: Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Customer Datasets, Model Weights and Notion AI Chats
articles.context: "Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were...
articles.full_text:
Fireworks AI disclosed on Monday that its investigation into a security incident first reported early last month uncovered further malicious activity, affecting account and billing information, alongside secrets, datasets, and incomplete models for a "limited set of accounts."

In a notice published on October 10, 2026, the company said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT.

At that time, the AI infrastructure provider said it only found evidence that environment variables, including API keys and tokens stored as secrets, were captured in certain affected accounts, adding that there were no signs that customer models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information were accessed.

In response to the incident, Fireworks AI took the step of revoking the compromised internal credentials and rotating service account tokens, along with affected Fireworks API keys and keys created by the threat actor.

The latest bulletin from the company reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously thought. The company said attackers reached its development environment via an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development (R&D) machines on October 23, 2026.

"On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," it added. "As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use."

The breach is said to have provided access to the following types of information -

Resource metadata: Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, and creation time

Billing information: billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage

Model weights and datasets: a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets for certain customers

Fireworks AI said payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not impacted by the security incident. It also said it's alerting customers whose data was impacted.

The company also noted that it has implemented security hardening procedures, such as credential revocation and rotation; isolating affected systems to prevent further unauthorized activity and lateral movement; tightening access controls; and improving its logging and monitoring systems.

"The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to large language models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways," it said.

The activity is assessed to be part of an emerging threat known as LLMjacking, which refers to the act of hijacking a victim's LLM through stolen credentials to fuel a criminal enterprise that thrives on peddling the access to other threat actors, while leaving the legitimate owner to pay the bill.

Last week, Google issued a warning that threat actors are increasingly targeting AI infrastructure for LLMjacking in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors.

Notion Impacted by Fireworks AI Incident

Popular productivity and note-taking application Notion has disclosed that the security incident targeting Fireworks AI impacted "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces." In a post shared on Reddit, one user said: "looks like all of us are part of that <1%."

While the initial assessment was that the breach allowed the threat actor to access Notion AI synthetic testing data, it has since come to light that it may also have involved potential customer data.

"Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results."

Notion has also emphasized that no other features across its platform were affected by the incident. The Insights feature has since been disabled as it continues to investigate the breach and the company is no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.

Affected customers are advised to review the impacted data securely inside their workspace. If those with affected workspaces have pasted sensitive information, passwords, API keys, or other credentials during the attack window, it's recommended to rotate them with immediate effect.

articles.title: Researcher bypassed Meta smart glasses’ safeguards to run her own code
articles.context: Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses
articles.full_text:
We’ve written before about what Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses can see and hear, and who might get to use that information. Those worries focus on how the glasses handle information during normal use. A security researcher has now shown how to bypass a safeguard meant to stop unauthorized software running on them.

Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. For the technical details I’ll gladly refer you to her own post about it.

The glasses are controlled by the Meta AI app on the owner’s phone. Developers can add their own apps to the glasses through a developer tool, and the phone sends that software to the glasses to install.

The glasses were supposed to check that the software really came from Meta. In older firmware (up to and including version 126), they didn’t check, so the researcher could swap in an app of her own.

Meta introduced a check in firmware version 127 to verify the app’s digital signature to prove that it came from Meta . The researcher found the on/off switch for that signature check came from a settings file passed along by the phone. The glasses only checked the file was correctly formed, not whether it had been tampered with. Changing a single byte in the file turned the signature check off.

Once her app was running, she could send commands to the glasses from the paired phone over a wireless connection.

The glasses have a camera, microphones and a wireless connection, and they sit on your face all day. A wearable that can be made to run unapproved code goes beyond a privacy-policy question. It becomes a security question about who controls the device. As we’ve seen, some cheaper smart glasses already are a security disaster.

In this case the person running the code would be the person that controls the phone. If malicious software running on the glasses could access the camera or stored recordings, it could potentially send footage to an attacker’s server. Pamoutaf’s research doesn’t demonstrate that scenario, but it raises questions about what that software might be able to access.

In her post she promised a follow-up exploring other potential ways to attack the glasses.

How to stay safe

Keep the glasses’ firmware and the Meta AI app updated, and avoid unofficial apps or modifications.

If smart glasses are just another gadget to you, I’d leave them on the shelf. If you rely on them as an accessibility aid, you deserve technology that helps you without putting your privacy or other people’s at risk.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

Malwarebytes Mobile Security protects you from phishing, scam texts, malicious sites, and more. With real-time AI-powered Scam Guard built right in.

articles.title: Ransomware recovery is now a client retention metric
articles.context: Track three numbers to see how you’re doing: Time to first client update: How long after detection does the client hear from you
articles.full_text:
The ransomware attack is over. Your team has restored the client’s data, brought systems back online and put business operations back on track. From a technical standpoint, the recovery was a success.

But the client still has questions. Why did updates go quiet for two days? What drove the recovery costs up? And where did the 31 hours of emergency labor on the invoice come from?

Recovering from ransomware is only part of the job. Clients also need to know what happened, what recovery involved and what it cost them. When communication falls short or unexpected charges appear, even a technically successful recovery can leave clients questioning the value of their MSP relationship.

The disruption may be behind them, but their doubts can carry into the next renewal conversation.

The trend: Slow, fragmented recovery erodes trust and renewals

Ransomware recovery can take days, even when teams have backups and a response plan in place. According to industry reports, only 16% of affected organizations fully recovered within a day. Over half (55%) recovered within a week. For businesses that depend on their systems to serve customers and generate revenue, every additional day of disruption carries a cost.

The stakes extend to the MSP, too. Kaseya’s 2026 Cybersecurity Outlook report found that 12% of MSPs lost clients following security incidents, with ransomware, account takeover and business email compromise among the main reasons.

When recovery involves delays, fragmented efforts or gaps in communication, clients struggle to understand what is happening and when they can expect normal operations to resume. They may also question unexpected costs or wonder whether their provider has the situation under control.

Clients expect cyberattacks to happen, but they also expect their MSP to respond quickly, coordinate recovery and keep them informed. When those expectations go unmet, a technically successful recovery may still leave clients questioning whether they should renew their contracts.

A successful recovery depends on both the technical response and the client experience. MSPs that set expectations early, communicate consistently and explain costs before they become surprises have a stronger chance of preserving client trust long after the systems come back online.

Resolve Incidents Faster and Keep the Clients You Recover For

Slow, disconnected recovery puts renewals at risk, even when the restore itself goes well.

Download the AI Playbook to see how MSPs use AI to cut resolution times and keep clients confident when it matters most.

Download the Playbook

Where your recovery process breaks down

Most MSPs have skilled people. The trouble starts when those people work across disconnected tools in the middle of a crisis.

Tool sprawl slows everyone down

Backup, monitoring, ticketing and billing live in separate consoles. Your techs spend incident hours piecing together context instead of restoring systems.

Handoffs break

An alert fires in one tool, a ticket opens in another and a restore job runs in a third. Nothing links them, so no one can say what the attack touched or what’s still down.

Billing falls through the cracks

Emergency labor, restore time and after-hours work often go untracked. Someone reconstructs those hours from memory days later. You either lose margin or send an invoice the client doesn’t recognize, and you do it at the worst possible time.

Client updates depend on who’s free

Without a single ticket trail, communication comes down to whoever has a spare minute. Some clients get a call every few hours. Others hear nothing until the work is done.

Each of these problems looks small by itself. Together, they turn a recoverable incident into a trust problem.

5 signs your recovery process is costing you client trust

Clients chase you for updates. They have to ask what’s happening instead of hearing from your team.

Your team scrambles across tools. Technicians waste valuable recovery time piecing together information from disconnected systems.

No one owns the full picture. Handoffs leave gaps in who knows what’s restored, what’s still down and what needs attention.

Recovery bills come as a surprise. Emergency labor and after-hours work appear on invoices without clear explanations.

Recovery ends without clear answers. Clients are left unsure what happened, what it cost or what you’ll do to prevent a repeat.

What good recovery looks like for an MSP

Strong recovery runs on one timeline and one source of truth. Everyone on your team sees the same facts, so your client hears the same story no matter who calls. Updates go out on a schedule you set, before the client asks.

When the incident closes, the invoice matches the work, because your team logged the work as it happened.

Track three numbers to see how you’re doing:

Time to first client update: How long after detection does the client hear from you?

Time to restore: How long until their critical systems run again?

Time to invoice: How fast can you send an accurate bill after closing the incident?

If any of these takes too long, you have a process gap that clients will notice. Closing those gaps takes more than working harder during an incident. It takes tools that share data from the start.

The fix: Unifying RMM, PSA and BCDR with Kaseya Trifecta

The 2026 Kaseya Cybersecurity Report found that two factors supported faster incident recovery: well-trained internal IT or security teams (35%) and integrated security and IT management tools (18%).

Kaseya Trifecta puts RMM, PSA and BCDR in one connected platform. The idea is simple. When your monitoring, ticketing and recovery tools share a workflow, your team stops stitching context together and starts fixing the problem.

Here’s how it maps to the breakdowns above:

Fragmented context: RMM, PSA and BCDR run on one workflow and one data set, so your techs see the full picture in one place.

Slow handoffs: Recovery events tie directly to tickets and endpoints. You know what’s affected and what’s restored without chasing updates.

Billing blind spots: Time and labor land in the ticket as the work happens, then flow to billing. Your invoice reflects what your team did.

Inconsistent updates: One auditable incident record gives every team member the same facts. Your client gets consistent communication, whoever is on shift.

This matches what the report found. Teams that recover quickly pair skilled people with tools that connect. Trifecta gives your people that connection.

Keep the client, not just the data

Surviving the attack is the baseline. Your clients expect it. What they remember is whether recovery felt organized, transparent and fair.

Faster resolution gives you the foundation for all of that. It shortens downtime, makes your updates credible and keeps your invoices accurate. Those benefits help protect renewals long after the incident closes.

articles.title: WhiteMatter Raises $20 Million in Series A Funding
articles.context: Cybersecurity startup WhiteMatter on Tuesday announced raising $20 million in a Series A funding round that brings the total raised by the company to $24 million
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity startup WhiteMatter on Tuesday announced raising $20 million in a Series A funding round that brings the total raised by the company to $24 million.

The investment round was led by Blumberg Capital, with additional support from previous investors Crew Capital and Sprout & Oak.

Founded in 2024 and previously known as QuilrAI, WhiteMatter has built a platform that helps organizations secure and govern every AI agent running in their environments.

According to WhiteMatter, enterprises can run every AI agent through its platform and gain visibility into where agents are built and used: across endpoints, cloud, SaaS, and code.

The solution deploys and governs every agent, model, and MCP server, observes and secures each action, and optimizes traffic through a single gateway.

WhiteMatter can deploy a dedicated guardian agent for every agent running in the environment, scaling if agents multiply autonomously, to ensure continuous policy-driven control.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The cybersecurity startup will use the new investment to accelerate research and development and expand its go-to-market organization. It will also build its executive team.

“Despite all the discussion about pausing AI development, enterprises are doing the opposite. AI technology is too powerful, the opportunity is too significant, and the competitive pressure is too real to put it back in the box,” said WhiteMatter founder and CEO Vidit Arora.

“Companies that slow down AI adoption risk being overtaken by competitors that move fast, stay secure, and scale AI with confidence, which is exactly why we built WhiteMatter,” Arora added.

WhiteMatter has headquarters in San Francisco and Austin.

articles.title: SAP Patches Critical ICM2SHELL, ProxyGate Vulnerabilities
articles.context: Enterprise software maker SAP on Tuesday announced the release of 42 new and updated security notes, including nine that resolve critical-severity vulnerabilities
articles.full_text:
Enterprise software maker SAP on Tuesday announced the release of 42 new and updated security notes, including nine that resolve critical-severity vulnerabilities.

Four of SAP’s new security notes address maximum-severity flaws in NetWeaver (Internet Communication Manager (ICM) and SAML2 Service Provider), Web Dispatcher, and Gateway.

The ICM and Web Dispatcher flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126, are a single weakness in the SAP kernel component that receives HTTP, HTTPS, and WebSocket traffic.

According to Onapsis, which calls the security defect ICM2SHELL, the issue is related to reassembling large WebSocket messages, which may be split into fragments during a server-browser exchange and then put together by the receiver.

“A specially crafted sequence of WebSocket messages makes the ICM or the WD write attacker-controlled data past the end of the memory it reserved for the connection. Depending on how that data is shaped, the result is either an immediate crash of the process or controlled corruption of its memory,” Onapsis explains.

ICM2SHELL, the enterprise application security firm says, could allow an attacker to execute operating system commands with <sid>adm privileges.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“This is not a theoretical outcome. The Onapsis Research Labs provided SAP a working exploit that achieves full, unauthenticated remote code execution end to end, running arbitrary commands as <sid>adm on the target system. The denial-of-service condition, in turn, reproduced on every SAP Kernel release tested,” Onapsis says.

The max-severity SAP Gateway flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-89103 and referred to as ProxyGate, could be exploited by unauthenticated attackers to achieve remote code execution (RCE) without user interaction.

It is related to the prxyinfo access-control list, which should restrict requests to trusted networks only. However, if left open, it allows an attacker to send a series of requests that appear to be originating from an internal network, tricking the gateway into accepting them.

This allows an attacker to execute OS commands with the <sid>adm privileges and gain full control over the SAP system, without providing a username, password, or certificate.

“Because the flaw is in the SAP kernel, it affects a broad range of releases, including kernel versions that are already out of maintenance. Further, the gateway runs not only on ABAP but also on AS Java, dual-stack, and standalone-gateway systems,” Onapsis explains.

SAP also resolved a max-severity missing authentication bug in NetWeaver (CVE-2026-120017) that, in certain configurations, could allow unauthenticated attackers to submit specially crafted data and impersonate arbitrary users, which could lead to full system compromise.

The remaining five critical notes in SAP’s November 2026 bulletin address vulnerabilities in NetWeaver (CVE-2026-109803 and CVE-2026-76965), S4CRM (CVE-2026-109795), Web Dispatcher (CVE-2026-89119), and BusinessObjects (CVE-2026-109798).

Additionally, SAP published 17 high-severity fixes, including for multiple memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS), and information disclosure bugs.

Since the scheduled October 2026 security patches, SAP released new notes dealing with the recently disclosed PHP2Shell and Node2Shell vulnerabilities in its Business AI Platform and updated several other notes and advisories. This brings the total to 43 new and updated notes released this month, Onapsis notes in its analysis of the patches.

articles.title: AI reverse engineering let researchers add a new feature to Slack
articles.context: The rebuilt Slack ran well enough that the team added a new feature to it: AI text autocomplete, powered by a small local model
articles.full_text:
Intezer researchers used AI agents to rebuild source code for Slack, Apple’s Finder and a TinyTurla-NG sample, from a backdoor family Cisco Talos attributes to the Turla group. They worked from the shipped programs and vendor documentation. The rebuilt Slack ran well enough that the team added a new feature to it: AI text autocomplete, powered by a small local model.

Software vendors that count on compiling their programs to keep source code private are the ones exposed. “Our research shows that an AI agent can reconstruct a working copy of an application when given the original software’s binary or package,” wrote the Intezer researchers behind the work. The same method that opens up a commercial app also opens up malware.

The backdoor rebuild has the numbers

Intezer set five tests for success. The code had to be readable enough to maintain, clean and idiomatic enough to compare with human-written source, compiled only from what the agents wrote, free of bundled third-party libraries, and identical in behavior to the original. Intezer rated TinyTurla the hardest of the three targets.

Codex, running GPT-5.6-sol-high, drove the workflow and made the engineering decisions, while Kimi K3 filled three separate roles in the setup. The agents produced about 3,100 lines of source in two files.

The rebuilt DLL is 296,960 bytes against the original’s 291,840, with 1,072 functions against 1,041 and identical imported symbols. BinDiff, a tool that compares how two binaries are put together, matched 1,034 of the original functions and scored the pair at 92.8% similarity with 98.7% confidence. Put plainly, the copy is built almost the same way as the original. “That is a statement about shape,” the researchers explained.

Intezer checked behavior separately. Its harness, the automated setup that runs the agents and tools, compared each rebuilt function with its original using Binary Ninja’s high-level intermediate language, a readable translation of machine code.

Slack and Finder still have gaps

Claude dug through Slack’s minified client code to identify the third-party libraries inside it. The client contains more than 500,000 functions, most of them from those libraries. Slack’s server is not downloadable, so the agents built a Slack-compatible one on SQLite, guided by network inspection of the real Slack app and Slack’s documentation.

Finder, a 25.8 MB executable, still has gaps around online-only files, sync status and actions that depend on other macOS services. Intezer did not publish how long the rebuilds took or what they cost.

Obfuscation is the suggested defense

Intezer’s advice is to use encryptors and obfuscators, tools that scramble code so it is harder to read. The researchers say these “raise the bar” for AI agents. “The software industry will have to adjust,” they wrote.

articles.title: Introducing JFrog Threat Hub: Turning Vulnerability Intelligence into Blast Radius Analysis
articles.context: A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment
articles.full_text:
A new supply chain attack hits the news. A CVE with a dramatic name starts trending. A malicious package turns up in npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face. Within minutes, your Slack channels fill up, your CISO wants an update, and someone asks the question every DevSecOps professional dreads:

“How are we affected?”

Providing a definitive answer should be simple. In practice it often takes hours, and sometimes even days to get the complete picture.

The pain: awareness is easy, blast radius is hard

Security teams are not short on information. Advisories, research blogs, vendor bulletins, social media threads, and mailing lists all announce new threats faster than anyone can read them. The challenging part is leveraging that information to understand how it affects your particular environment.

Until now, that process usually looked something like this:

Separating the signal from the noise. Relevant intelligence is scattered across dozens of sources. Some of it is vetted, some of it is speculation, and some of it is a repost of a repost. Someone has to read it, judge its credibility, and decide whether it deserves attention.

Translating general threats into actionable responses. A blog post describes an attack. It doesn’t hand you a clean list of the affected packages and versions. Someone has to extract the package names, version ranges, and CVE identifiers, and hope nothing was missed.

Figuring out where affected components are hiding. Today, software applications are assembled from many open-source components. Unfortunately, the vulnerability that was just discovered is rarely a direct dependency. It’s usually buried several layers deep in a transitive dependency which is part of a Docker image, or sitting in a build from last quarter. Your artifacts are spread across multiple repositories, projects, teams, and pipelines, making it difficult to identify all the affected components across the entire software supply chain.

Stitching together a holistic view from disparate tools. One tool tracks vulnerabilities, another tracks builds, and a spreadsheet maps services to owners. Correlating these sources manually is a slow and error-prone process, especially in the middle of a high profile security incident where nobody has the time to do it.

Prioritizing remediation with imperfect data. Published severity scores don’t always match real-world exploitability. A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment. Without context analysis, teams either over-react or under-react because they lack the proper information.

All of the above happens while the clock is ticking. The window between disclosure and exploitation keeps shrinking, and every hour spent hunting for an answer is another hour attackers can use to exploit weaknesses in your application. The real cost is often not the vulnerability itself but the time it takes to figure out the most effective strategy for defending against it.

Meet JFrog Threat Hub: taking you from “what happened?” to “what’s affected?” in a single unified interface

JFrog Threat Hub is designed to close the gap. It brings both publicly published security research and JFrog’s own threat intelligence directly into the JFrog Platform, to help determine how it affects your development environment.

What is JFrog Threat Hub?

JFrog Threat Hub is a detailed threat intelligence dashboard accessed from within JFrog Xray. It includes a daily-updated feed of vetted posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages. Most of the security intelligence is based on reports from the JFrog Security Research team, which monitors public registries such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face, runs automated scanners on every new and updated package, and analyzes CVEs for real-world exploitability. Relevant external advisories are also included in the feed.

Each post includes the name of the source, publish date, CVSS score, and descriptive tags, along with a public label that groups the affected packages and versions. A severity mismatch indicator flags cases where JFrog’s research rates a threat differently from its published score, so teams can prioritize by actual, rather than perceived, risk.

One of the most important features is the Check Impact button. With one click, it runs an impact search across your organization and lists every affected artifact, along with its repository, vulnerable component version, scan date, and runtime status. Teams can export these results, set Xray policies, or move straight into triage and remediation all within a single unified platform.

Threat Hub includes updated CVE advisories and impact search across the entire supply chain

Instead of reading about an attack in one place and searching for exposure in another, Threat Hub brings both steps into one seamless workflow. It not only provides early awareness, but also helps map out the true blast radius, taking you directly from reading about a threat to understanding your exact exposure.

Curated intelligence, delivered where you already work

Threat Hub consolidates security posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages, updates it daily, and then sorts it according to customer preference. In addition, intelligence from the JFrog Security Research Team is integrated as well, including:

Continuous monitoring of open-source repositories such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face for the latest security issues

Running automated scanners across new and updated packages

Deeply investigating suspicious findings

Analyzing new and existing CVEs for real-world exploitability

Disclosing newly discovered malware to repository maintainers

For our customers, this means original, vetted research sits alongside the external advisories that matter, without the noise of an open-ended news feed. Each post shows its source, publish date, and tags such as which ecosystems are affected. When a post is tied to a known attack, it applies a label that puts together groups of affected packages and versions, and may link to a fix or advisory.

Just one click to gauge CVE impact

When working from the JFrog Xray interface, the Threat Hub dashboard can be accessed by selecting Xray > Overview. One of the most powerful features of the Threat Hub console is the “Check Impact” button. Click it, and Threat Hub opens an Impact Search specifically for your organization. If you are affected, it shows the matching artifacts and their scan dates, so you can see where the problem lives across your scanned artifacts and decide what to fix first.

For supported CVE and malicious package posts, there’s no manual extraction of package names, no custom queries, and no stitching together results from separate tools. The research and the results are presented side by side.

CVE Severity you can act on

Published scores don’t always tell the whole story, so some posts also show a Severity Mismatch Indicator when JFrog Security Research’s assessment differs from the severity of a publicly available CVE or advisory. JFrog’s research severity reflects real-world exploitability and impact, not just the published score, which gives you the context you need when prioritizing your remediation strategy.

What this changes for your team

Operations and Security teams gain these important advantages:

Faster incident scoping. The question “How are we affected?” can get an answer faster, with less cross-tool detective work.

Less context switching. Reading the research, understanding the impact, and identifying affected artifacts all happen in one centralized interface.

Improved prioritization. Vetted research and severity context from JFrog’s own researchers helps focus on the threats that are more likely to be exploitable.

More precise communications. When leadership asks for a status update, you can present them with the specific affected artifacts and scan dates instead of “we’re still looking.”

See JFrog Threat Hub in action

The next major supply chain attack is a question of when, not if. When it arrives, the teams that respond best won’t be the ones who read the most blog posts. They’ll be the ones who can understand how a specific threat affects their particular environment in the fastest way possible.

articles.title: Dreeze raises $33 million to automate recovery of entire cloud applications
articles.context: “With cyber threats increasing and AI introducing new risks, enterprises need to assume that critical applications will go down
articles.full_text:
Dreeze emerged from stealth with $33 million in seed funding and announced the general availability of its Application Revival platform for Amazon Web Services (AWS). Norwest and Bessemer Venture Partners led the round, with participation from Claltech. The platform helps enterprises recover complete cloud applications by restoring data, infrastructure, and dependencies in the order they need to come back online.

A successful backup can still leave a business offline. Cloud applications rely on infrastructure, configurations, identities, secrets, keys, and connections that must be restored alongside the data. When those pieces are missing, IT teams have to track down credentials, consult old runbooks, and rebuild dependencies by hand. Dreeze calls this the “recovery scramble.” It can leave an application offline for days or even weeks after its data has been restored.

“Our customers have moved production workloads into the public cloud, and most of them can back up that data without much trouble. Recovery is what worries them: getting a whole application running again, with every dependency in the right order,” said Jeremy Miller, CEO of Coravant. “Dreeze was built around that problem, which is why we wanted to work with them from the start.”

Application Revival gives teams a way to test recovery before an outage. The platform maps each application’s dependencies as its environment changes, backs up the resources it needs, and automatically generates a recovery plan. Teams can run that plan end to end to verify that it brings the application back online.

“Companies have spent years getting better at backing up data, but getting the data back doesn’t mean the business is back,” said Ziv Kedem, CEO of Dreeze. “With cyber threats increasing and AI introducing new risks, enterprises need to assume that critical applications will go down. We started Dreeze because recovery needs to go further. Our goal is to make Application Revival the new standard, so companies know they have a proven path to bring their applications back when something goes wrong.”

Introducing Application Revival

Know – Autonomous Dependency Mapping: Maps cloud resources and dependencies to the applications they support and generates a recovery plan based on the live environment as it changes.

Protect – Vaulted Backup: Backs up the data, configurations, keys, and other resources an application needs to run. Backups are stored in an immutable, air-gapped vault, with optional replication across regions.

Orchestrate – Revival Automation: Runs the recovery plan, restoring data, infrastructure, configurations, identities, and connections in dependency order.

Validate – Revival Confidence: Runs an automated, end-to-end recovery test that brings up a working application without affecting production or requiring manual cleanup.

“At Kashya, Zerto and now at Dreeze, Ziv, Oded and Avi have spent decades together building recovery technology that enterprises rely on. They know first-hand how the market needs to evolve,” said Dror Nahumi, general partner at Norwest. “As cloud environments grow more complex and the cost of downtime rises, enterprises need a better way to prepare for failure. Few teams understand the recovery problem as deeply as this one.”

Dreeze for Microsoft Azure is in early access, with general availability planned for early 2027.

articles.title: Cloud Vulnerabilities Surge Fourfold in Less Than a Year
articles.context: ” Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds
articles.full_text:
The median number of high or critical vulnerabilities in cloud workloads increased fourfold between May and November this year, due to the impact of frontier AI, Datadog has claimed.

The cloud observability and security specialist revealed the findings in its State of Cloud Security 2026 published on November 10. It’s based on analysis of the cloud security posture of thousands of customer organizations around the world.

Datadog claimed that the median number of high/critical severity flaws in cloud workloads surged from four in May, when Anthropic’s Mythos model was released, to 14 in June and 16 in November.

The data was sourced from analysis of vulnerabilities in third-party libraries used by applications monitored through Datadog Code Security’s Software Composition Analysis (SCA) feature, the report noted.

“This data reveals that the increased number of vulnerabilities in the CVE database isn't a theoretical risk,” it added. “It affects an increasing number of real-world applications running in cloud environments, reinforcing the need for cloud security foundations that limit the blast radius of compromised applications.”

Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds.

The report also highlighted the challenge of long-lived credentials; specifically related to cloud-hosted AI inference services and CI/CD pipelines.

Datadog warned that such credentials are consistently ranked as one of the most common causes of cloud breaches, with automated tools continuously scanning the web for weaknesses.

“Red-team frameworks like Pacu and Datadog’s own Pathrunner along with secret scanners like TruffleHog reliably find over-permissioned credentials and exposed keys at scale,” it said. “That same tooling is available to autonomous attackers, who enumerate for long-lived credentials first because they’re the highest-value, longest-lived prize in the environment.”

The report revealed that nearly half of organizations using Gemini use long-lived Gemini API keys, while the percentage of cloud users with access keys older than three years has reached nearly 30% for AWS IAM and Google Cloud Service Account users.

“Rather than static Bedrock or Gemini API keys, you should access AI inference services through the calling workload’s short-lived identity when supported (IAM role, managed identity, or service account) so the model is reached with the same federated credentials as other cloud resources and not a separate long-lived key,” Datadog explained.

Cloud Dependencies Expose Users to Machine-Speed Attacks

Supply-chain attacks are increasingly run autonomously and at machine speed, with hijacked dependencies one of the most popular routes to compromise, Datadog claimed.

Part of the challenge is the speed with which new dependency versions are adopted by users. If adopted automatically without proper vetting, they can result in the rapid compromise of cloud credentials and services.

Some 60% of organizations Datadog analyzed run versions that were released less than 24 hours earlier, with these versions appearing in more than a fifth (21%) of cloud applications.

The risk is amplified the more dependencies there are, and Datadog found that app workloads running in the cloud have on average 149 software dependencies. The figure across the average organization is 568.

“Organizations should implement dependency cooldowns to lower the risk of malicious dependencies reaching their cloud environments, because the community usually identifies and contains hijacked libraries within a few hours,” the report recommended.

articles.title: Chrome zero-day whack-a-mole continues as 2026 tally hits 8
articles.context: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar
articles.full_text: Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar. The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks. The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited. Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit. The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine. The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited. The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight. That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess. Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

articles.title: Over a Dozen Organizations Hit in Qubole Supply Chain Attack
articles.context: A threat actor used the compromised IAM credentials for an AWS account associated with big-data platform Qubole to steal data from over a dozen organizations, cybersecurity...
articles.full_text:
A threat actor used the compromised IAM credentials for an AWS account associated with big-data platform Qubole to steal data from over a dozen organizations, cybersecurity researchers discovered.

The credentials allowed the attackers to assume IAM roles organizations had set up for Qubole’s AWS account and access their AWS environments.

Cross-account IAM roles are normal for SaaS platforms that operate within customers’ AWS environments. During onboarding, customers create a role for Qubole, and the vendor’s AWS account can assume the role when needed, typically via an External ID.

The leaked Qubole credentials allowed the threat actor to assume this role and pull data from the AWS environments of over a dozen companies.

“The doors the attacker used were old ones. Qubole roles were still in place long after companies had stopped using Qubole, and those roles could read nearly all of the data the attacker went after,” cybersecurity firm Sentra notes.

The roles stayed dormant until the campaign kicked off on October 14. They were used until October 26 to enumerate resources, collect secrets and configurations, and access data.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The attacks came from a rented OVH server and the Mullvad VPN, and none of the observed activity originated from Qubole’s network, Sentra says.

“The threat actor used role session names that followed a consistent format of the prefix quiam-, followed by a suffix describing the actions taken. This includes session names such as quiam-enum and quiam-scope-full,” Wiz, which analyzed the campaign alongside Sentra, says.

Following enumeration, the attackers harvested secrets from common AWS storage locations, then used TruffleHog to test the credentials. Next, the threat actor exfiltrated data from the victims’ S3 buckets.

“The threat actor appears to have been opportunistic. Rather than looking for specific data, it read from whatever buckets each role could reach, in some cases downloading entire buckets in a single session,” Wiz says.

The cybersecurity firm also identified an ISO file designed to be remotely booted on victim machines to harvest data, but has no evidence of its deployment.

“Wiz has not identified any ties between this campaign and other publicly reported activity. The targeting and data theft appear opportunistic and do not match typical state-backed priorities; however, we don’t have any direct insight into the motivation of the threat actor or how they may use the stolen data,” the company says.

Wiz also discovered a separate campaign involving Qubole integrations, active between October 8 and October 11, in which customer-owned AWS access keys were tested against victim environments, and in some cases used for compromise.

articles.title: Update Chrome now to fix a flaw attackers are exploiting
articles.context: A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available
articles.full_text:
On November 9, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. It includes nine security fixes, including one for an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability.

A zero-day vulnerability is a security flaw disclosed or exploited before an official fix becomes available.

Hong Kong’s Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) rates the overall risk as “Extremely High.” Its bulletin says some of the vulnerabilities address in the update could allow denial of service, security restriction bypass, and remote code execution.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome 157.0.8103.51 is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Google also released Chrome 157.0.8103.50 for Android on November 9. Google says it includes the same security fixes as the desktop release unless otherwise noted. Android users should check Google Play for the update.

Technical details

Let’s take a closer look at that zero-day vulnerability.

Google says it was notified about a vulnerability by an unnamed third party on November 6. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-125350 and rated as a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome’s XML component.

XML is a data format Chrome uses to read and process certain kinds of structured web content. XML stands for Extensible Markup Language: it labels information with tags, rather like HTML, but allows authors to define their own tags to describe their data.

A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code.

Google only says that it is “aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” It has not named the attackers, the targets, the delivery method, or what the exploit can do.

articles.title: Before you buy an advent calendar, check these warning signs
articles.context: Partnerships are announced by the retailer too, not only by the seller

In this article

Store-added reviews and countdowns that keep resetting make products look popular and deals urgent

Missing contact details can make it harder to resolve a problem with an order

AI-generated images and unverified brand partnerships promote products with no licensing information

Learn how to check an online seller before you buy

Advent calendar buying guides are already appearing across the holiday shopping coverage this year. Social media can also put unfamiliar sellers directly in shoppers’ feeds. We found several stores using the same website template, product images with an AI-generated content watermark, and a TikTok account using one store’s branding to link straight to its product page.

We examined stores selling a Legend of Zelda music calendar, a Michael Jackson music calendar, a Lord of the Rings figure calendar, and Harry Potter character plant pots. Other stores, including one selling a Metallica calendar, use the same layout, low-stock warning, and recycled marketing lines. We found no licensing information on the stores, which is reason enough to avoid them.

Fake reviews and countdowns create a false sense of demand

Each store sells a single product. Its page surrounds polished product images with urgency cues: a sale that ends today, a low-stock warning, a five-minute cart reservation timer, a count of orders placed in the last day, and star ratings with thousands of reviews. Testimonials appear underneath, with “verified buyer” badges and timestamps such as “three hours ago.”

None of it is connected to anything. The ratings, review counts, and testimonials are entered into the site theme manually, rather than generated by a review system. The timestamps don’t change, and countdowns reset and run again—on some stores, every day.

Checkout runs through Shopify. That doesn’t establish whether orders will arrive or match their descriptions, and our investigation found no evidence that these pages were designed to steal card details. The risks we can support are misleading sales claims and the possibility of paying for something that never arrives or is very different from what was advertised. Several stores also offer optional checkout add-ons, including shipping protection, a queue-skip fee, and a mystery gift. On one store, these add-ons total nearly $35.

The Zelda calendar’s description contradicts itself

The clearest finding needs no technical analysis. The listing says each of the 25 discs holds a small chip storing your track data, and that the included player reads it and plays music through a built-in speaker with no app, no subscription and no Wi-Fi. Elsewhere on the same page it says the discs work with Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube, and that you can re-link any disc to a new song using a chip-writing app on your phone.

These claims cannot all be true. A device without a network connection can’t stream music from those services. And the instructions for linking discs to new songs suggest that each chip stores a link to a track, rather than the track itself. That’s how the legitimate version of this product works, according to our research: the chip holds a link, and a phone plays the music. Someone appears to have copied that mechanism and bolted a fictional standalone speaker onto it.

The bundle pricing also doesn’t add up. Two bundles claim savings of $15 and $33, but the prices shown below them work out to about $19 and $43 in savings.

The stores are copies of one another

Despite their different names, the stores we examined are nearly identical. They use the same commercial theme version and share an internal fingerprint indicating that their theme files are copies of one another. They also block right-clicking and access to developer tools.

The most direct link was left behind by accident, in that one store’s theme is still named after the file it was exported from, and that filename includes the web address of another store in the group. Other pages contain leftover text from a previous shop, including a warranty promising to replace costumes that don’t inflate properly and a scrolling banner with the unedited placeholder “use code X for X percent off.”

The stores’ files are timestamped from mid-July to the second week of September, with the newest store only days old when we examined it. Most merchant accounts are registered in Romania, while prices are shown in dollars. None of the calendar stores we examined listed a business address or phone number.

The pattern runs well past unlicensed character merchandise. We found advent calendars for fishing lures, squishy toys, charm bracelets, and wearable jumpers, with the same countdowns, stock warnings, and paid add-ons. Most appear to sell real, inexpensive goods at a steep markup. Their add-on prices differ, so we can’t conclude that the same person runs all of them. The evidence points to a shared sales playbook, not necessarily a shared owner.

What the evidence shows, and what it doesn’t

Product images from two of the calendar stores triggered a provenance checker for a watermark, indicating they were produced with OpenAI tools. The filenames agree: across three stores every product image follows the same automated naming pattern, and one store’s entire photography set is timestamped to a single afternoon.

A TikTok account uses one store’s name and branding and links directly to its product page. Several videos claim the store is collaborating with Walmart. They show retail scenes, including an oversized character figure outside a store and pallets of branded boxes. We found no evidence of such a partnership. The videos also depict scenes that don’t appear to be real. Combined with the shared website template and the filename linking two stores, this suggests that one operator or a closely connected group may be involved. It doesn’t establish who is behind the stores.

How to spot a questionable store before you pay

In our survey earlier this year, 22% of respondents said they had been “misled by AI-generated photos or product reviews.”Here are some checks that can help you spot warning signs.

Be wary of endless urgency. If a sale keeps “ending today” or low-stock warnings never change, don’t treat them as proof of a genuine deal.

Check that the product could exist. Search the product type and read how the real version works. If the listing claims something the technology can’t do, stop there.

Don’t arrive through a link. These stores sell largely through social video. Search the brand name separately and look for history, press, or customers outside its own website.

Treat partnership claims as claims. A video saying a brand is stocked by a retailer isn’t evidence that it is. Partnerships are announced by the retailer too, not only by the seller.

Look for a real business. A postal address, company registration and working phone number are easy for a legitimate seller to provide and were absent from these.

Reverse-image search the photos. Generated images usually have no history anywhere else online. A complete absence of results is itself informative.

Read the small print against itself. If a calendar’s warranty talks about inflatable costumes, the page wasn’t written for the product you’re buying.

Check the spelling, including on the box. We found a misspelled artist name in a product title, a mangled savings line, and a calendar with the word spelled “calindar” on the packaging artwork itself. A real manufacturer proofreads its own box.

Pay with a method that offers buyer protection. A credit card or payment service with buyer protection gives you a route to a refund. Bank transfers can be harder to reverse.

Tools that help

Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks scam sites, which can help when a link appears in your feed before you’ve had a chance to look up the seller.

Malwarebytes Scam Guard lets you check a suspicious link, message, or screenshot when something feels off but you can’t say why.

If a purchase leads to follow-up texts or calls about delivery fees, customs charges, or a refund, Malwarebytes Scam Number Check can tell you whether the number has been reported. A follow-up message can turn a bad purchase into something worse.

Something feel off? Check it before you click.

Malwarebytes Scam Guard helps you analyze suspicious links, texts, and screenshots instantly.
