articles.title: AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier
Ransomware threat blares from Vanderbilt University computers during cyberattack
articles.context: Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware...
articles.full_text: Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group BYOD. Vanderbilt announced on Monday morning that it was dealing with "an active cybersecurity incident," and that the fallout may affect university devices, systems, and cloud-based services. The Nashville-based university initially told students and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi. It warned them to watch for unexpected prompts, altered files or permissions, unfamiliar applications, and unsolicited authentication requests. Campus computers reportedly began playing an audio threat attributed to BYOD. Student newspaper The Vanderbilt Hustler cited posts on campus social network Fizz showing the message. "You have been compromised by BYOD," the recording said. "We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one." By Monday evening, Vanderbilt had restored access to campus Wi-Fi, but warned that access to most systems remains restricted. "We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university," it said. "Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation." Students were told to attend classes as scheduled on Tuesday and contact instructors about flexibility on coursework deadlines. Staff were instructed to report to work normally. Vanderbilt's Athletics department said that its ticketing system was unavailable, and that students were unable to claim tickets for the college's football game against Alabama on Saturday. BYOD claimed responsibility for the attack on Vanderbilt on Monday, along with extensive data theft. "If you could not tell already, your databases are locked [and] we have your entire estate and research data," it said via its leak site. "Over 1 million SSNs, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, student and employee records, full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess." Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's claims about the extent of its access or the data allegedly stolen. BYOD may be a familiar name to some. articles.title: Microsoft’s AI bug hunter finds Rust flaw that went undetected for nearly 11 years
articles.context: Microsoft said the researchers found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions they examined and assessed practical exploitation as unlikely
articles.full_text:
Microsoft researchers have uncovered a memory-safety bug in Rust’s standard library that had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, alongside other flaws that can trigger undefined behavior even in applications written entirely in safe Rust. Two of the findings affect stable Rust, including a separate issue that could cause applications to access freed memory.

The nearly 11-year-old bug involves Rust’s process::exit function. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab researchers found that calling the function from a child thread could cause the runtime to remove the main thread’s alternate signal stack while it was still running. If the main thread subsequently experienced a stack overflow, the operating system could be unable to deliver the signal correctly, resulting in a segmentation fault instead of Rust’s intended stack-overflow handling.

“The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years,” the researchers wrote in a blog post. Microsoft said the researchers found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions they examined and assessed practical exploitation as unlikely.

The research used Hyenas, FORGE Lab’s AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system, to investigate unsafe code in Rust’s standard library. Hyenas is the lab’s research version of codename MDASH, Microsoft’s agentic vulnerability-discovery system.

Microsoft said some of the bugs were found with help from Hyenas. Researchers then examined the underlying code, reproduced the issues, assessed their security impact, and reported them to Rust maintainers.

Microsoft said the practical risk is limited. Each flaw requires unusual conditions to trigger, and a bug in the standard library becomes “a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way,” the researchers wrote.

Unsafe code challenges Rust’s safety guarantees

Rust’s ownership model and type system are designed to prevent memory-safety problems commonly associated with languages such as C and C++. However, its standard library relies on unsafe code internally for operations that the compiler cannot verify.

Components such as Vec and String use these operations but expose them through safe APIs. Microsoft said these APIs must meet a strict soundness requirement: “no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.”

Microsoft grouped the findings into three categories: unsafe code that assumes operations will not panic, code that trusts user-provided implementations to behave correctly, and code that makes incorrect assumptions about the underlying system.

The first involved a panic-safety problem in Rust’s MapWindows::clone implementation. The function created a buffer before fully initializing its contents and then called a user-provided clone operation to populate it. If that operation triggered a panic, Rust’s unwinding mechanism could invoke the buffer’s destructor, which would attempt to access uninitialized memory. Microsoft said the reported fix prevents the partially initialized buffer from being destroyed before initialization is complete.

Another finding involved str::replace. The researchers found that the function could make an incorrect assumption about a custom implementation of the nightly Pattern trait. A custom implementation could supply a non-ASCII byte where the code expected an ASCII character, causing the replacement operation to produce invalid UTF-8 data. Subsequent string operations could then trigger undefined behavior, Microsoft said.

System-level bugs affect stable Rust

Microsoft said the first two categories of weaknesses were already being studied in 2021 through Rudra, a static analyzer developed by members of the research team. The standard library had also addressed panic-safety problems as far back as 2015, but similar weaknesses continue to appear in its implementations.

The third category involves interactions between Rust and underlying operating systems and C libraries. Besides the process::exit issue, researchers identified a problem in Rust’s CommandExt::exec functionality involving the process-wide environment variable array.

Microsoft found that the function could modify this shared state while holding a read lock, potentially allowing other threads to access inconsistent data. Under certain conditions, concurrent operations could leave the environment pointer referencing freed memory.

Microsoft said both the process::exit and CommandExt::exec findings affect stable Rust. A proposed fix for the environment-variable issue, which avoids modifying the shared array by calling execve directly, was under review when the blog was published.

Two issues reported by Microsoft’s team remained open at publication. The blog also discussed related reports from other researchers and fixes still under review.

Findings feed into Microsoft’s security products

Microsoft said the research findings can also feed into Microsoft Perception, its multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work across broader security workflows. It would therefore help the company improve the development of MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender.

For example, Microsoft’s Web App Pen Test Agent can use MDASH findings to prioritize testing, assess exploitability against live applications, and provide information to support remediation, the researchers wrote.

“Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs,” the researchers wrote, but to identify meaningful issues and improve the safety of foundational software developers and organizations depend on. The Rust project had not responded to a request for comment from CSO at the time of writing.

articles.title: Anthropic Rolls Out Mythos 5.2 With Improved Bug Hunting, Fewer Sandbox Escapes
articles.context: Anthropic on Monday released Claude Mythos 5
articles.full_text:
Anthropic on Monday released Claude Mythos 5.2, the latest version of its access-restricted AI model, and Mozilla says it roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery results of Mythos 5.1 in Firefox.

Mythos 5.2 and Claude Fable 5.2, which was released alongside it, share the same underlying model. The difference lies in the guardrails: Fable, which anyone can use, carries protections against cybersecurity and biology misuse, while Mythos ships without some of them.

Direct access to Mythos is reserved for vetted organizations, which can apply through Anthropic’s Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs.

“We’ve worked closely with the Anthropic team all year to harden Firefox with successive generations of Claude models, and each round has left fewer, subtler bugs to find. Even so, Mythos 5.2 roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery metrics of Mythos 5.1 across respective scanning campaigns,” said Brian Grinstead, distinguished engineer at Mozilla.

Internally, Anthropic measures progress with CVE Rediscovery, which gives a model the code of a project from before a known CVE was patched and checks whether the model spots the flaw without help.

In an October run covering 1,829 CVEs, Mythos 5.2 achieved a success rate of 89.6%. Mythos 5.1 scored 78.3%, and Opus 5.5, tested without safeguards, scored 81.3%.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Anthropic also shared results from testers, including a security company that found that one in six confirmed bugs uncovered by Mythos 5.2 had gone unnoticed by every other frontier model it ran.

In a footnote, however, Anthropic noted, “On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5.”

Claude Enterprise customers who are not part of the Cyber Verification Program have another route to the latest Mythos. Claude Security, Anthropic’s code vulnerability scanner, now uses Mythos 5.2 among other models.

In Fable 5.2, classifiers stop penetration testing, exploit generation and other risky cyber tasks, and users get a response from Opus 4.8 instead.

Anthropic says these protections are as robust as those in Fable 5.1 but are triggered less often by legitimate work. Early testing showed roughly 60% fewer cybersecurity blocks compared with Fable 5.1.

The company tested how readily the model escapes containment in an experiment of more than 1,800 scenarios. The sandbox contained an intentional flaw, and most tasks could only be completed by getting out of it.

Mythos 5.2 relied on credentials or files that Anthropic had left outside the sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios. That is a sharp drop from Mythos 5.1 (21%) and Mythos 5 (39%), and close to the 3.3% rate for Opus 5.5.

articles.title: IRISSCON 2026 puts preparedness for cyberattacks and hybrid threats in focus
articles.context: Recent incidents include cyberattacks targeting supermarket refrigeration systems in Ireland and elsewhere in Europe, bomb threats that disrupted flights to and from Ireland,...
articles.full_text:
Ireland risks being dangerously unprepared for increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks and hybrid threats unless the Government acts urgently to strengthen the country’s national security capabilities, according to Brian Honan, head of the Irish Reporting and Information Security Service (IRISSCERT) and founder of BH Consulting.

The warning comes ahead of IRISSCON 2026, IRISSCERT’s annual cybersecurity conference, which takes place at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin on Wednesday, 11 November. Help Net Security will be attending the event.

Recent incidents include cyberattacks targeting supermarket refrigeration systems in Ireland and elsewhere in Europe, bomb threats that disrupted flights to and from Ireland, and emailed bomb threats that forced evacuations and disrupted operations at Irish media organisations, including RTÉ.

The incidents come as Ireland prepares to host major EU political meetings. Honan said they highlight how quickly threats can disrupt businesses and public services, and raise questions about Ireland’s ability to detect and respond to incidents that can interrupt essential services and undermine public confidence.

“While Ireland has a National Cyber Security Strategy, we still lack an overarching national security strategy that brings together all the elements needed to defend our country against modern threats,” Honan said.

He warned that without a national strategy, agencies and organisations risk responding in isolation. A coordinated approach, he said, would help ensure they have the resources they need and can work together when an incident affects several sectors at once.

Honan called on the Government to complete the transposition of the EU’s NIS2 Directive into Irish law and address questions about the cybersecurity resources available to the Defence Forces, the Garda National Cyber Crime Bureau and the National Cyber Security Centre.

He said the Government also needs to consider how it supports Irish businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises. Many are increasingly exposed to cyberattacks and lack the resources, expertise and practical guidance to protect themselves, keep operating during an incident and recover afterwards.

“Cybersecurity is no longer simply an IT issue. It is an economic security issue, a national security issue, and ultimately an issue of public safety. We cannot afford to wait for a major national crisis, similar to the ransomware attack against the HSE in 2021, before taking it seriously.”

Responsibility for the recent incidents remains unclear. Honan said Ireland must be ready to respond whether an attack comes from cybercriminals, politically motivated groups or hostile states. He called for national infrastructure, public services and businesses to be better prepared to withstand attacks, maintain essential services and recover quickly.

“One of the biggest challenges with hybrid threats is that we may never establish with certainty who is behind an attack. But that uncertainty cannot become an excuse for inaction,” he said.

IRISSCON 2026 will bring together international cybersecurity experts, researchers, industry professionals and law enforcement representatives to discuss emerging threats and how organisations can prepare for them. The programme will cover threats to telecommunications infrastructure, cybercrime, emerging attack techniques and the role of human factors in security incidents.

articles.title: Default Admin Password Let Researchers Unlock and Start Cars
articles.context: Test Car Unlocked and Started From a Hijacked Account In early 2026, the researchers bypassed the web application firewall (WAF) in front of the login servers and found the...
articles.full_text:
Researchers been able to take over customer accounts at two car brands. They then demonstrated how they could remotely unlock and start a test car after finding an administration console on the brands' login servers still protected by its default password.

Security researchers Shubham Shah and Sam Curry detailed the work in a write-up published November 7. Customer logins for both brands ran on OpenIDM, identity management software from ForgeRock, now part of Ping Identity. The brands were not named, at the automakers' request.

The researchers reported the flaw to the two automakers and pointed to ForgeRock's hardening guidance to remove or protect the console before deployment.

Test Car Unlocked and Started From a Hijacked Account

In early 2026, the researchers bypassed the web application firewall (WAF) in front of the login servers and found the console still accepted its documented default credentials. From there they ran their own code on the identity servers and changed the email address and password on a test account.

Logging in as that customer through the normal app, they unlocked and started the test car with its owner present. The session also exposed the vehicle's location and telemetry.

The researchers wrote that they could have created a session for any customer account on the affected deployments. Changing an account's login details also left the owner's existing app session active, and the researchers could divert the app's notifications away from the owner's phone.

Both automakers fixed the issue about two hours after the flaw was reported and rotated affected credentials, according to the write-up.

Read more on default passwords in connected systems: CISA, FBI Urge Action to Protect Industrial Refrigeration Networks

Australian Systems Exposed Through Hardcoded Credentials

In a companion post, Shah described a separate chain against one of the automaker's Australian systems, researched in July 2026.

The chain could start from a car's number plate. Hardcoded administrator credentials, a WAF bypass and a misconfigured multi-factor authentication (MFA) step then allowed account takeover and remote unlocking.

The exposed data included customers' names, phone numbers and password hashes. Together, the write-ups covered vehicles in Australia, the US and Canada. The researchers wrote that they tested only on cars they owned or had permission to use.

Shah's post does not say when the Australian findings were reported or whether they have been fixed. Neither post reports malicious use or says whether the researchers checked for it.

articles.title: Your Artifact Repositories Need a Firewall
articles.context: Attackers publish malicious packages, hijack legitimate projects, and turn routine dependency download into opportunities for credential theft or a build compromise
articles.full_text:
Most organizations spend a lot of time looking for vulnerabilities in the software they build. But what about the malicious packages that enter before development even begins?

Attackers publish malicious packages, hijack legitimate projects, and turn routine dependency download into opportunities for credential theft or a build compromise. Malicious packages can run code during installation, when a developer or build system may already have access to source code, tokens, cloud accounts, or publishing credentials.

CI pipelines and AI agents add to the volume of package requests. They can resolve and install dependencies automatically, often without a human reviewing each request. That makes the point where packages enter the development workflow an important place to evaluate risk.

A repository or package firewall checks dependency requests against threat intelligence and policy before components reach developers, agents, or builds. The protection depends on the quality of that intelligence and where the firewall can evaluate a request.

Recent Attacks Show How Much Can Hide in a Package

In October 2026, a hijacked release of the TensorLake TypeScript SDK used an install hook to search for credentials and accept remote commands.

Sonatype's analysis found code that could modify repositories accessible to the compromised account and could expose collected data through a GitHub fallback. The investigation did not confirm that data was published, repositories were modified, or downstream systems were affected.

Other campaigns used different routes into the same workflows:

Hijacked packages and new malicious packages: Six npm packages delivered the same malware. Three appeared to be hijacked legitimate packages, and three were published with the malicious payload already included. The malware used Ethereum transactions to find infrastructure hosting additional payloads.

Large-scale package flooding: Sonatype identified nearly 850 components in the Flooding Dropper campaign. The packages downloaded and launched additional payloads on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Credential theft and propagation: The Mini Shai-Hulud wave affected more than 2,200 component versions. Malicious releases of legitimate packages used install hooks to steal credentials and, where publishing access was available, compromise more packages.

Install-time execution: Miasma waves abused binding.gyp and node-gyp to execute during installation, rather than relying only on familiar lifecycle scripts. The Leo Platform compromise report tracked 23 malicious package versions.

These incidents show why package risk is not limited to suspicious names or newly created projects. Malicious code can arrive in a familiar package, run as part of installation, and act with the access available to the developer, build, or agent that requested it.

What a Repository or Package Firewall Does

A repository or package firewall checks dependency requests as they pass from a development environment toward package sources. It evaluates a requested component against security intelligence and, depending on the product's capabilities and configuration, can block or quarantine components that appear malicious or violate policy.

Once a package has been installed, teams may need to investigate the affected machine, identify exposed credentials, check for persistence, and determine whether the package reached other systems. Blocking a known malicious package at the point of entry can help prevent that cleanup from starting in the first place.

A firewall is one layer of software supply chain protection. It does not replace endpoint security, code review, or other controls. It addresses a specific risk: malicious or policy-violating components entering through package requests. And like any control, its coverage depends on which developers, pipelines, agents, and package sources route through it.

What to Look for in a Package Firewall

A repository or package firewall should do more than sit between a repository and a registry. As you evaluate options, consider whether or not it can:

Block malicious components before download, at the point where a package is requested.

Use current, in-depth threat intelligence that can help identify more than known vulnerabilities or suspicious package names.

Protect requests from developers, CI pipelines, and AI agents that can access public package sources.

Fit your repository tools and package sources without requiring a change to established workflows.

Cover the package ecosystems your teams use, and make clear which registries, mirrors, and private sources are included.

Strong firewall protection helps teams stay ahead of threats by identifying and blocking malicious components before they enter the development process. By evaluating package requests at the point of intake, it can reduce the risk of compromised builds and the investigation and rework that follow, while helping teams keep development moving.

How Sonatype's Intelligence Informs Firewall Decisions

A firewall's decision is only as useful as the evidence behind it. Sonatype Firewall combines machine-learning signals with AI-powered analysis, alongside the expertise of Sonatype's security research team, to identify suspicious packages and investigate if they contain malicious code.

By analyzing release behavior, examining package contents, and correlating findings across multiple sources, Sonatype can detect threats earlier, uncover additional affected packages, and turn new discoveries into actionable intelligence that informs Firewall's blocking and quarantine decisions.

That work can involve several kinds of analysis:

Activity and release patterns can help surface packages that behave differently from their project's history or from typical ecosystem activity.

Behavioral analysis can flag unusual signals around a package or release. Researchers can investigate those findings to confirm whether a component is malicious.

Payload analysis examines what the code actually does, including behavior such as credential theft, code injection, or downloading another payload.

Secondary expansion follows the code beyond the original package. Advanced Binary Fingerprinting can help identify embedded or renamed code that may not appear in a package's declared dependencies. In one investigation, Sonatype researchers found code associated with the flatmap-stream incident in 12 additional npm components.

Together, these methods provide context that a package name or manifest alone cannot. That context helps a firewall make a more informed decision about whether to allow, block, or hold a request for review.

Give Every Package Request a Safer Path

Every dependency starts with a request. A developer adds a package, a pipeline pulls it into a build, or an AI agent selects it for generated code. That request is an opportunity to assess a component before it becomes part of your software.

Sonatype Firewall helps teams bring security and development together at the moment open source enters the software supply chain. Backed by Sonatype's research and designed to work with supported repository environments, it helps organizations block malicious components earlier before they reach developers or workflows. That gives teams a chance to stop known threats at the point of entry, reduce avoidable disruption, and keep development moving with greater confidence.

Even if your existing repositories support secure component selection, malicious packages can still make their way into development. The difference comes down to how threats are identified, how quickly new malicious activity is detected, and whether that intelligence can stop a package before it's downloaded. Sonatype Firewall is that difference. Since it's designed to work with a wide range of repository managers, you can add an additional layer of protection to block known risks and avoid downstream work.

See how Sonatype Firewall can help protect your repositories from malicious packages.

Written by Aaron Linskens

Aaron is a technical writer at Sonatype. He works at a crossroads of technical writing, developer advocacy, and information design. He aims to get developers and non-technical collaborators to work better together in solving problems and building software.

articles.title: Claude Mythos 5.2 arrives with stronger bug hunting and less sandbox-breaking behavior
articles.context: In the first, a 1983 result showed that black holes form abruptly as such universes heat up, but only in large ones
articles.full_text:
Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2. The two versions share an underlying model, with stricter safeguards for cybersecurity and biology tasks in the broadly available Fable.

Fable blocks fewer requests

Fable’s safety classifiers block high-risk cybersecurity tasks such as penetration testing and exploit generation, as well as most biology research tasks. When Fable blocks a request in either category, Anthropic serves a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity or Opus 5 for biology. Organizations can apply for Mythos access through the recently expanded Cyber Verification Program and Life Sciences Verification Program.

In early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, Anthropic recorded about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 than with Fable 5.1. Cybersecurity blocks fell by about 60%, and biology blocks fell by about 40%. The company says the safeguards are as robust as those in Fable 5.1.

Mythos outscores Opus in bug-finding

Anthropic calls Mythos 5.2 its most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. In the company’s CVE Rediscovery benchmark, which covered 1,829 previously published vulnerabilities, Mythos 5.2 rediscovered 89.6%, compared with 81.3% for Opus 5.5 with safeguards disabled. That represents a 10.2% relative increase. Anthropic also says an unnamed security firm reported that one in six confirmed bugs Mythos found had been missed by every other frontier model the firm tested.

CVE Rediscovery (Source: Anthropic)

“Claude Mythos 5.2 is astonishingly good. We’ve worked closely with the Anthropic team all year to harden Firefox with successive generations of Claude models, and each round has left fewer, subtler bugs to find. Even so, Mythos 5.2 roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery metrics of Mythos 5.1 across respective scanning campaigns,” said Brian Grinstead, Distinguished Engineer at Mozilla.

Claude Enterprise customers can use Mythos 5.2 through Claude Security even if they are outside the Cyber Verification Program. Claude Security scans code for vulnerabilities, monitors repositories as code changes, and tracks if findings are fixed.

Fable finishes a calculation physicists abandoned

Anthropic says Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics involving black holes and the effort to reconcile relativity with quantum mechanics. Both rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes with gravity can be described by a quantum theory without it.

In the first, a 1983 result showed that black holes form abruptly as such universes heat up, but only in large ones. A 2003 calculation for very small universes was too laborious to finish. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 completed it, largely on its own, and found the transition is abrupt there too. In the second, the model found the exact limit of a technique used for more than 15 years to rule out quantum gravity theories in a simplified universe.

Testing for sandbox escapes

Anthropic assessed the risk of unsafe behavior in high-stakes situations as low. The UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design, and METR tested the underlying model before release.

The company tested more than 1,800 scenarios in a deliberately weakened sandbox, and most could only be solved by escaping it. Mythos 5.2 used credentials or files placed outside the sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios. Opus 5.5 did so in 3.3%, Sonnet 5.5 in 5.1%, Mythos 5.1 in 21%, and Mythos 5 in 39%.

Both Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 expressed suspicion that they were being evaluated more often than any other recent Claude model did. Anthropic says this makes it harder to predict how the models will behave in real-world settings. The company draws on monitoring during training, reviews of internal transcripts, external testing, and interpretability research.

Defending against distillation

Anthropic says illicit distillation, in which another model is trained on Claude’s outputs, takes place at industrial scale and can reproduce capabilities without Claude’s safeguards. Fable 5.2 uses Anthropic’s strongest protections against distillation to date. The company previously reported that the techniques used in Fable 5.2 reduced the amount of data distillers collected by 90% to 99%. Anthropic has extended its preserved thinking feature to all API accounts. The feature prevents distillers from editing Claude’s earlier context in an attempt to extract its reasoning.

During training, Anthropic limited gains in certain research capabilities that could accelerate AI development, such as optimizing accelerator kernels and improving language model architectures. The company says performance in those areas is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 and that the training changes left related capabilities such as agentic coding unaffected.

Privacy and enterprise monitoring

The models’ safeguards monitor usage across multiple requests to detect patterns of misuse. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards feature runs automated monitoring on prompts and responses stored in the customer’s own infrastructure, making the setup compatible with Anthropic’s zero data retention option.

The feature is in private beta with customers including Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe. Eligible customers can continue using the models with zero data retention before they adopt it. Other customers have 30-day retention for safety monitoring.

Availability and pricing

Fable 5.2 is available on Anthropic’s platforms and through Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can access it on the Claude Platform using the model ID claude-fable-5-2. Standard pricing for both models is $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Fast mode costs $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens and is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. Mythos 5.2 fast mode is limited to organizations in Anthropic’s verification programs.

articles.title: Beyond the Alert: The Case for Rich Network Data
articles.context: It’s the reason we have detections in the first place
articles.full_text:
At some point your security will fail. This isn’t pessimism. It’s not because your team and tools aren’t sophisticated enough. It’s the reason we have detections in the first place. And, it’s why once we accept that prevention has its limits, we arrive at an interdiction strategy: finding and disrupting what got in.

After the alert

The alert tells you something happened. However, gaining access to your network doesn’t necessarily mean attackers have stolen data or disrupted the systems they were targeting. They may need to obtain additional access, move to another machine, or further explore the network. Being able to see and understand that activity is the intervention opportunity.

People naturally gravitate toward detections during product evaluations. They’re tangible, easy to compare and quantify, and address the question everyone wants an answer to: Will they catch the attack? There’s often an assumption that the rest will follow, meaning, if the detections are good, surely the investigation will be as well, right?

Whether you can trace the attack, understand the scope, and respond in time to intervene depends largely on the data behind that detection. In network security, a product can have good detections and still leave an analyst struggling to investigate. Perhaps the analyst can see the connection that triggered the alert but can’t follow what happened next. If a search returns nothing, does that mean the activity didn’t happen or that you weren’t collecting the evidence needed to see it?

This, and the arrival of AI defense, is why data quality has recently been getting so much attention.

Data vs. data

Investigation success takes knowledge of both attacker behavior and your own environment. You need to understand what you’re looking for, but also what your data can actually tell you.

The difference in network data shows up when investigating an alert. Both shallow and rich data provide investigations with a starting point, but one can rapidly lead to a dead end. Shallow data is often just composed of timestamps, IPs, and basic connection information. Rich data retains greater transaction details and adds context. It correlates and lets you pivot and reconstruct, answering not just what triggered the alert but what happened before, after, and elsewhere.

To evaluate the data quality of a security tool, consider key questions such as:

Are full transaction details provided or just a summary?

Is packet content or file extraction available?

How far back can we search, and how fast?

Can I follow a connection across hosts and time?

AI <3 data

AI-powered SOC tools can now process data at a scale that human teams simply cannot match. The more data points AI has, the more effectively it can surface events. While shallow data limits what AI can correlate, richer data allows it to identify subtle patterns across hosts and behaviors, potentially exposing previously unseen indicators of compromise or providing opportunity to intervene before an attack escalates.

AI can help when something unfamiliar is encountered. Nobody knows every service, process, or log format. An assistant can help explain what you’re looking at, suggest questions to pursue, or write a script to make a large set of data easier to examine. That can save a lot of research time. It can also help an analyst get past a point where they would otherwise be stuck.

But we’re certainly not at the point where we can trust what AI claims 100% of the time. You still need to test what it gives you. If an assistant suggests an explanation, check whether the evidence supports it. If it produces a query or script, test what it does. And before running a suggested command, ask what else it might affect. A model can be so focused on solving the immediate problem that it overlooks the rest of the system.

As AI takes on more investigative work, the ability to inspect the underlying evidence becomes another essential aspect of modern data quality.

Unfamiliar territory is the test

When evaluating data from network security products—NDR in particular—take an alert from a demonstration and investigate it properly. But don’t follow the guided path. Dig deep and put yourself in unfamiliar territory. You’ll get a much better sense of how the product helps analysts when they’re dealing with an event they haven’t seen before.

Look at the transactions behind the alert

Ask what packet content or extracted files are available

Follow the activity backwards and forwards in time

Ask a question that wasn’t anticipated

These questions and tasks probably won’t be part of a typical demo. That’s the point. They’ll let you see if the data provides the fidelity, reach, and context to actually solve investigations or just a starting point with nowhere to go.

Detections get the attention, but data determines the outcome. The real question is can your team use the data to fully understand an incident and decide what to do?

About Corelight:

Your AI SOC is only as effective as the data behind it. Corelight network detection and response (NDR) delivers data that’s open, transparent, and explainable—helping detect evasive threats, reduce triage time, and enable agentic AI throughout the SOC. Corelight’s structured network evidence preserves protocol-level context to produce a more complete dataset for investigation and AI. When analysts and AI can reason from evidence instead of isolated alerts or metadata, they can validate findings, reconstruct activity, and reach more reliable conclusions. Learn more about Corelight at https://corelight.com/cp/elitedefense

articles.title: Vanderbilt University Takes Systems Offline After Cyber Incident
articles.context: Campus WiFi was also confirmed to be available
articles.full_text:
Vanderbilt University has been hit by a cyber incident, resulting in systems and applications being taken offline.

The Nashville-based institution disclosed that it was responding to an active incident at 10.45am CST on November 9, which it said may impact university devices, systems and cloud-based services.

“We are asking all members of the university community to shut down university devices, disconnect from university WiFi, and remain extremely vigilant. Take immediate action if you notice any unusual or suspicious activity on your devices,” the University wrote in the update on its website.

Such suspicious activity included unexpected pop-ups, warnings or security notifications; unusual changes to files, folders, or permissions in cloud storage platforms; and unexpected requests to enter passwords or approve authentication requests.

A later update by Vanderbilt at 7.15pm CST confirmed that classes will proceed on a normal schedule from November 10, while student services will also be operating normally. Campus WiFi was also confirmed to be available.

However, access to most Vanderbilt systems and applications remains restricted.

“We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university. Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation,” the update added.

The Vanderbilt Hustler, the official student newspaper for Vanderbilt University, reported on November 9 that university IT staff entered classrooms across campus, alerting that school-issued computers were not safe to use.

Read now: Copenhagen University Breach Compromises Data on Half a Million People

Vanderbilt Incident Claimed by BYOD Ransomware

Vanderbilt did not give any details on the nature of the incident, or any alleged perpetrator. However, cyber intelligence firm Venarix reported on X that the BYOD ransomware gang has listed Vanderbilt University on its data leak site.

The group claimed to have locked the university’s databases and accessed a vast volume of data held in its systems.

This includes Vanderbilt’s research data, over one million social security numbers, full names, emails, phone numbers, student and employee records, and a full takeover of the university’s domain controller.

articles.title: France Blames Iran for Supermarket Fridge Hack, Requests International Arrest Warrants
articles.context: Laure Beccuau, the Paris Public Prosecutor, said on social media the investigation found links between the October 11 to 12 cyber-attack and the Shahid Kaveh and Shahid...
articles.full_text:
The recent wave of cyber-attacks targeting refrigeration control systems across 700 supermarkets sites in France was coordinated by Iranian hacking groups, according to French authorities.

Laure Beccuau, the Paris Public Prosecutor, said on social media the investigation found links between the October 11 to 12 cyber-attack and the Shahid Kaveh and Shahid Shoostari groups, two elite offensive cyber units tied to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

In a technical attribution notice published on November 9, the French Computer Emergency and Response Team (CERT-FR) said Shahid Kaveh is linked to a range of purported hacktivist groups, including CyberAveng3rs, Soldiers of Solomon, Mr. Soul and Cyber Isnaad Front.

Investigators from the Anti-Criminality Office (OFAC) and the French domestic intelligence service (DGSI) found IP addresses linked to Iran-based endpoints and observed Farsi words in the traces left by the hackers.

Additionally, the techniques, tactics and procedures (TTPs) employed by the attackers were consistent with previous Shahid Kaveh campaigns.

CERT-FR named three leaders of the IRGC and Shahid Kaveh linked to the cyber-attacks.

The Paris prosecutor's office has now opened a judicial investigation into the cyber-attacks and the damage caused.

France Vows to Take Punitive Measures

According to another statement issued by the French government on November 9, Paris intends to take a series of diplomatic and punitive measures in response to the cyber-attacks.

The government announced that it would summon Iran’s Ambassador to France to formally convey its strongest condemnation of the attacks.

It also stated that it would urge its European partners to introduce additional sanctions targeting Iranian individuals and entities allegedly involved in the cyber-attacks against France, as well as other malicious cyber activities.

The French government stressed that it reserves the right to take further measures, both public and undisclosed, should they be deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to the cyber threats.

Frist Nation-State, Sabotage-Focused Cyber-Attack on French Soil

Historically, France has rarely attributed cyber-attacks to a single country, making this move particularly significant.

“This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, marking the first cyber-offensive campaign carried out purely for sabotage purposes on French national territory,” the French government explained in its statement.

Commenting on the attribution, Gary Barlet, public sector CTO at Illumio, said he is also “impressed” that France is planning to pursue sanctions at a European level.

“It's not yet clear what form those sanctions will take, so that will be interesting to see. But this needs to happen more often. Too often an attack gets publicly called out, there's outrage, and then nothing happens. It sends a message to attackers that the cost of doing this is close to zero,” Barlet added.

In the CERT-FR technical notice, the French Cyber Crises Coordination Center (C4) said this attack added to a series of other incidents that have been attributed to IRGC-linked groups since at least 2020. These include destabilisation campaigns targeting satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and a French digital display company in 2024, in the context of the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

This attribution does not include the cyber-attack on the French Blood Service (EFS) that occurred in early November.

articles.title: Apple Patches iMessage Group Chat Privacy Flaws and Bluetooth Pairing Vulnerabilities
articles.context: An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it
articles.full_text:
An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix.

The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected.

The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27.

The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960.

Which Updates Carry the Fixes

Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update.

The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes.

The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away.

The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component.

All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do.

Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

articles.title: Windows settings backup is on by default starting with Windows 11 26H2
articles.context: The company renamed the feature, which launched in August 2025 as Windows Backup for Organizations, and moved the management of roaming settings into the same policy tools
articles.full_text:
Starting with Windows 11, version 26H2, Windows settings backup will switch on by default on eligible devices. The company renamed the feature, which launched in August 2025 as Windows Backup for Organizations, and moved the management of roaming settings into the same policy tools.

What gets saved

The feature backs up supported Windows settings and the list of installed Microsoft Store apps. When restore is available, users can select a backup profile to recover their settings and app list on a new, reset, or reimaged PC.

Soon after the launch, Microsoft added first sign-in restore, extending support to more device types and hybrid-managed environments.

Four changes

IT teams can keep their existing policy settings, Cloud Solution Providers, and Group Policy paths. The rename requires no policy migration or reconfiguration.

Enterprise State Roaming (ESR) lets supported Windows settings follow users across devices associated with their Microsoft Entra ID accounts. Since the transition period ended in June 2026, administrators have managed ESR through Windows settings backup and restore policies. The same settings remain supported, and applicable licensing requirements still apply.

Windows continues to honor policies that explicitly enable or disable backup. Organizations that want to keep backup off can explicitly disable it by policy. Administrators still need to configure restore separately.

Available starting with Windows 11, version 24H2, the restore summary shows the restored personalization settings and the Microsoft Store app list. Users can reach it through a notification on the new device or by going to Settings > Accounts > Windows backup. The summary opens in a browser and offers an export option. It becomes available about an hour after a successful restore and remains accessible for seven days after device setup.

Source: Microsoft

Tools for administrators

Microsoft provides the WindowsBackupAdmin PowerShell module to help administrators manage backup profiles. Administrators with the appropriate permissions can view profile attributes, export backup information for governance, and delete a user’s backup data or profiles. The module gives administrators access to profile information only.

The scripts wrap existing Microsoft Graph beta APIs and are available through the PowerShell Gallery and GitHub.

Tested inside Microsoft

Microsoft says it has deployed backup policies across its own organization. Brian Fielder, Vice President of Microsoft Digital, said the feature helps “free IT teams from the heavy lifting of device reimaging.”

Shilpa Narang, Senior Product Manager at Microsoft, described the goal as helping employees pick up where they left off on a new PC while making device transitions easier for administrators.

articles.title: N-able Takes N-central Offline as Researcher Drops Over 30 Zero-Days
articles.context: The security researcher released proof-of-concept (PoC) code targeting every flaw and reportedly explained that the zero-days were dropped after N-able failed to patch security...
articles.full_text:
N-able on Monday took hosted N-central environments offline in response to a security researcher’s public disclosure of more than 30 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities.

“As a precautionary measure, we are temporarily taking our Hosted N-central environment offline while we take the necessary actions to secure the environment and implement appropriate remediation,” the company said.

While N-central and the related services remain inaccessible, N-able says it has made progress validating the flaws and creating a fix, which should roll out around midday on November 10.

On-premises N-central deployments should also be kept offline until patches are released, the company says.

“N-able Engineering continues to make progress on the N-central hotfix and associated validation activities. The work remains on track with no setbacks, and our teams are progressing as quickly as possible while maintaining the validation required for a safe remediation,” the company said.

N-able also pointed out that it has no evidence that the vulnerabilities have been exploited against its N-central environments.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The zero-day bugs were published on GitHub on Sunday by security researcher Sean Bales and have yet to be assigned CVE identifiers. Bales dubbed the flaws Able2Shell.

According to the researcher, the weaknesses could be exploited to achieve remote code execution (RCE) with ‘nable’ or root privileges, to execute arbitrary commands, create unauthorized administrative accounts, or leak sensitive data, such as configurations and credentials.

Additionally, Bales describes four exploit chains that could also lead to RCE with ‘nable’ or root privileges.

The security researcher released proof-of-concept (PoC) code targeting every flaw and reportedly explained that the zero-days were dropped after N-able failed to patch security defects he previously reported in another product.

articles.title: Anthropic sharpens AI coding and security capabilities with Mythos 5.2
articles.context: However, Claude Enterprise customers can use the model’s vulnerability detection capabilities through Claude Security without joining those programs, the company said
articles.full_text:
Anthropic has introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, claiming significant improvements in handling complex software engineering tasks while cutting API prices by 20% compared with the previous versions.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model but have different safeguards. Fable is broadly available, while direct access to Mythos is restricted to vetted cybersecurity and life sciences organizations to limit potential misuse.

The models are both priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50, respectively. Anthropic said the newer versions can generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors.

The company reported substantial gains in coding performance. Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% on the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark at its Xhigh effort setting, compared with 32.4% for Fable 5.1. The benchmark assesses whether maintainers of open-source projects would accept AI-generated changes to their code.

Performance and costs could entice enterprises

The models’ improved performance and lower prices could make long-running AI agents viable for software migrations and scientific research, according to Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at Omdia. Higher task completion rates could further reduce deployment costs, he said.

Anthropic said Fable 5.2 at its “High effort” setting achieved a coding benchmark score comparable to Opus 5.5 at its highest setting, at roughly half the cost per task. The comparison suggests that Fable could be more economical for some demanding assignments, although the savings would depend on the workload and effort setting.

“Anthropic has cut the price of a token, not the price of a thought,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research. He urged CIOs to treat AI processing effort as a budget consideration and measure costs against successfully completed tasks.

Anthropic also recommends Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge work, with Fable and Mythos intended for more demanding assignments.

Reliability challenges persist

In an internal experiment, an Anthropic engineer tasked Fable 5.2 with building a prototype operating system. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced software that could boot on a laptop.

Su said the improvements bring enterprises closer to highly autonomous software development, although widespread deployment will depend on addressing persistent operational limitations.

“Reliability remains an issue without human supervision,” Su said.

Coordinating multiple AI agents across enterprise tools and internal teams also remains difficult, he added. Organizations will need to monitor agent activity and run these systems in appropriately isolated environments. Critical changes should remain subject to human approval, with sufficient visibility into agent behavior to support audits.

Pareekh Jain, CEO of Pareekh Consulting, said complex legacy systems and the need to meet business requirements could limit how much software development enterprises can delegate to AI agents.

Faster vulnerability discovery raises concerns

Anthropic said Mythos 5.2 identified 89.6% of vulnerabilities in its internal CVE Rediscovery evaluation, compared with 78.3% for Mythos 5.1.

Conducted against 1,829 previously disclosed vulnerabilities, the test assessed whether models could independently rediscover flaws in software snapshots taken before the vulnerabilities were fixed. The company said Mythos 5.2 was also better at reproducing vulnerabilities and developing fixes.

Anthropic has restricted direct access to Mythos 5.2 through its verification programs. However, Claude Enterprise customers can use the model’s vulnerability detection capabilities through Claude Security without joining those programs, the company said.

According to Su, “Mythos 5.2 shifts the balance towards defenders in controlled enterprise settings.”

Jain, however, cautioned that advances in AI-powered vulnerability discovery could also help attackers identify software weaknesses more quickly. “This creates an AI-powered race between attackers and defenders,” he said.

Data retention raises compliance questions

Anthropic said customers eligible for zero data retention can continue using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 under those arrangements, while other customers face 30-day retention for safety monitoring.

The company has also introduced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, currently in private beta, which allows automated safety monitoring to run on prompts and responses stored within customers’ infrastructure.

Gogia said data retention requirements could outweigh the benefits of lower API prices for regulated enterprises. He urged procurement teams to obtain written confirmation of zero-retention arrangements before deploying the models for sensitive workloads.

The article originally appeared on InfoWorld.

articles.title: Binance Investigates ShinyHunters Breach Claims
articles.context: 3bn in virtual currency from Binance after a months-long, multi-stage attack that involved fake job interviews and zero-day malware
articles.full_text:
Binance is actively investigating claims from a notorious extortion group that it has obtained 335 million customer records.

ShinyHunters posted an ad on PwsForums on November 4 claiming it was selling 335.9 million lines of records including private key wallets, user account passwords, transaction histories, email addresses and phone numbers, internal infrastructure information, KYC data including ID cards and passports, and “crypto assets in Binance’s hot wallet.”

It also demanded $900,000 from the cryptocurrency exchange, claiming it had two remaining choices: “pay or leak.”

However, a message sent to a Binance user by the firm’s customer support account on X said that, based on the sample information and the description of the data “this appears likely to be a scam rather than evidence of a Binance systems breach.”

Read more on ShinyHunters: ShinyHunters Claim Hack of Rival Ransomware Gang Clop

“We have found no evidence that Binance systems, customer KYC data, account credentials, wallet private keys, or internal infrastructure information were compromised in connection with this listing,” the message continued.

“Several aspects of this claim are inconsistent with how Binance stores and protects user data: Binance does not store user passwords in plaintext; Binance does not hold private keys for users’ external wallets; and the listing references jurisdictions where Binance no longer operates.”

Binance said that listings similar to this that have appeared in the past were often the result of infostealer malware installed on victims’ devices rather than a breach of the firm’s systems.

However, it urged users to be on the lookout for follow-on phishing attempts seeking passwords, 2FA codes, seed phrases and private keys.

Laundering Activity Continues

In the meantime, Binance continues to deal with the fallout from a huge theft of cryptocurrency from its platform by North Korean actors at the end of October.

The TraderTraitor group stole around $6.3bn in virtual currency from Binance after a months-long, multi-stage attack that involved fake job interviews and zero-day malware.

The group is now trying to launder the stolen funds by creating meme coins to disguise money flows, according to blockchain investigators.

“Anyone can create a new crypto token, and thousands of new tokens appear every day. Most are meme coins: tokens built around a joke, an animal or a celebrity, and traded on hype rather than any underlying use,” explained Elliptic chief scientist and co-founder, Tom Robinson.

“The launderers' tokens are made to be used once and thrown away. Nobody outside the laundering operation buys them, and their price is whatever the launderers choose to set. That makes them useful as a container, allowing stolen funds to go in on one side of a liquidity pool and come out on the other.”

Image credit: miss.cabul / Shutterstock.com

articles.title: When everything is a threat, nothing feels safe
articles.context: A vulnerability described as critical does not necessarily create the same level of risk for every business
articles.full_text:
When you leave home, you lock the door. When you get into the car, you fasten your seat belt. These are familiar safety habits. We understand their purpose, know how to perform them and rarely need to stop and think about them.

Our digital lives are different. We shop, bank, work and keep in touch with family and friends online, often without clear signs of where a danger begins or which precaution matters most. We receive a steady stream of warnings about new scams, stolen credentials, data breaches and software vulnerabilities. The messages vary in urgency, but many seem to demand our immediate attention.

The result can be an uncomfortable contradiction: information intended to make us safer can also leave us overwhelmed and less willing to act.

In conversations with people inside and outside the technology field, I keep hearing variations of the same concerns. There is a new scam every week, and no way to keep up. If major companies can be breached, how can an individual protect themselves? Almost anything done online seems risky.

These are reasonable questions. As a cybersecurity professional, I believe our response should go beyond repeating that threats exist. We need to help people understand which risks are relevant, what they can do about them and where their responsibility ends.

When a warning becomes background noise

There are good reasons to monitor the threat landscape. Criminals adapt their techniques, fraud schemes evolve and vulnerabilities sometimes require urgent remediation. Ignoring those developments is not a sensible strategy.

But a threat’s existence is not the same as a person’s or organization’s exposure to it. A vulnerability described as critical does not necessarily create the same level of risk for every business. The answer depends on which products are in use, whether affected systems are exposed, what safeguards are already in place and the potential business impact.

A critical flaw in technology that an organization does not use may be worth noting without requiring emergency action. A less dramatic issue affecting a business-critical, internet-facing service could deserve immediate attention. The headline alone cannot make that distinction.

Yet headlines are often how people encounter cybersecurity. When warnings arrive without context, prioritization or practical guidance, they compete for a limited amount of attention. What should be exceptional starts to feel routine. An alert that genuinely requires action may disappear into the noise.

There is a meaningful difference between staying informed and feeling compelled to remain on high alert every moment of the day.

Security fatigue is not simply a lack of interest

Researchers have a name for part of this experience: security fatigue. In a 2016 qualitative study, researchers at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) interviewed 40 everyday computer users about security and privacy. Signs of fatigue appeared in 25 interviews, even though fatigue was not the study’s initial focus.

Participants described frustration with repeated requirements and advice, along with feelings of resignation and diminished control. The researchers connected these experiences with decision avoidance, choosing the easiest option available, and disregarding protective guidance. The study was small and qualitative, so it should not be treated as a measure of how widespread fatigue is today. Its value lies in explaining behavior that security teams may otherwise label as carelessness.

When someone dismisses yet another warning, they may not be indifferent to security. They may simply have lost the ability to tell what matters, what is urgent and what action is expected of them.

This distinction matters for security leaders. If every message is marked urgent, we should not be surprised when urgency stops working. More warnings are not automatically better communication.

Replace headline volume with decision criteria

I do not believe people need to memorize every new phishing technique or follow every vulnerability disclosure to practice sound digital security. Nor is it sustainable for security teams to treat every issue as equally important.

A better approach starts with three questions whenever a new alert appears:

1. Does this affect me or my organization? Is the alert about a service, device, account or process I use or oversee?

2. Does it require action now? Is there credible guidance and a concrete reason for urgency, or is this general information about a possible threat?

3. What is the most effective action available to me? Should I install an update, verify an unusual request through another channel, enable a safeguard or notify the appropriate team?

This is not a guarantee of safety. It is a way to separate useful information from noise and preserve attention for decisions that matter.

For individuals, a consistent baseline is more valuable than trying to recognize the scam of the week: keep devices and applications updated, use long and unique passwords with a password manager, enable multifactor authentication and verify requests that demand immediate action or sensitive information. These habits are easy to describe, even if implementing them sometimes requires help.

For organizations, the equivalent is a risk-based process that connects alerts to actual assets, exposure, business priorities and clear owners. A security bulletin should answer who is affected, what the organization knows, what needs to happen and by when. When no action is required, saying so is also useful.

The burden cannot rest entirely on users

It would be unfair to finish this discussion by giving people another long list of obligations. If staying secure requires every employee to interpret technical warnings, navigate confusing settings and make the correct choice every time, the design of the system is part of the problem.

Organizations and technology providers should make secure behavior easier by default. That includes sensible protective settings, automated updates where appropriate, effective filtering, straightforward reporting channels and clear instructions when a real decision is necessary. It also means preparing for mistakes through detection, response and recovery rather than assuming flawless human behavior.

NIST’s work on human-centered cybersecurity makes a similar case: systems and guidance should account for people’s actual needs, capabilities and limitations. The goal is to make safe actions easier to take in practice, not merely to issue more instructions.

Security leaders can put that principle to work by reviewing the warnings employees receive. Are several teams sending overlapping messages about the same threat? Do alerts explain the action and its owner? Are we asking employees to solve problems that technical control could prevent? Can people report a suspicious message without fearing blame?

These questions recognize that user behavior matters, but it always takes place within a system that can support or undermine good decisions.

Build awareness through confidence

I want security awareness to treat people as partners, not as the weakest link to be frightened into compliance. Good risk communication should explain why something matters, whom it affects and what realistic next step is available. It should also be able to say when there is no reason to panic.

Confidence does not mean assuming nothing will go wrong. It means understanding the most relevant risks, knowing which protections are in place and knowing where to turn when something unusual happens.

We should therefore be careful about how we measure awareness. The number of alerts distributed, or training messages delivered tells us little about whether people can act on what they have learned. I would rather ask a more demanding question: After receiving our guidance, are people better equipped to make a sound decision?

If the answer is no, we need to change how we communicate cybersecurity.

Awareness should not be about frightening people. It should provide knowledge, a sense of control and practical ways to act.

articles.title: Google patches eighth Chrome zero-day exploited in attacks this year
articles.context: Google has released emergency security updates to patch a new Chrome vulnerability exploited in zero-day attacks, the eighth such flaw since the start of the year
articles.full_text:
Google has released emergency security updates to patch a new Chrome vulnerability exploited in zero-day attacks, the eighth such flaw since the start of the year.

"Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said in a Monday security advisory.

As Google explained, this flaw stems from a Use-After-Free (UAF) weakness in the XML component of the Google Chrome web browser, which occurs when the browser's XML parser processes data, deletes an object from the computer's memory, but fails to clear the pointer referencing that object.

Attackers can exploit this high-severity memory corruption vulnerability when the browser later tries to use or read that "freed" memory space to manipulate the memory layout and execute malicious code.

While Google has found evidence of attackers exploiting this zero-day bug in the wild, it has not shared additional details about these incidents.

"Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix. We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed," it noted.

Google has now fixed the zero-day for users in the Stable Desktop channel, with new versions rolling out to Windows, macOS (157.0.8103.50/.51), and Linux users (157.0.8103.50). Although Google says the security update could take days or weeks to reach all Chrome users, it was available immediately when BleepingComputer checked for updates today.

If you don't want to update the web browser manually, you can also let Chrome check for updates on its own, as it will automatically install them after the next launch.

​Since the start of the year, Google has addressed seven other actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities:

An iterator invalidation bug (CVE-2026-2441) in CSSFontFeatureValuesMap (Chrome's implementation of CSS font feature values), which Google addressed in mid-February.

Two other Chrome zero-day bugs exploited in attacks were patched in March: an out-of-bounds write weakness in the Skia 2D graphics library (CVE-2026-3909), and an inappropriate implementation vulnerability in the V8 JavaScript and WebAssembly engine (CVE-2026-3910).

A use-after-free weakness in Dawn (CVE-2026-5281), the underlying cross-platform implementation of the WebGPU standard used by the Chromium project, which Google patched in April.

An out-of-bounds read and write vulnerability in Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine (CVE-2026-11645), exploited in the wild and patched in June.

And out-of-bounds write (CVE-2026-87491) and type confusion (CVE-2026-85046) flaws in the V8 JavaScript engine, fixed in September.

Google fixed eight more zero-days exploited in attacks in 2025, many of them reported by the company's Threat Analysis Group (TAG), which tracks zero-day exploits used in spyware attacks.

articles.title: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 Beats GPT-6 Cyber in Multi-Stage Cyberattack Benchmark
articles.context: Average success rates were 97% in vulnerability research and exploitation, 98% in network attack simulation, and 63% in evasion
articles.full_text:
Anthropic on Monday released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models, which it said exhibit improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision.

During pre-release training, the large language models (LLMs) helped its engineers "complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours."

The artificial intelligence (AI) company said high-stakes risks arising from misalignment remain low, and claimed the models matched or performed better than Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most alignment measures, resistance to misuse, honesty, and factuality.

"It was roughly an order of magnitude less likely than Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 to publish harmful content to public package registries without encouragement, though it still did so when encouraged by the simulated user," Anthropic noted in its system card.

On Irregular's CyScenarioBench, which measures whether a model can plan and execute a multi-stage cyber operation in a realistic environment, Fable 5.2 completed 76.3% of all challenges, compared to 61.7% for Fable 5.1 and 61% for OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber.

In a pair of reports published over the last month, Irregular said Google's Gemini 4 Argon solved 12 challenges in the subset of the CyScenarioBench suite end to end, up from 5 for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and none for Gemini 3.1 Pro.

"On CyScenarioBench, GPT-6 Cyber completed 11 of 11 long-horizon scenarios at least once, compared with 8 of 11 for GPT-6 Astra. Its average success rate was 61%, an increase of 7 percentage points," the AI testing lab said. "On Atomic Challenges, GPT-6 Cyber solved all 22 challenges. Average success rates were 97% in vulnerability research and exploitation, 98% in network attack simulation, and 63% in evasion."

Fable 5.2 also scored 89.6% on the CVE Rediscovery benchmark, Anthropic's own internal evaluation of whether an AI model can independently rediscover known vulnerabilities given only the affected source code. The assessment includes 1,829 advisories for open-source projects published in October 2026.

Describing Claude Mythos 5.2 as its "most capable model for cybersecurity engineering," Anthropic said it can flag more vulnerabilities than prior models, while simultaneously getting better at reproducing and fixing them.

As before, the model's cyber capabilities are accessible through its Cyber Verification Program. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.

The development comes as Anthropic updated Claude Security with continuous code scanning and automatic fix tracking to help security teams monitor and address vulnerabilities as code changes.

"Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project's threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what's actually reachable first," Anthropic said.

articles.title: Fireworks AI discloses new breach after cloud provider hack
articles.context: After revoking compromised internal credentials, affected Fireworks API keys, and keys created by the attackers, Fireworks discovered another security incident on October 23
articles.full_text:
AI infrastructure startup Fireworks has disclosed a new security breach in which attackers accessed its development machines after breaching a third-party cloud provider.

FireWorks provides a high-performance inference platform for developers who want to deploy and run open-source artificial intelligence models (such as Mistral, Meta's Llama, or Google's Gemma) without worrying about hardware bottlenecks and complex infrastructure tasks.

The company notified law enforcement and customers of another security incident in early October after attackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts.

"The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to Large Language Models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways, known as 'LLMJacking'," Fireworks said at the time.

After revoking compromised internal credentials, affected Fireworks API keys, and keys created by the attackers, Fireworks discovered another security incident on October 23.

In the new breach, the threat actors accessed resource metadata (e.g., Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation time), billing information (e.g., billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage), and incomplete model weights and datasets for some customers.

However, the company said the attackers couldn't access customer payment card numbers because Fireworks doesn't store them.

"A third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks R&D machines experienced a security incident on October 23. On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," Fireworks noted in a Monday advisory.

"We detected this activity on the same day, and followed our incident response processes to take immediate remediation measures and close known critical vulnerabilities. As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use."

Since the attack, Fireworks revoked and replaced credentials and service accounts, restricted unauthorized network pathways, isolated affected systems, and tightened access to data storage and analytics systems to block public or unauthorized access to stored data.

The company is now working with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 incident response division to secure its systems against future attacks and further investigate the incident's full scope and impact.

One week ago, researchers at Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant reported that large language model hijacking attacks (also known as LLMjacking) are driving record costs for compromised organizations, with cloud AI charges reaching as high as $1 million due to fraudulent calls using stolen API keys.
