articles.title: Hackers Compromise Ethersphere's bee-js and Swarm Desktop to Deliver Wallet-Stealing Malware
articles.context: The macOS app was signed with the project's Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS displayed only its normal first-launch prompt, the firm found
articles.full_text:
Attackers used the Ethersphere project's own release automation to publish malicious versions of two of its tools for the Swarm decentralized storage network: bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2.

Both releases download and run code built to steal the wallet key that Swarm Desktop keeps for its node, along with the stored password that unlocks it. The code is also built to install a backdoor on Windows, macOS, and Linux machines.

The bee-js package is the JavaScript library behind Swarm Desktop and the swarm-cli command-line tool. Swarm Desktop runs a Swarm node on a user's own computer and saves the node's private keys there.

Both malicious releases have been taken down, and the project's maintainers released a clean Swarm Desktop update today. Neither step removes a backdoor already installed nor protects a key already sent. No theft of funds had been reported at the time of writing.

Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 appeared on GitHub at about 00:36 UTC today and was withdrawn about 8.5 hours later. The app's built-in updater could offer it to Windows x64 computers and Apple Silicon Macs within about 10 minutes, according to an incident analysis by Socket, a supply chain security firm. Intel Macs were never offered it, and Linux installs do not update automatically.

The bee-js release, version 13.3.0, was the latest version on npm for about 75 minutes, from 00:09 to 01:25 UTC today. Its code runs as a postinstall script, which npm executes automatically during installation unless install scripts are disabled. A project did not need to import the library for the code to run.

The project's own swarm-cli and bee-dashboard packages, and the Swarm Desktop source code, accepted version ranges that included 13.3.0. A fresh install within that window could have pulled in the malicious version.

None of the reports gave a count of infected machines. The firm's rough estimate is that bee-js 13.3.0 was downloaded about 10 times, including by security scanners and mirrors. Swarm Desktop 0.56.2's download count reached 65 by 08:27 UTC, including researchers.

Ethersphere's maintainers withdrew 0.56.2 and replaced it today with a clean release, version 0.56.3. In the change that set up the new release, one of them wrote that 0.56.2 "was published by an attacker using stolen CI credentials and has been withdrawn."

Version 0.56.3 is the same code as the previous version, 0.56.1, signed with a newly issued Developer ID certificate, according to that maintainer's incident note. The note says the app's auto-updater will move installs of 0.56.2 to it, although Linux packages still need to be replaced by hand. A comparison of the two versions' source code by The Hacker News found no changes beyond the version number and release notes.

When The Hacker News checked npm today, 13.2.0 was again the latest bee-js version, and 13.3.0 could no longer be downloaded from the registry.

What to Do

The GitHub advisory for bee-js 13.3.0 says: "Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised." SafeDep, a software supply chain security company, offers the same advice for any computer on which Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 was installed.

If you use bee-js in a project or CI job:

Search lockfiles, package caches, internal registries, and CI install logs for @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0, including copies pulled in by other packages.

Pin 13.2.0, and clear cached copies of 13.3.0, including any npm mirror you install through.

If 13.3.0 was installed with install scripts turned on, treat that machine or CI runner as compromised, even if the install log shows no errors. The code hides its own network errors.

From a clean computer, rotate every password, token, and key that the installing user or CI job could read.

If you run Swarm Desktop:

Look for the line Bee Desktop version: 0.56.2 (production) in the app's log file, bee-desktop.log. Version 0.56.2 is written at every launch, just before the malicious code runs.

The log folder is ~/Library/Logs/Swarm Desktop/ on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Swarm Desktop\Log\ on Windows, and ~/.local/state/Swarm Desktop/ on Linux.

Install 0.56.3. On Linux, replace the package by hand.

If 0.56.2 ever ran, treat the node's key and password as stolen. From a clean computer, move the node's funds, chequebook, and stake to a new key.

On any machine where the code ran:

Remove the ~/.solidity/ folder, the solidity-langsupport-runner.service user service on Linux, the com.solidity.langsupport.runner LaunchAgent on macOS, and the ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df) service on Windows.

Updating, reinstalling, or removing the app or package does not remove them.

Where possible, rebuild the machine from a trusted image instead of cleaning it in place.

How the Malware Works

Both releases carry the same loader, SafeDep found in its technical analysis. It is a few lines of code that download more code from api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and run it with the user's permissions. In bee-js the loader is the postinstall script, and in Swarm Desktop it runs each time the app starts.

The downloaded code looks for two files in Swarm Desktop's data folder: config.yaml and data-dir/keys/swarm.key. If both are there, it sends them to the attackers' server.

The key file is an encrypted Ethereum keystore, but Swarm Desktop keeps its password in plain text in config.yaml. With both files, the attackers can take the node wallet's xDAI and xBZZ tokens, its chequebook funds, and its stake, the company says.

The downloaded code also installs a backdoor. On Linux and macOS, it is a Go remote shell called evjawbreaker, saved in a hidden ~/.solidity folder. It runs in the background as a user service on Linux and as a LaunchAgent on macOS.

The shell reads the address of its control server from an Ethereum smart contract, so the attackers can change that address at any time. They had updated it 29 minutes before the malicious bee-js code was added.

On Windows, the downloaded code installs a genuine ScreenConnect remote-access client, signed by its maker, ConnectWise. The client runs as a system service and connects to the attackers' relay.

If the user is an administrator, the code gets administrator rights through a known way around the User Account Control prompt. If not, it shows the prompt again whenever the user cancels. With those rights, it adds a Microsoft Defender exclusion and installs the client silently.

How the Releases Got Out

Both releases came from bee-worker, the account Ethersphere uses to automate its releases. Neither change was signed nor submitted as a pull request.

For bee-js, the attackers published a GitHub release for the new version, which started the project's npm publishing workflow. That workflow needed no approval and published the package to npm in 73 seconds, according to Socket.

Because the project's real workflow built it, the package carried valid provenance, the record that links an npm package to the repository and workflow that built it. Provenance shows where a package was built, not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it.

For Swarm Desktop, the attackers manually started a build workflow that had the project's Apple and Windows signing certificates and needed no approval. The macOS app was signed with the project's Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS displayed only its normal first-launch prompt, the firm found.

The maintainers have since made the app's signing jobs wait for approval from the project's DevOps team and run only from the main branch.

How the attackers gained access remained unclear at the time of writing. The maintainer's incident note blames the theft of CI credentials and secrets.

The firm's analysis indicates that two GitHub accounts were used: bee-worker and a long-time maintainer's account. None of the reports explained how the credentials were stolen.

Links to Earlier Attacks

The payloads share an Ethereum contract, a ScreenConnect relay, and file names with fake extensions for Solidity developers that appeared on the Open VSX marketplace in September. Researchers at Pluto Security described those extensions in their October 1 EtherDuck analysis.

Pluto ties them "with high confidence" to the group behind the original SleepyDuck extension, which read its server address from a different Ethereum contract in 2025. Socket says the same group is behind the bee-js and Swarm Desktop releases.

Indicators of Compromise

Defenders can search logs and machines for the following.

Domain: api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz

URL path: /v1/analytics (bee-js loader)

URL path: /v1/electron (Swarm Desktop loader)

URL path: /v1/assets/ (further payloads)

URL path: /v1/swarm/report (stolen wallet files)

HTTP header: X-Ethersphere: 1

IP:port: 193[.]57[.]9[.]155:4912 (evjawbreaker control server)

IP:port: 185[.]232[.]84[.]169:8041 (ScreenConnect relay)

Ethereum contract: 0xf8a900Db50b3331be6B768bA460BB59f3E40C344

Path: ~/.solidity/

systemd unit: solidity-langsupport-runner.service

LaunchAgent: com.solidity.langsupport.runner

Service: ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df)

SHA-256: 9b73e7cd4e1425e770392549d8df46c706139ef476f4f7b9ac405165dc8d9696 (linux_amd64)

SHA-256: b601776817363b96295119f7221338a122d5247a35a77a64b04f286e1bbcc565 (linux_arm64)

articles.title: PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security
Simplify cross-partition access with AWS IAM outbound identity federation
articles.context: IAM integration – You control access with the same IAM roles, trust policies, and permissions policies you already use
articles.full_text:
You can now use tokens from AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) outbound federation to assume roles in other Amazon Web Services (AWS) partitions.

When your workloads run across AWS partitions such as Commercial, China, GovCloud (US), and European Sovereign Cloud, a workload in one partition might need to access resources or communicate with AWS services in another partition. AWS partitions are hard isolation boundaries with independent instances of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), so a credential issued in one partition isn’t valid in another. As a result, direct role assumption with sts:AssumeRole doesn’t work across partition boundaries and resource policies can’t reference principals that exist in another partition.

AWS IAM outbound identity federation already lets your workloads obtain a short-lived, AWS signed JSON Web Token (JWT) and use it to authenticate to external services. Today, we’re extending it with cross-partition support. Your workloads can now use that same mechanism to federate into another AWS partition. A workload in one partition obtains a short-lived JWT using sts:GetWebIdentityToken and exchanges it for temporary credentials in another partition using sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with no long-term credentials to store or rotate.

This post walks through configuring cross-partition identity federation using Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) data access as an example, but the same steps apply to any cross-partition API call.

Important: If your workload requires cross-partition access, consult your compliance team to make sure that your implementation aligns with your regulatory or compliance obligations. A non-exhaustive list of examples are FedRAMP, ITAR, DoD CC SRG, GDPR, and others.

Why use IAM outbound identity federation for cross-partition access?

IAM outbound identity federation provides several benefits, including:

Carry origin identity into authorization decisions – The destination trust policy can condition on the source identity’s context, its AWS account, organization ID (org_id), source AWS Region, and principal, so you authorize based on who and where the request originated, not only that a token is valid.

Cross-partition audit trail – AWS CloudTrail events in the destination Region include the source principal Amazon Resource Name (ARN), source Region, and a token ID that correlates back to the source Region’s GetWebIdentityToken CloudTrail event.

Temporary credentials end to end – Your workload authenticates with a short-lived, signed JWT and receives temporary credentials, so every stage of cross-partition access uses credentials that expire automatically.

Fully managed token infrastructure – AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) issues, signs, and publishes verification keys for the JWTs. You don’t need to implement a public key infrastructure (PKI) or host your own OpenID Provider.

IAM integration – You control access with the same IAM roles, trust policies, and permissions policies you already use. Destination accounts can condition on subject, audience, source Region, account, organization ID, and principal ID.

Session revocation – You can revoke credentials that have already been issued. Scope the revocation by origin or apply a deny on the destination role.

How cross-partition identity federation with IAM outbound identity federation works

Cross-partition identity federation works by obtaining a signed JWT from AWS STS in the source partition and exchanging that JWT for temporary credentials from AWS STS in the destination partition.

For example, a workload running in the AWS Govcloud (US) partition in the us-gov-west-1 Region can obtain a JWT and exchange it for temporary credentials valid in the AWS Commercial partition in the us-east-1 Region.

Architecture overview

The following diagram shows the elements and workflow used to support cross-partition access.

Figure 1: Cross-partition flow diagram

The cross-partition flow works as follows:

Token request – Your workload, running in a Region from the source partition calls sts:GetWebIdentityToken API.

Token issuance – AWS STS returns a short-lived, cryptographically signed JWT. The token contains claims that assert your workload’s AWS identity, including the account ID, the principal ARN, source Region, and more.

Token presentation – Your workload calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity on the AWS STS endpoint in a Region in the destination partition, passing the JWT as the web identity token and the ARN of the target role in the destination partition.

Fetch verification keys and metadata – AWS STS in the destination partition retrieves the public verification key from your OpenID Connect (OIDC) Issuer URL’s JWKS endpoint.

Validation: AWS STS in the destination partition verifies the token’s signature and evaluates the target role’s trust policy.

Return temporary credentials: AWS STS in the destination partition returns temporary credentials scoped by the policies attached to the role.

Cross-partition resource access – Your workload uses the temporary credentials to access resources in the destination partition, such as an S3 bucket.

Setting up cross-partition identity federation

In this walkthrough, we use the example of a workload running in the us-gov-west-1 Region that needs to access data in an S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region.

Prerequisites

For this walkthrough, you need the following:

Two AWS accounts: one in the source partition, AWS GovCloud (US), where the workload runs and one in the destination partition, AWS Commercial, that holds the data.

In the source account: an IAM principal with permissions to enable outbound web identity federation (iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation) and to call sts:GetWebIdentityToken to obtain a signed JWT representing its identity.

In the destination account: an IAM principal with permissions to register the source account’s issuer as an OIDC identity provider (iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider) and create an IAM role whose trust policy allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from that provider, conditioned on the token’s aud and sub claims.

An S3 bucket in the destination account that holds the data you want to access from the source partition.

A local installation of AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI)

So you can run and verify every step from your own command line, this walkthrough has you assume the workload role as the token-creating identity. In production, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, AWS Lambda function, or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (AWS EKS) Pod runs as that role automatically through its instance profile or execution role with no assume-role step.

Step 0: Configure credentials for the GovCloud and Commercial AWS CLI profiles

This walkthrough runs commands in two partitions, so configure a named AWS CLI profile for each. For example, GovCloudCredentials for the source account and CommercialCredentials for the destination. Use the --profile parameter matching the partition where you run each command. In this walkthrough we configure our profiles in the ~/.aws/config file:

[profile GovCloudCredentials] region = us-gov-west-1 # GovCloud account credentials / SSO [profile CommercialCredentials] region = us-east-1 # Commercial account credentials / SSO

Step 1: Enable outbound identity federation on the source account

Enable outbound identity federation on your GovCloud account to generate a unique issuer URL that hosts the OIDC discovery endpoint needed for cross-partition trust. This needs to be performed once in the source account.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation.

Run the following command.

aws iam enable-outbound-web-identity-federation --region us-gov-west-1 --profile GovCloudCredentials

Copy the issuer URL from the command output. For GovCloud, it looks like: https://<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws

Note: IAM has a single endpoint per partition. The --region parameter simply targets that partition’s IAM. Enabling outbound web identity federation is an account-wide setting, so you only need to run this once.

Step 2: Allow your IAM principal to generate JWTs in the source partition

Create an IAM policy that grants permission to call the sts:GetWebIdentityToken API and attach it to the IAM principal that will generate tokens. This example uses an IAM role.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:CreateRole and iam:PutRolePolicy.

Save the following trust policy to a file named workload-trust-policy.json. This policy controls who can assume the workload role; the role’s ARN is what becomes the token’s sub. So that you can run the walkthrough from the AWS CLI, we set the principal to the identity behind your AWS CLI profile. In production, set it to the compute service that runs your workload, for example "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" }, which removes the need to assume the role manually.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowCliRoleToAssume", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-cli-role>" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] }

Run the following command to create the workload role with the preceding trust policy:

aws iam create-role \ --role-name <your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --assume-role-policy-document file://workload-trust-policy.json \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --profile GovCloudCredentials

Save the following policy to a file named get-web-identity-token-policy.json. This policy grants permission to call sts:GetWebIdentityToken, with conditions that restrict the token audience and limit the token lifetime to 300 seconds:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowTokensForDestination", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sts:GetWebIdentityToken", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "ForAllValues:StringEquals": { "sts:IdentityTokenAudience": "<your-audience-name>" }, "Null": { "sts:IdentityTokenAudience": "false" }, "NumericLessThanEquals": { "sts:DurationSeconds": 300 }, "StringEquals": { "sts:SigningAlgorithm": "ES384" } } } ] }

Run the following command to attach the permissions policy to the role:

aws iam put-role-policy \ --role-name <your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --policy-name AllowGetWebIdentityToken \ --policy-document file://get-web-identity-token-policy.json \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --profile GovCloudCredentials

For the full detailed walkthrough of these steps, see Getting started with outbound identity federation.

Step 3: Configure trust in the destination account

Create an OIDC identity provider and a trust policy in your Commercial account using the issuer URL from Step 1.

Using the AWS CLI:

Ensure your IAM principal has permission to call iam:CreateOpenIDConnectProvider and iam:CreateRole.

Run the following command to register the source account’s issuer URL as an OIDC identity provider in the destination account:

aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider \ --url https://<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws \ --client-id-list "<your-audience-name>" \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Note: --thumbprint-list is optional; IAM retrieves the issuer’s certificate thumbprint automatically. Because the AWS STS issuer endpoint uses a certificate from a trusted certificate authority (CA), AWS validates it against its trusted root CAs.

Save the following trust policy to a file named trust-policy.json. This policy allows the role to be assumed only with tokens matching the expected audience and originating from us-gov-west-1:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowTrustedGovCloudSourceRole", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:oidc-provider/<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:sub": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:aud": "<your-audience-name>", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:source_region": "us-gov-west-1", "<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws:org_id": "<your-source-org-id>" } } } ] }

Run the following command to create the role with the preceding trust policy:

aws iam create-role \ --role-name <your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Run the following command to attach a permissions policy granting access to the destination S3 bucket:

aws iam attach-role-policy \ --role-name <your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:policy/<your-s3-access-policy> \ --region us-east-1 \ --profile CommercialCredentials

Step 4: Cross-partition resource access

With the setup complete, your workload requests a JWT from the source partition, exchanges it for temporary credentials in the destination partition, and uses those credentials to access the S3 bucket.

Using the AWS CLI:

Assume the workload role. In production your workload already runs as this role through its instance profile or execution role, so it skips this step. To trace the flow from the AWS CLI, assume the workload role so the token you create carries that role as its sub. This command uses jq to parse the JSON:

WORKLOAD_CREDS=$(aws sts assume-role \ --role-arn arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name> \ --role-session-name trace-cross-partition \ --region us-gov-west-1 --profile GovCloudCredentials) export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.AccessKeyId') export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SecretAccessKey') export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo "$WORKLOAD_CREDS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SessionToken')

Create the signed JWT from AWS STS and capture it as a variable:

WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN=$(aws sts get-web-identity-token \ --audience "<your-audience-name>" \ --signing-algorithm ES384 \ --duration-seconds 300 \ --region us-gov-west-1 \ --query WebIdentityToken --output text)

Run the following command to exchange the JWT for temporary credentials in the destination partition:

CREDENTIALS=$(aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name> \ --role-session-name <your-session-name> \ --web-identity-token "$WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN" \ --region us-east-1)

Export the temporary credentials from the output:

export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.AccessKeyId') export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SecretAccessKey') export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=$(echo "$CREDENTIALS" | jq -r '.Credentials.SessionToken')

Run the following command to transfer data from the destination S3 bucket:

aws s3 cp s3://<destination(us-east-1)-bucket>/data.csv ./data.csv --region us-east-1

For applications, the following AWS SDK for Python example creates a session that handles the token exchange and refreshes the credentials automatically:

import boto3 import botocore.session from botocore import UNSIGNED from botocore.config import Config from botocore.credentials import DeferredRefreshableCredentials def cross_partition_session(role_arn, audience, source_region, dest_region, session_name="cross-partition-session", duration_seconds=300, signing_algorithm="ES384", source_session=None): ''' This helper method creates a self-refreshing boto3 session object using IAM outbound federation. ''' source_session = source_session or boto3.Session() source_sts = source_session.client("sts", region_name=source_region) dest_sts = boto3.client("sts", region_name=dest_region, config=Config(signature_version=UNSIGNED)) def refresh(): token = source_sts.get_web_identity_token( Audience=[audience], SigningAlgorithm=signing_algorithm, DurationSeconds=duration_seconds, )["WebIdentityToken"] creds = dest_sts.assume_role_with_web_identity( RoleArn=role_arn, RoleSessionName=session_name, WebIdentityToken=token, )["Credentials"] return { "access_key": creds["AccessKeyId"], "secret_key": creds["SecretAccessKey"], "token": creds["SessionToken"], "expiry_time": creds["Expiration"].isoformat(), } botocore_sess = botocore.session.get_session() botocore_sess._credentials = DeferredRefreshableCredentials( refresh_using=refresh, method="cross-partition-identity-federation") return boto3.Session(botocore_session=botocore_sess, region_name=dest_region) # Build a cross-partition session, then use it like any other boto3 session. # Credentials refresh automatically as they near expiry, no manual re-minting. session = cross_partition_session( role_arn="arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<destination-role>", audience="<your-audience>", source_region="us-gov-west-1", dest_region="us-east-1", ) # Confirm which identity we're operating as in the destination partition. print(session.client("sts").get_caller_identity()["Arn"]) # Use the session for real work, e.g. read an object from the destination bucket. session.client("s3").download_file("<destination-bucket>", "data.csv", "data.csv")

Security best practices

We recommend the following best practices for cross-partition access using IAM outbound identity federation.

Principle of least privilege – Grant only the minimum permissions needed in the destination partition role. Scope to specific resources and actions.

Use condition keys – In the source account, restrict token audience and duration through IAM policy conditions. In the destination trust policy, use the aud and sub conditions to control which tokens can assume which roles.

Short token lifetimes – Use the shortest practical duration.

Monitor with CloudTrail – Enable CloudTrail in both accounts. The source GetWebIdentityToken event records responseElements.webIdentityTokenId, and the destination AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event records the same value as requestParameters.webIdentityTokenId alongside the source principal ARN and source Region. Matching those two fields correlates access end-to-end across partitions.

Verify compliance – Consult your compliance team to ensure cross-partition data movement meets regulatory requirements.

Access Path – Access should be initiated from the more restrictive partition to the less restrictive partition.

Controlling cross-partition access by origin

Cross-partition federation is not enabled by default. You enable it at an AWS account level and configure a federation provider. Once enabled, you can control the providers that are allowed to federate in. The condition key aws:FederatedProvider can be used to restrict which federation provider or partitions are allowed, or to deny API calls from credentials federated from a source account or provider. A new condition key introduced with this release, aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion can be used to deny API calls federated from a source Region.

Allowlist approved origins

To constrain which origins can federate in, apply an RCP on sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Because RCPs are deny-only, you express an allowlist as a deny on anything outside your approved set, enforced before any credentials are issued.

Note that sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is used by all OIDC federation such as GitHub Actions, Amazon EKS, and others, not just cross-partition. Each policy pairs the allowlist with a StringLike that matches any IAM outbound identity federation issuer (*.tokens.sts.*), so the deny applies only to cross-partition federation and leaves your other OIDC providers untouched. The following two examples demonstrate allowing specific issuers or partitions:

Allowlist trusted issuers. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringNotLike on the OIDC provider ARN to deny federation from any issuer outside your approved set.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowlistApprovedIssuer", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.*" }, "StringNotLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": [ "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/<issuer-host>" ] } } } ] }

Allowlist a partition. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringNotLike on the issuer domain to deny federation from any partition you have not approved, without enumerating individual issuer ARNs. Include any cross-partition issuer you want to allow in the policy.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowlistApprovedPartition", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.*" }, "StringNotLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": [ "arn:*:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" ] } } } ] }

Use policy to control or revoke access after role assumption

Because AWS authorizes requests against the policies in effect, a deny on either key stops in-flight sessions on their next API call. The following examples use an SCP and give you three levers, from one issuer up to an entire partition:

Deny one issuer. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringEquals on the OIDC provider ARN to deny every API call made with credentials federated from a single source account.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySessionsFromSourceIssuer", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:oidc-provider/<unique-id>.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" } } } ] }

Deny one Region. Use the new aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion condition key to deny every API call made with credentials whose originating JWT was created in a specific source Region.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySourceRegion", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:CrossPartitionSourceRegion": "us-gov-west-1" } } } ] }

Deny whole partition. Use aws:FederatedProvider with StringLike on the issuer domain to deny every API call made with credentials federated from an entire source partition, without enumerating OIDC ARNs or Regions.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenySourcePartition", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "aws:FederatedProvider": "arn:aws:iam::*:oidc-provider/*.tokens.sts.us-gov.api.aws" } } } ] }

You can also attach a policy directly to the role in the destination partition to revoke access. For more information, see Deny access to all IAM role sessions associated with a role.

Auditing cross-partition access with CloudTrail

The source partition logs a GetWebIdentityToken event when the JWT is issued, and the destination partition logs an AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event when the token is exchanged for temporary credentials, both carrying the same JWT ID (webIdentityTokenId). Matching that ID lets you trace and audit a single token from issuance in one partition to its exchange for AWS STS credentials in the other. In the following sample pair of CloudTrail log entries, the cross-partition calls were made from an EC2 instance using its instance role.

Source partition:

{ "eventName": "GetWebIdentityToken", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventTime": "2026-09-10T18:33:01Z", "awsRegion": "us-gov-west-1", "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "arn": "arn:aws-us-gov:sts::<source-account-id>:assumed-role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>/<instance-id>" }, "requestParameters": { "audience": ["<your-audience-name>"], "durationSeconds": 300, "signingAlgorithm": "ES384" }, "responseElements": { "webIdentityTokenId": "6318f9f3-bccf-4d00-8e77-920e810f395c", "expiration": "2026-09-10T18:38:01Z" } }

webIdentityTokenId: The unique identifier on the source partition that correlates this event to the destination AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity CloudTrail event.

Destination partition:

{ "eventName": "AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventTime": "2026-09-10T18:33:01Z", "awsRegion": "us-east-1", "requestParameters": { "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<destination-account-id>:role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name>", "roleSessionName": "<your-session-name>", "webIdentityTokenId": "6318f9f3-bccf-4d00-8e77-920e810f395c", }, "responseElements": { "subjectFromWebIdentityToken": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "audience": "<your-audience-name>", "assumedRoleUser": { "arn": "arn:aws:sts::<destination-account-id>:assumed-role/<your-destination-partition-iam-role-name>/<your-session-name>" } }, "additionalEventData": { "crossPartitionData": { "sourcePrincipalArn": "arn:aws-us-gov:iam::<source-account-id>:role/<your-source-partition-iam-role-name>", "sourceRegion": "us-gov-west-1" } } }

sourcePrincipalArn: The IAM principal that obtained the JWT in the source Region.

sourceRegion: The Region where the JWT was issued.

webIdentityTokenData: The unique identifier on the destination partition that correlates this event to the source GetWebIdentityToken CloudTrail event.

Availability and pricing

Cross-partition IAM outbound identity federation is available in all Regions within the AWS Commercial (aws), China (aws-cn), GovCloud (US) (aws-us-gov), and European Sovereign Cloud (aws-eusc) partitions, at no additional cost. Note that same-partition identity federation isn’t supported with IAM outbound identity federation; for cross-account access within a single partition, use sts:AssumeRole.

Alternative option for cross-partition access

Organizations that already operate a public key infrastructure (PKI) can also use IAM Roles Anywhere to give workloads access across partitions. IAM Roles Anywhere can use your existing certificate authority (CA) or AWS Private Certificate Authority to issue and manage x.509 certificates to specific workloads and applications. To learn more about this alternative, see the blog post Transfer data across AWS partitions with IAM Roles Anywhere.

Conclusion

Cross-partition identity federation gives your workloads a way to reach across AWS partition boundaries without storing or rotating long-term credentials. Short-lived JWTs handle authentication at every stage, and standard IAM roles handle authorization, so the security model is consistent with what you already use inside a single partition. Cross-partition identity federation operates exclusively across AWS partition boundaries. Same-partition federation isn’t supported using IAM outbound identity federation. To learn more, see Federating AWS identities across AWS partitions in the IAM User Guide.

Partitions are isolation boundaries by design with independent IAM instances and separate credentialed access between Regions in different partitions. Treat cross-partition access as an exception and before you establish any, confirm it’s permitted under your regulatory, compliance, and security requirements. For more detail on partitions as a fault isolation boundary, see AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries and Meeting data residency requirements on AWS.

Bill Wells

Bill is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS with over 20 years of IT experience that began in the U.S. Air Force. Drawing on a diverse background across multiple organizations, Bill specializes in architecting secure, compliance-aligned cloud solutions that help federal partners achieve mission outcomes with AWS.

Nithin Jayakar Padala

Nithin is a Software Development Engineer on the AWS IAM team. He works on the core identity systems behind the temporary credentials that customers rely on for short-term access to AWS services at massive scale. He enjoys working on hard problems at the intersection of distributed systems, identity, and security. Outside of work, Nithin can be found traveling, value investing, watching anime, or volunteering with local charities.

articles.title: Jailbroken AI Agent Ran Two-Week Attack on European Telecom
articles.context: Read more on AI-driven attacks: Chinese Hacker Uses DeepSeek AI to Orchestrate Vulnerability Exploits Autonomous Agent Adapted When Its Attacks Were Blocked The operator's...
articles.full_text:
A jailbroken AI agent has spent more than two weeks attacking a European telecommunications provider and 13 organizations hosted on its data center and cloud infrastructure.

Malbear Labs, which has dubbed the campaign Operation Snowball, detailed the activity in research published November 8 after finding the attacker's working directory during a routine sweep for exposed open directories. The unprotected directory held more than 70 session transcripts and the agent's own reports.

The custom agent framework ran on DeepSeek Flash, with a jailbreak prompt of about 78,000 characters that told the model to treat any refusal as a malfunction. Malbear wrote that the transcripts contained no recorded refusals.

Read more on AI-driven attacks: Chinese Hacker Uses DeepSeek AI to Orchestrate Vulnerability Exploits

Autonomous Agent Adapted When Its Attacks Were Blocked

The operator's messages, translated from Chinese, were brief. Besides prompts such as "Go on" and "Stop," they set a target subnet, put three internal hosts off-limits and followed up on the agent's vulnerability list. Malbear wrote that the operator "delegated the intrusion to an AI and checked in asynchronously to review progress."

The agent entered the telecom by exploiting CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XML external entity (XXE) flaw in Cisco BroadWorks. Cisco fixed the flaw in August.

The agent went on to exploit Liferay (CVE-2020-7961) for root access on a host spanning several internal networks and JBoss/RichFaces (CVE-2013-2165) for a second foothold. Malbear listed more than a dozen other flaws the agent targeted, found or kept in its toolkit, none marked as exploited.

When endpoint security blocked an attempt to exploit the Linux flaw PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034), the agent changed its approach without operator direction. After a tunneling tool was blocked, it wrote a replacement.

Access Claims Extended to Patient and Monitoring Data

According to Malbear, the recovered transcripts showed the agent extracting dozens of credential sets, private keys and a healthcare organization's Active Directory data.

The agent also reported reaching subscriber billing records and what Malbear described as millions of patient records, through a TrakCare Oracle database that still used default credentials.

Its reports also listed about 80 Zabbix monitoring backups covering the provider's managed-services customers.

The post does not say whether Malbear checked these claims with any victim, what was taken rather than staged or whether all 13 organizations were breached.

Malbear assessed the activity as consistent with a Chinese-origin operator and did not link it to a state actor. Its recommendations included treating internet-exposed, end-of-life JBoss Application Server 6 instances as compromised and watching internal traffic for tunneling.

articles.title: NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure
QNAP Warns Users as Plex2Shell Flaws Are Used to Hack NAS Devices
articles.context: QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server through the QNAP App Center after reports that threat actors exploited the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain to compromise NAS devices
articles.full_text:
Taiwanese vendor QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server after reports of NAS compromises through the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain.

QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server through the QNAP App Center after reports that threat actors exploited the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain to compromise NAS devices.

“QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through these vulnerabilities, and QNAP Technical Support is assisting the affected usersadvisory published by QNAP. ” reads the report published by the vendor. “The QNAP Product Security Incident Response Team (QNAP PSIRT) has confirmed that the vulnerabilities exist only in Plex Media Server; QTS, QuTS hero, and other QNAP operating systems are not themselves affected.”

Plex Media Server is designed to make movies, music, and other media available across devices. But when a server is exposed to the internet and runs vulnerable software, it can become an entry point for attackers who have little interest in your film collection.

On October 16, 2026, security researcher Zach Main published technical details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code for a vulnerability chain dubbed Plex2Shell. Within a day, researchers had observed attackers using the exploit against an internet-facing honeypot, deploying cryptocurrency-mining malware and proxy software. The incident is a reminder of how quickly a public exploit can be weaponized by threat actors.

The chain combines four vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. Together, they can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers without valid credentials, provided the required conditions are met. The code runs with the privileges of the Plex service, giving attackers an opportunity to install additional software and abuse the host.

The technical details are available in Main’s original analysis, Plex2Shell. Plex had been notified of the vulnerabilities on July 27 and acknowledged the report on August 4, awarding a bug bounty. The company released fixes in September, before the exploit code became public.

The loader does not check the library’s name, executable permissions, digital signature, or symbols. As a result, the library’s ELF constructor can run with the same privileges as the Plex service.

“It doesn’t check for a lib prefix, doesn’t require the execute bit, doesn’t verify any signature, and doesn’t look for any specific symbol.” reads the report published by zmain.com. “When dlopen loads a shared object, it runs the ELF’s DT_INIT_ARRAY (constructor functions) before doing any symbol resolution. A .so that only has a constructor and no exported symbols will still execute its code on load. We then trigger a second transcode. The codec directory gets re-enumerated, the .so we wrote in Stage 4 gets loaded, and the constructor runs as uid=1000(plex).”

That detail matters because the final stage can exploit how Plex loads shared libraries. The chain uses a setting related to transcoding to influence execution, allowing a specially crafted library to run when Plex loads it. The result can be code execution under the service account, without requiring the attacker to obtain an interactive login first.

QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server immediately, users should go to App Center, open My Apps and update Plex Media Server to version 1.43.3 or later. They should then check in Plex Web, under Settings and General, that the installed version is 1.43.3.10861 or later. QNAP will release further updates after verifying them, but users should not wait.

If Plex was reachable from the internet while running version 1.43.2 or earlier, users should treat the NAS as potentially compromised. This may apply if Plex Remote Access was enabled, port 32400 was forwarded, or the port was opened automatically through UPnP or router settings. Updating alone will not remove anything an attacker may have installed.

In those cases, users should follow QNAP’s FAQ to perform a clean reinstall, check for signs of compromise and reset both their Plex and NAS credentials. The company also advises disabling Plex Remote Access if it is not needed and avoiding port forwarding for port 32400. Users who need remote access should use a VPN instead.

QNAP also recommends keeping QTS or QuTS hero and all installed apps up to date. Step-by-step instructions are available in the Plex2Shell: Check and Remediation FAQ for QNAP NAS Users.

CISA added Plex2Shell flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 20, 2026, urging federal agencies to addresse them by October 23, 2026.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, QNAP)

articles.title: Bitter Hackers Deploy New PapRAT Backdoor in Cyberespionage Campaign Targeting South Asia
articles.context: The PapRAT malware delivered via the MSI installer in the second attack chain is designed for remote control
articles.full_text:
The South Asian cyber espionage group known as Bitter (aka APT-C-08, APT-Q-37, Hazy Tiger, Orange Yali, T-APT-17, and TA397) has been observed targeting South Asian organizations with a previously unreported remote access trojan called PapRAT.

"PapRAT has both C++ and Rust implementations," Fortinet FortiGuard Labs researcher Cara Lin said. "Its capabilities include command execution, file uploads and downloads, file deletion, directory and drive enumeration, and screenshot capture. The Rust variant adds PowerShell execution and other commands."

The campaign is notable for making use of three different infection chains -

A Windows Shortcut (LNK) file that abuses the native "ftp.exe" utility to run scripts and create scheduled tasks designed to maintain contact with a command-and-control (C2) server.

A VHDX disk image containing a LNK file that launches a lure Microsoft Excel spreadsheet, while running an MSI installer in the background to deploy PapRAT.

A URL shortcut (URL) file that fetches a LNK file via WebDAV, which then leads to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT.

The living-off-the-land (LotL) approach is designed to execute commands from a remote server ("goodnfortunes[.]com"), allowing it to collect directory and task lists, directory information from Desktop, Documents, and Downloads, installed antivirus product data, and mounted drives.

The harvested reconnaissance information is saved as "abc.pdf" and exfiltrated back to the C2 server via a curl command, after which the staged file is deleted from the host.

A second version of the script has been found to retrieve a file called "talk.log" from "techtalkhelp[.]com." The payload contains a Base64-encoded script to obtain additional instructions from the same server and execute them as PowerShell commands.

"This staging model gives the attacker operational flexibility, while the commands are updated server-side without pushing a new binary, avoiding PE drops and process injection that some security appliances could easily detect," Fortinet said.

The PapRAT malware delivered via the MSI installer in the second attack chain is designed for remote control. It supports eight commands -

MSG, for remote shell

FDD, for directory listing

DEL, for file deletion

RUN, for arbitrary file execution

GDR, for drive enumeration

SS1, for screenshot capture

UPP, for uploading local files to the C2 server ("rivingtonclarks[.]com")

DWW, for downloading files from the C2 server

A Rust version of the malware incorporates three more commands -

MS2, for PowerShell command execution

SLP, for sleeping and polling resumption

BYE, for process termination

A notable aspect of the third attack chain is that it combines the salient aspects of the first two sequences by using a script to download an MSI installer via curl. Like before, the MSI installer serves as a conduit for PapRAT, which then proceeds to drop WmRAT, a malware previously identified as used by Bitter.

The findings indicate that the threat actor continues to refine its custom arsenal to establish and maintain access to targeted systems.

"These changes underscore the importance of monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Fortinet said. "Organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages."

articles.title: Email Addresses of 2.2 Million Sega Customers Leaked in Vendor Breach
articles.context: Sega has revealed that around 2
articles.full_text:
Sega has revealed that around 2.2 million customer email addresses have been exposed as result of a third-party incident.

The video gaming giant revealed on November 9 that an unauthorized third party leaked the email addresses after gaining access to Arara Inc., a Japanese email delivery provider used by Sega to distribute its email newsletter.

“We deeply apologize for the great inconvenience and concern caused to our customers and all parties involved,” Sega wrote.

“Currently, Arara is working to identify the causes of unauthorized access and prevent further damage, and we are working with Arara and related companies to confirm the details of the leaked information.”

The Japanese firm said the breach is limited to 2.196 million email addresses for various email newsletters, and 92,273 items related to distribution.

The leaked information does not include customer names, dates of birth, genders, addresses, phone numbers, credit card information or login passwords.

No misuse of the leaked data has been currently confirmed. However, Sega has warned customers to be vigilant for suspicious emails purporting to be from Sega or Sega Fave Corporation, or using product or service names operated by both companies.

Sega Fave is a subsidiary of the broader Sega group, which focuses on the production of toys and arcade machines.

“Please do not open or reply to URLs or attachments provided in emails you do not recognize. Accessing URLs or opening attached files may lead to entering personal information or affecting your device. Neither our company nor Sega Fave will ask you for your password or credit card information by email. If you receive such an email, do not access the reply or the provided link; delete it,” the company said.

Sega Breach Part of Large-Scale Third-Party Incident

Arara revealed it had been compromised in a statement issued on October 29, which said that unauthorized access was gained to certain server systems of its email distribution service a day earlier, on October 28 after a hacker exploited vulnerabilities in web servers.

The distribution service ‘Arara Message’ was suspended on October 31 and remains offline at the time of writing, according to a dedicated incident page set up by the firm to provide updates.

According to a report by The Japan Times, Arara’s parent company Paycloud Holdings confirmed on November 2 that hackers gained unauthorized access to servers operated by the subsidiary, which exposed information held by around 380 corporate clients using the service. This included 77 million email addresses.

Paycloud also noted that depending on the company, the breached data also included names, telephone numbers and addresses. However, it said that no credit card details have been exposed.

articles.title: Outlook.com bounces legit emails as Microsoft's authentication crackdown goes sideways
articles.context: In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day
articles.full_text: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails. The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures. Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information. The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails. The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required. Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed. Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more. SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both). The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response. To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place. A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation." "Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue." Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected. Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well. It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

articles.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: SSHole Exploited, APT Root RCE, Robot Takeovers, 15K Hacked Sites, and More
articles.context: " Zyxel Fixes 0-Day exploited to Hack About 1,000 Network Switches — Zyxel has fixed a zero-day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches that threat actors exploited...
articles.full_text:
A system doesn't always need a complicated bug to let someone in. Sometimes, a blank password is enough. That's one of the bigger stories this week. And it gets worse when the tools meant to keep systems updated or running safely become part of the attack.

Elsewhere, attackers are hiding inside normal web traffic, stealing credentials from network devices, and finding new uses for exposed systems. AI is helping some of them move faster, but old mistakes are doing plenty of the work too. Even forgotten settings and small changes made months ago are coming back to cause trouble.

There's a lot packed into this week's news, including some strange research findings, fresh attacks, and a few warnings worth taking seriously. Here's the full recap.

⚡ Threat of the Week

OpenSSH Flaw Sees Exploitation Attempts — Threat actors are attempting to exploit a recently disclosed security flaw impacting OpenSSH that can enable sign-ins to accounts that have no password set. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score: 8.1) and codenamed SSHole (or *sshole), impacts Linux systems that run OpenSSH on the musl C library with Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) disabled, including Alpine Linux's default OpenSSH server configuration. As of November 9, 2026, a total of 20 exploitation attempts have been recorded from 13 unique IP addresses from Denmark, Iran, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Singapore, Sweden, Switzerland, and the U.S.

Harden Your CI/CD Pipelines With Drop-in Replacements for 1,000+ GitHub Actions

SHA pinning guarantees immutability, not security. If a pinned action is vulnerable or compromised, it still runs in your pipeline with access to your secrets. Chainguard Actions provides 1,000+ continuously hardened, drop-in replacements for standard GitHub Actions. Try it free for 30 days.

Try Chainguard Actions ➝

🔔 Top News

Trojanized CWP Web Server Used to Deliver CWPdoor — A new Linux malware called CWPdoor is being distributed via a trojanized version of cwpsrv, the built-in daemon and web server that powers the Control Web Panel. According to XLab, a shell script named "cwpsrv_update.sh" is used to download "cwpsrv" from a remote server ("136.0.141[.]71") and replace the legitimate file on the system. "The downloaded cwpsrv is a passive backdoor that can be triggered by specific headers in HTTP/HTTPS traffic to remotely execute commands specified by the attacker," XLab said. "Its backdoor logic is triggered only when it receives a specially crafted request from the attacker. At the same time, it suppresses logging for that request, leaving no trace of the interaction in the access logs. This combination of directly replacing the legitimate cwpsrv binary, passive triggering, and log suppression makes CWPdoor exceptionally stealthy."

Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Allows Code Execution as Root — A vulnerability in the APT package manager (CVE-2026-109518, CVSS score: 7.7) can be exploited to install a package under certain conditions and achieve code execution with elevated privileges. The issue affects Ubuntu and Debian operating systems. "Under specific conditions, when APT is configured to use HTTP package sources with retry settings enabled, a third-party with a network position between the host and the package mirror can cause APT to install a package that did not pass verification," Amazon said in an advisory. "Maintainer scripts within that package then run with elevated privileges."

CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks Targeting Financial Organizations — The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has disclosed that an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted threat actor it tracks as Crafty Falcon is targeting organizations in the Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) sectors in the country. Calling it a "significant escalation" in attacks, the threat actor is said to be re-targeting entities that were originally targeted last month after incomplete remediation, adding that the intrusions "have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response."

Zyxel Fixes 0-Day exploited to Hack About 1,000 Network Switches — Zyxel has fixed a zero-day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches that threat actors exploited to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-107441 (CVSS score: 8.8), is an out-of-bounds write flaw that could "allow a LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker to exploit the flaw and potentially execute OS commands via a crafted HTTP request." The activity has been attributed to a Chinese-speaking threat actor tracked as Kapibala (aka Red Heron). The attacker has been found to weaponize the flaw to deploy the JITTERLY backdoor and SIXZUT, a ring 3 rootkit.

cPGuard Update Mechanism Hijacked to Deliver Backdoor — Unknown threat actors compromised the update infrastructure for the cPGuard web security suite to distribute a backdoor and a data-stealing script. "On 2 November 2026 at 02:06 UTC, an unidentified attacker used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to OPSSHIELD's update distribution infrastructure (CDN)," OPSSHIELD said. "The attacker used this access to distribute a malicious script through the cPGuard update channel." The attacker is said to have gotten in through its billing application at manage.opsshield[.]com and logged in to a customer account they had registered.

mSecure Urges Customers to Change their Passwords — Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed. "mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company said. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist." However, the company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information. The lack of specifics has understandably riled up customers, with one user on Reddit stating "their silence on this is mind-bending." In December 2025, Germany's cyber agency BSI found that mSecure's maker could, in theory, access the data users store in it.

‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs

Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-16305, CVE-2026-16306 (INFINITT PACS), CVE-2026-13684, CVE-2026-13639, CVE-2026-13673, CVE-2026-6205 (Synology DSM), CVE-2026-58868, CVE-2026-58882 (Google Android), GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (Ruby on Rails), CVE-2026-102703, CVE-2026-102704 (Xen), CVE-2026-109518 (Debian apt), CVE-2026-98432, CVE-2026-121639, CVE-2026-121638, CVE-2026-121640 (WatchGuard), CVE-2026-76506 (Cisco), CVE-2026-119741 (rsync), CVE-2026-121156, CVE-2026-121229, CVE-2026-121246, CVE-2026-121035, CVE-2026-121247, CVE-2026-121203, CVE-2026-121126 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-98432 (Veeam), CVE-2026-83844 (Microsoft Paint), CVE-2026-19868 (SonicWall SonicOS), CVE-2026-123158 (OpenSSH), and multiple vulnerabilities in the BaseChat Android app version 9.8.1.

🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars

Your SOC Has an Identity Blind Spot — Here's How Attackers Exploit It and How to Close It → Your SOC may be tracking threats, but is it missing the identities behind them? As attackers increasingly exploit human, machine, and AI identities, traditional security tools often lack the context needed to detect and contain threats quickly. Join this free webinar to learn how connecting identity security with SOC operations can expose hidden risks, reveal attack blast radius, and accelerate incident response.

Your GitHub Actions May Still Be Vulnerable — Even With SHA Pinning. Here's Why → Think your GitHub Actions are secure because you use SHA pinning? Think again. Attackers can exploit hidden weaknesses in CI/CD workflows, even when standard security measures are in place. Join this expert-led webinar to discover how these attacks work, why SHA pinning alone isn't enough, and what you can do to protect your software supply chain.

📰 Around the Cyber World

The Russian-speaking ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation known as Qilin (aka Agenda) has recorded 179 publicly reported attacks in 2024, and more than 1,000 claimed victims in 2025. This year alone, it has claimed more than 900 victims, making it one of the most active ransomware groups. "Affiliates commonly gain access through phishing, stolen credentials, vulnerable internet-facing systems and remote-management tools," Acronis said. "Qilin uses a flexible ransomware platform that allows affiliates to tailor attacks to the victim environment, including the encryption of local files, network shares and virtual machine infrastructure." One notable Qilin affiliate is Securotrop, which continues to operate within the Qilin affiliate network, while maintaining an independent channel for publishing stolen victim data.

Exposed Dixell/Copeland XWEB PRO refrigeration controllers are being turned into abuse infrastructure, according to SecurityScorecard, which uncovered a suspected SMTP botnet that includes confirmed refrigeration controllers. Attackers are said to be using compromised Dixell/Copeland XWEB PRO refrigeration controllers as proxy exits and spam senders. "The SMTP cluster consists of nine IP addresses, three of them confirmed XWEB controllers," Security Scorecard said. "Of 1,041 targets, 508 were contacted by at least two nodes. The three most active nodes had approximately 47% of their target lists in common, the report’s strongest signal of coordination."

A targeted Browser-in-the-Middle (BitM) phishing operation dubbed PhantomDOM is using custom DOM-mirroring to hijack Microsoft 365 sessions. "The attack began with a SharePoint-themed PDF distributed from an apparently legitimate sender and progressed through redirects and browser checks before presenting Microsoft authentication inside an attacker-controlled remote browser," ZeroBEC said. "The victim saw a familiar sign-in experience. The attacker controlled the browser in which that experience actually ran." According to the email security company, PhantomDOM goes beyond cloned login pages and conventional reverse-proxy phishing. "Its client reconstructs the remote DOM, forwards keyboard and clipboard interactions over WebSocket, survives connection interruptions and supports live operator control," it added.

According to a report from the non-profit AI Alignment Foundation, AI agents assigned a sandboxed coding task to fix a broken pricing service "shared a private token and ran untrusted code in exchange for help from an agent forum." In an experiment tested against nine models, GPT-6.1-Sol refused every swarm request in 50 of 50 trials, while Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Sonnet 5.5 trials were cut short by their providers' content filters.

A zero-day vulnerability has been disclosed in CPython that could enable bad actors to breach AI hosting platforms. "A memory-safety flaw in the CPython interpreter allows attackers to escape a code sandbox and execute code hidden in a specially crafted model," RunSybil said. "By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests. They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads." The findings build upon a previous out-of-bounds read in CPython that could result in a sandbox escape. The issue has been fixed and backported to 3.13, 3.14, and 3.15 branches.

The U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has issued an order effectively cutting off MEXC Global's access to the U.S. financial system under Operation Economic Outcast. "MEXC Global is a convertible virtual currency exchanger that has facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions connected to Iranian, North Korean, and Russian sanctions evasion, as well as cybercrime, including by transacting directly with sanctioned actors," FinCEN said.

A new study of 25,964 U.S. government-related domains has found 43 whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. In one case, a misspelled domain's SPF configuration ("amzonses[.]com" instead of "amazonses[.]com") authorized at least 32,066 unique IP addresses to send email on behalf of a U.S. county. "These external dependencies authorize third-party senders, route incoming mail, provide DNS delegation, and receive security telemetry," SH Consulting said. "The government domains themselves can remain registered and be considered protected, because there are no signs to suggest anything is wrong." SH Consulting said it defensively registered 17 of these dangling DNS dependencies to prevent abuse.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland and a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia. Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government from 2021 until his arrest in August 2023 and has agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months. "He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict," said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.

Huntress has warned of a "couple waves of activity across multiple organizations involving GeoVision camera software," pointing to broad exploitation of the platform to deliver malware. The activity originates from the IP addresses 45.32.117[.]34 and 156.246.94[.]183.

A single AI-augmented threat actor (AAT) has been observed using a mesh of 12 AI agents called BOSSAI to conduct persistent campaigns in several countries. The mesh consists of combining HexStrike AI, Hermes, CyberStrikeAI, and HalberdStrike, alongside Grok, OpenClaw, and Claude Code, with some acting as infrastructure builders and maintainers, while others scan for vulnerabilities and attack. The findings once again show how a lone actor can mount offensive operations at scale. "Using the BOSSAI mesh, the operator targeted hundreds of organizations spanning government emergency services, banks and lenders, universities, military systems, phone directories, e-commerce platforms, and gambling sites in eleven countries," Acronis said. "It's unclear if the attacker has any specific affiliation or goal beyond compromising as many organizations as possible, presumably to monetize the activity." The threat actor is believed to be a single individual based in Hualien City, Taiwan.

Truffle Security has launched the Secrets Revocation Program, a free initiative that helps API key issuers revoke 1.4 million secrets that have been confirmed to be live and leaked on GitHub, Docker Hub, npm, Hugging Face, and others.

Gnosis Pay said it detected unauthorized access to the system powering its Gnosis Pay-branded cards on November 3, 2026, leading to the exposure of customer information. "The data breach was limited to the system powering Gnosis Pay-branded cards, which was already scheduled for retirement on 20 December 2026," it said. "We have increased our monitoring of card activity and wallets to detect fraud or attempts to access user funds. We have also implemented an extra verification step (3D Secure) and made it mandatory for all online card payments. These measures will stay in place until the B2C system is fully retired as planned on 20 December 2026." The company said it directly notified users about what information was accessed from their account, but did not reveal the number of customers impacted.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned four individuals and 41 entities that are tied to scam compounds in Cambodia, Madagascar, and other countries across Southeast Asia and Africa. The sanctioned parties are said to have supported the business network of Prince Group. "Cyber scam syndicates continue to steal billions of dollars from American victims while relying on sophisticated international business networks to launder their illicit proceeds," said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. "The newly designated individuals and entities have helped sustain Prince Group TCO’s illicit global operations after the October 2025 and June 2026 designations by managing offshore corporate structures, concealing beneficial ownership, facilitating commercial activities, and providing administrative and financial services to senior Prince Group TCO executives."

The U.S. Treasury also sanctioned Chui Kok Wa for his role as the leader of a scam compound in Madagascar that was dismantled earlier this year. Late last month, Wa was charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, as the leader of the NFT investment scam. "In the scheme, scammers posed as beautiful women who met victims on dating websites, eventually enlisting them to connect their cryptocurrency wallets to fraudulent websites associated with the NFT investments," the Justice Department said. "Once connected, the scammers willed the victims to continue to fund their cryptocurrency wallets, and then surreptitiously pulled money from the victims’ wallets without their knowledge." Wa's phones also allegedly contained employment contracts, detailing overnight work schedules in Madagascar and providing employees with bonus payments tied to money stolen, as well as scripts or guides for what scammers should say to victims and a roster containing employees' names, passport information, salary, hours, disciplinary actions taken against them, along with a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the employees.

Vercel has launched Security Review, a new capability in Vercel Agent that scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories. "Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI," Vercel said. "With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings." In tandem, Vercel said it's starting the rollout of Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) for vercel[.]com to make it harder for stealer malware to siphon session cookies from a device. Google rolled out DBSC support in Chrome earlier this April.

Fortra has revealed that attackers are creating convincing travel-booking pages that imitate trusted rental platforms. "The fake sites use familiar branding, realistic property listings, reservation details, and urgent messages to persuade travelers to provide sensitive data such as credit card information, usernames and passwords, and more," Fortra said.

Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, has pleaded guilty today to wire fraud and money laundering related to using his access as an FBI agent to steal cryptocurrency. "From 2017 through early 2025, Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, worked at the FBI Boston Division on an investigative squad focused on an adversarial nation-state," the Justice Department said. "From February 2025 to July 31, 2026, Yaroch worked in the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, with access to FBI systems that contained cryptocurrency credentials that the FBI had collected as part of its investigations. Beginning no later than December 2024, Yaroch used his position to steal cryptocurrency from wallets controlled by the subjects of various other investigations or by adversarial nation-state actors, and from at least one wallet the FBI created to use in an operation. Throughout his wire fraud scheme, Yaroch conducted approximately 100 fraudulent transfers using credentials related to 35 separate FBI investigations. He illicitly gained approximately $2,474,380.66 in fraudulent proceeds." The stolen funds were used to pay off his debts and finance a new life abroad, even asking ChatGPT how to maximize profit from investments and where to live in the European Union. Yaroch will be sentenced in March 2027.

DigiCert said it identified an event involving unauthorized access to one of its business systems, leading to exposure of names and email addresses. In some cases, driver's licenses, passports, utility bills, and other documents containing a name and address that its customers provided as proof were also compromised. The incident has been traced back to a February 2025 change that moved the internal business system to a different network segment, causing it to be opened to the public internet for more than 16 months. Unknown attackers abused a self-registration feature in the system's account manager to create a read-only account that had access to archived data between June 27 and July 2, 2026. Although DigiCert blocked the unauthorized account on July 2, it subsequently determined in October that the account was used to access archived customer contact information, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses.

OpenAI announced 2 that it is increasing payouts in its Security Bug Bounty program. The objective is to get the broader research community hunting for flaws that its own testing may have missed. "A critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000," OpenAI said. "Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses."

Three people accused of using AI to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to plunder about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies and attorneys at major law firms in order to trick employees into sending large payments to bank accounts under their control between 2024 and 2026, according to the Justice Department. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain in June and August 2026, respectively, while Sheetrit was arrested in the U.K. in September 2026.

A fake download campaign is targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers hosted on bogus sites to distribute multiple payloads. "We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device [WorldProxyPool], enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform [CharityEngine and BOINC], or installing additional utility-style software [AW Manager or Windows Manager], often without users' informed knowledge or consent," Microsoft said.
