"These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks."

A Chinese-language exploitation framework called Greeter has targeted Flowise honeypots with thousands of chat messages reading only "hello" while weaponizing an old code injection flaw (CVE-2024-58351) to execute malicious instructions. The framework conducted system discovery, extracted environment variables, probed cloud metadata services, searched for SSH keys and other credentials, tried to set up persistence, and ran quick checks to determine whether the host could run payloads from memory. Era Security said it counted 4,372 Flowise instances exposed online, out of which 703 (21.5%) had no authentication enabled. "It reveals a new exploitation framework designed to turn exposed AI applications into entry points for code execution, credential discovery, and potentially broader cloud compromise," Era Security said. "The framework’s most consequential feature was its ephemeral, per-request execution model. Attack instructions were supplied through overrideConfig.javascriptFunction, while stored user messages contained only 'hello.' The malicious function could change with each request without altering the saved chatflow, leaving an incomplete picture for defenders inspecting workflow definitions or chat history alone."

A threat actor has been abusing fake "suspended account" notices to hide phishing content from users revisiting its lookalike pages masquerading as business banking and treasury logins. The campaign, active since May 2026, has been relying on more than 300 fake domains, including 248 impersonating 189 U.S. financial institutions. The first domains were registered in late 2025, but most of them appeared between July and September 2026. "What ties them together is one mechanism: the kit remembers every visitor’s IP address, so the first visit gets a bank login page, and any return visit gets what looks like a closed hosting account. We call this cluster the 'Suspended' infrastructure," KELA said. "Most domains follow the same recipe, [keyword]-[bank].com, with keywords such as secure, disable, protect and cancel, which makes the cluster findable in newly registered domain feeds."

Meta said it paid nearly $1.2 million in bug bounties to researchers who found and responsibly disclosed issues in its Muse AI assistant. The bug bounty program went public in September 2026. "The largest single award was paid out four months before launch for a bug that allowed a researcher to get access to conversations and tokens in pre-release VMs used by employees and engineers testing the product," Meta said. "An authentication check treated a header added by a local HTTPS proxy as proof that a request came from a trusted source. During a system migration, the environment gained a second proxy layer. That meant requests from outside could carry the trusted header too. A researcher found this and demonstrated the exploit." Meta paid a $300,000 bounty for this report.

Chinese nation-state threat activity declined by 41.4% in the six months from April to September 2026, according to a new study by Trellix. The change is "a shift in operational focus, we assess, rather than reduced intent, and one that warrants vigilance rather than reassurance," it added.

QNAP is urging users to update Plex Media Server on their NAS instances to the latest version available in the QNAP App Center following reports of active exploitation of a set of vulnerabilities known as Plex2Shell. "QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through these vulnerabilities," it said. "The QNAP Technical Support team is assisting affected users and has confirmed that no data loss has occurred."

MetaMask has disclosed that the security incident it identified on September 28, 2026, resulted in unauthorized access to part of its infrastructure, and that it took steps to contain the incident and secure affected systems. "We have identified no indication that MetaMask wallets or our wallet infrastructure were compromised as a result of this incident," it said. "We have not identified evidence that the incident enabled unauthorized access to or withdrawal of customers' staked principal. However, a limited amount of execution-layer staking rewards was diverted during the incident." The attacker is said to have briefly altered the addresses used to receive execution-layer staking rewards for certain validators, diverting approximately 0.385 ETH in rewards. "These rewards are separate from customers' staked ETH," MetaMask added. "We have found no evidence that customers’ staked principal or withdrawal keys were compromised, and the affected systems have been secured."

Infected security-themed GitHub projects are being used to target cybersecurity professionals to deliver backdoors and infostealer malware. According to Doctor Web, more than 2,000 PCs have been affected. The malicious code is embedded in Visual Studio project files, Python scripts, and Go source files. Once launched, the malware establishes persistence on the infected host, escalates privileges, disables security and recovery features, and deploys additional payloads, including AsyncRAT, a clipper malware, and an information stealer. The malware also attempts to remove ESET, McAfee, and Malwarebytes antivirus tools from the host and interferes with Windows backups. "The attackers behind these compromised development projects target blockchain game enthusiasts and (most intriguingly) information security professionals," the Russian cybersecurity company said. "The first infected repositories emerged two years ago. The early uploads targeted crypto wallet users – back then attackers used repositories containing Visual Studio projects related to blockchain games, game bots and cheating."

Security researcher Scott Helme has revealed that about 15,579 websites are currently infected with malicious JavaScript delivering credit card skimmers, ClickFix lures, iOS exploitation kits like Coruna and DarkSword, and malicious redirects. These websites receive more than 135 million visits every month.

A new report from Layer3 Intel has found that residential proxy traffic has exited through the White House network (AS2650) 236 times over a 30-day period between October 5 and November 3, 2026, with 28 separate residential proxy services able to route traffic through six of its addresses. "Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning," Layer3 Intel said. "That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them." In a post shared on X, Synthient said "several White House staffers are running a Windows 11 machine with InfaticaSDK installed," adding it found "a number of Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices beaconing to known proxy providers like Geonode, Infatica, and Mellowtel." The root cause is believed to be Rave[.]io, a shared streaming app that bundles 12 proxy SDKs into the platform. Rave allows users to watch content from YouTube, Netflix, and Disney+ with friends and runs on Mac, iPhone, Android, and Windows.

A set of five vulnerabilities has been disclosed in Reachy Mini, an open-source, expressive companion robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face, that, when chained together, can allow an attacker to "execute attacker code, escalate to a persistent root via the robot’s passwordless sudo, and ultimately gain control of the device's motor," JFrog said. "A second variant of the attack works through the browser, where the operator visits a malicious web page, which silently compromises the robot."

A phishing campaign built around fake registration pages for OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic events is luring marketing employees with rewards like "3 months of ChatGPT Pro" or "3 months of Grok Heavy" to get them to sign in with their work accounts. "This campaign uses them in email-delivered invitations that lead to AitM and device code phishing, expanding the use of AI-themed lures across various payload types," Push Security said. "Employees want access to the latest AI tools, making them excellent bait for attacks." The Microsoft option launches a device code phishing flow run through the Kali365 phishing-as-a-service platform, while clicking "Continue with Google" opens a VoidProxy reverse proxy of Google's sign-in page. It is unclear how the attackers initially distribute the phishing links. The kits used to build and deploy the fake event invite lure pages as ZoomMock and MSDRoot. Similar campaigns have been reported by ANY.RUN and Cofense in recent months.

A U.S. school estate was compromised by the 3AM ransomware group as part of a hybrid human-AI operation, according to Bitdefender. The exact initial access vector used is unknown, but the first recorded activity started on September 10, 2026. "Some parts show a human operator at the keyboard while others behave like an agentic loop, a language model reading each result and retrying with different commands," Bitdefender said. "With the exception of the encryptor itself, the whole operation was built on legitimate, built-in tools, which is standard for ransomware operations. What is different is how the attacker behaved, and several things point to an agentic loop, a program that feeds each result back to a model and runs what comes back. The retries behave like a loop too."

Conclusion

The strange part is how many of these attacks start with something small. A setting nobody checked, an update nobody questioned, or a system left online longer than it should have been. Add a little patience from the attackers, and suddenly a minor mistake becomes a much bigger problem. Not every attack needs a clever trick.

That's it for this week's roundup. Some of these stories will fade, while others may get worse as more details come out. Either way, there's enough here to keep security teams busy. Check what applies to your systems, fix what you can, and we'll be back next week with whatever turns up next.

articles.title: AI Security
articles.context: AI Security Two weeks ago, I attended the [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco
articles.full_text:
AI Security

Two weeks ago, I attended the [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. It was an excellent event: three days of very dense talks about all aspects of AI security. (My talk was about integrous AI, and I will post it when it is online.)

AI security can be divided into three broad topics. It’s important for researchers to understand which one they are working on. And it’s important for us as a community to work on them all. They are: security of AI, security with AI, and security from AI. [un]prompted had good talks about all three.

Tags: AI, conferences, Schneier news

Posted on November 9, 2026 at 7:05 AM • 1 Comments

articles.title: CISA and the FBI Warn Of Attacks against Industrial Refrigeration Controllers
articles.context: Attackers may exploit flaws in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to change settings remotely and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles
articles.full_text:
US agencies warn attackers are going after industrial refrigeration controllers. The fixes are basic, and most start with getting them off the internet.

CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA and the Department of Transportation published a joint advisory on attacks against industrial refrigeration controllers and cold chain monitoring systems. The activity is global. Healthcare, chemical, food and transport companies use these systems to watch temperatures, keep logs, run defrost cycles and save energy, including in refrigerated trucks.

“The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities.” reads the advisory published by CISA. “The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”

The targets are electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold-storage sites. Attackers may exploit flaws in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to change settings remotely and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles. In plain terms, someone could cook your freezer from the other side of the world.

The agencies identify three ways in: bypassing authentication, injecting arbitrary code, and exploiting weak configurations. Once inside, an attacker can change temperatures, which can shorten equipment life, create a fire hazard and destroy stock. Spoiled products that reach consumers can also create a safety risk.

“The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.” continues the adviosry.

An attacker can also hide the damage. Operators lose sight of current temperatures, and that’s a bad moment to learn a cold room has been warm for hours.

CISA’s Chris Butera adds that every organization that depends on these systems should assume it’s a target. The advice follows the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals from CISA and NIST, a minimum set of practices for any organization.

Start with exposure. Keep controller panels off the internet, and if you need remote access, put an up-to-date firewall or similar gateway in front of it. Then separate industrial equipment from the office network with its own virtual network.

Next, fix the basics. Change default passwords, use strong ones, and add phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where you can. Update firmware, and retire or replace devices the maker no longer supports.

Allow only trusted devices and IP addresses to change system settings. Keep tested backups in a separate location, disconnected from the network. Enable logging and regularly check the logs. If devices do not record activity, monitor the network traffic between them.

U.S. organizations should report suspicious activity to CISA’s 24/7 operations center or the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. Healthcare organizations can also contact HHS.

Reports should include the date, time and location of the incident, a description of the activity, the number of people affected, the equipment involved, and a contact person within the organization.

One control gets forgotten more than the rest. A controller shouldn’t be able to push a freezer past what’s safe, whoever is giving the orders.

“The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems.” concludes the report. “To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT“

CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology

CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security

CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

articles.title: Web3Auth Flaw Exploited to Steal Keplr Crypto, Provider Empties Other Wallets for Safety
articles.context: Josh Lee, a Keplr co-founder, gave an early estimate in his initial findings: about 20% of Google and Apple login accounts were affected, and only a fraction of those appeared...
articles.full_text:
Some people who set up a Keplr crypto wallet with their Google or Apple account have had money stolen by an attacker.

Keplr uses a company called Web3Auth to run that Google and Apple sign-in. The attacker used a security flaw at that company to reach the wallets, both companies said late last week.

Web3Auth then used the attacker's own route to empty other at-risk wallets before the attacker got to them, it said. It moved that money, with help from the wallet maker, into recovery wallets for safekeeping. So an empty balance may mean the money was rescued, not stolen.

Wallets made with a recovery phrase (a backup list of 12 or 24 words) or a hardware wallet are not affected, the wallet maker said. It has paused Google and Apple sign-in while it investigates.

What Affected Users Should Do

The wallet maker has given this user guidance for accounts created with Google or Apple login:

Do not send new funds to the account.

Do not re-import the account or recreate it anywhere.

Move any funds that are not staked or locked to an account that uses a recovery phrase or a hardware wallet.

Trust updates only from the official accounts of the wallet maker and the login provider, and ignore direct messages or links that offer "recovery."

Staked and locked assets are taking longer to secure. The wallet maker is also working with the login provider on a way for users to check whether their account was affected.

In the meantime, the login provider has published a recovery address list, which it says lets people tell its own transfers apart from possibly malicious ones.

It has also warned users not to assume that an unfamiliar destination address is linked to the attacker.

What Went Wrong

In an incident update, Web3Auth said a security issue in its own infrastructure affected certain wallets it provides inside the Keplr app.

Keplr went further, saying the flaw led to a "private key breach" for some users who signed in with Google or Apple. A private key is the secret code that approves payments from a wallet, so whoever holds it can move the money.

Neither company has said how the flaw worked, when the attacker first used it, or whether that route is now closed.

Where the Money Went

No dollar figure for the theft has come from either company. Josh Lee, a Keplr co-founder, gave an early estimate in his initial findings: about 20% of Google and Apple login accounts were affected, and only a fraction of those appeared to have been exploited.

GoPlus, a Web3 security company, said in a security alert that at least about $1 million had been stolen. It did not explain how it reached that figure.

The rescued money went into what the login provider calls secure recovery wallets, on 11 blockchains in the Cosmos family and eight Ethereum-style chains.

Bitquery, a blockchain data firm, counted at least $6.01 million moving from more than 44,000 wallets into the recovery wallets by late last week. The firm first reported the transfers as theft. It has since issued a corrected analysis that treats them as the rescue, though it says it cannot check who controls the recovery wallets.

The first of these transfers came 21 minutes before the login provider's first public notice, the firm's data shows. Most of the wallets, 86%, were emptied after the wallet maker warned users.

The moved funds are safe, the login provider said in its recovery thread, and it is working with the wallet maker to return them to users. It has not said how or when.

Beyond Keplr

The login provider said the issue affects its services used by some other companies, but Keplr is the only one it has named. It paused its embedded wallet service, which other apps use to build wallets for their users. Its status page still shows its login service as down today.

Consensys, the company behind the MetaMask wallet, bought the login provider in June 2025. Its acquisition announcement said the deal would let MetaMask users create and recover wallets with social logins. The provider said its initial investigation found "no evidence that MetaMask users are impacted."

articles.title: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Targeted in Reported $133m Heist
articles.context: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out
articles.full_text:
A leading French banking group has moved to reassure customers that their funds are safe after reports emerged of a $133m heist.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa issued a statement on November 4 confirming that it had been a victim “of an attack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out.”

The hackers reached the bank’s network via the platform of a service provider, it added in an FAQ on the incident.

“The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms,” it said.

“They did not, therefore, use customer accounts belonging to its federations or subsidiaries. We have communicated that this incident has no financial consequences for our customers. As soon as this attack was identified, our teams immediately activated the necessary security measures to contain the incident and prevent any further fraudulent activity against us.”

Read more on big-money heists: Brazilian Fintech Giant Sinqia Reveals $130m Heist Attempt

Suspicious Withdrawals Traced Across Multiple Exchanges

The incident first came to light on November 2 when blockchain investigator, “ZachXBT,” claimed in a Telegram post that an unnamed “EU entity” had lost $106m from “multiple centralized exchange accounts.”

ZachXBT ruled out the involvement of notorious North Korean hackers the Lazarus Group.

“Over the past 24 hours the illicit actor has been aggressively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring to instant exchanges (WellWallet, Kyrrex, etc), converting to XMR via Wagyu, and bridging across multiple chains,” they explained.

The investigator posted an updated the day after claiming to have spotted an additional $27m of fraudulent centralized exchange account (CEX) withdrawals.

“My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it’s currently being covered up,” they said. “No proper incident disclosure has resulted in $30m+ being laundered away which could have been frozen by EU law enforcement.”

However, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa noted in its FAQ that it was “still too early” to say for sure how much was taken.

“Our teams are continuing their work to precisely assess the financial consequences of this attack: some of the funds involved have been frozen, and other actions are underway to recover them,” it said.

“We can already confirm that the amounts involved are in no way likely to jeopardize the financial health and stability of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.”

The bank urged customers to be on the lookout for potential phishing attempts in the aftermath of the incident and resulting publicity.

The news comes just days after North Korean hackers stole an estimated $6.3bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what has been described as the biggest theft of its kind ever seen.

articles.title: LNbits Urges All Operators to Shut Down Their Bitcoin Lightning Wallet Servers Amid Attacks
articles.context: The attack ran from 09:22 to 14:00 UTC yesterday, starting more than three hours before the project's first warning at 12:33 UTC
articles.full_text:
Everyone running LNbits, a free, open-source Bitcoin Lightning wallet system, should shut down their servers now because of a wave of attacks, the project said yesterday.

It has several security fixes to release and asked operators to be careful until they are out. One operator said new accounts used an exploit to withdraw 2,285,545 satoshis, about 0.023 bitcoin, from his server before he could stop it.

The shutdown notice came about 80 minutes after a first, narrower warning. That warning asked operators to disable Paywall, an add-on that makes people pay to view content, while the project looked into a possible bug.

As of 09:00 UTC today, the project had not released a fixed version. On X, it had not canceled the notice, offered another option, or told operators how to check whether their servers were hit before they were shut down.

Ben Arc, an LNbits developer, said in a patch estimate yesterday that patches "should be merged and available within 24-48hrs." Counted from his post, that means between about 14:00 UTC today and 14:00 UTC tomorrow.

The project also switched off all the LNbits instances it runs for users on its cloud service, my.lnbits.com, later yesterday. It said in a hosted-service notice that all services would be back within 24 hours, or by about 17:20 UTC today.

Kevin Ravensberg, the operator who reported the loss, said in a loss report on X that his server was exploited before the shutdown notice. The attack ran from 09:22 to 14:00 UTC yesterday, starting more than three hours before the project's first warning at 12:33 UTC.

He has promised to repay users of BitTipBot, a Telegram bot. They cannot reach their funds until the project fixes the flaws.

Later yesterday, Ravensberg said in a follow-up post that Arc and a team of security testers had confirmed "which exact extension exploit was used" on his server. Neither he nor the project had named that extension in posts on X as of 09:00 UTC today. The project also had not said whether it is Paywall, the add-on named in its first warning.

The shutdown notice covers LNbits servers and does not mention Lightning nodes or other wallet software. It did not say how many servers were attacked or how much was taken.

articles.title: DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185,000 Times Since Trump Took Office
articles.context: To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only...
articles.full_text:
Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that normally takes on transnational crime, estimates it has sent out at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration, according to a recent court filing. The figure shows how HSI has increasingly relied on this warrantless authority to conduct investigations.

To put HSI’s estimate into perspective, a previous WIRED analysis found that in the more than six and a half years from the start of 2016 to mid-August 2022, ICE agents only sent out around 170,000 of a type of administrative subpoena called a 1509 customs summons.

The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed as part of a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security filed by the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the nonprofit, says the EFF hopes to get more details about the 185,000 estimate. The EFF originally asked for information about how many administrative subpoenas were sent to technology companies, internet platforms, and service providers by ICE or DHS since January 20, 2025. It’s not clear if that count is just for administrative subpoenas sent to those types of companies or if it includes a much broader set.

Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked investigative tool. Unlike with a grand jury subpoena or a court order, the government doesn’t have to explain to the courts why it needs the documents or what data it’s requesting from a company.

Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government has used DHS’s administrative subpoena power to try to unmask anonymous online critics and pursue broad customer records about protesters. This includes, for example, a list of people in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific green beanie from REI.

Congress originally granted the use of 1509 customs summons to the then stand-alone US Customs Service nearly a century ago, with the idea that it would let customs officers inspect business records related to importing merchandise and figure out whether they owed customs duties. In 2003, Congress transferred that agency’s powers, including the ability to issue customs summons, to the newly formed Department of Homeland Security.

In the past, DHS has maintained that customs summons could be used only for specific purposes. The DHS inspector general admonished Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Professional Responsibility in 2017 for trying to use a customs summons to unmask an anonymous Twitter poster, pointing out that its own procedures manual said that customs summons could only be used to obtain information related to customs or immigrations laws.

articles.title: Anti-Money Laundering Watchdog FATF Targets Scam Compounds
articles.context: Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment...
articles.full_text:
A leading anti-money laundering (AML) organization has called for global action to disrupt the scam compounds responsible for a considerable volume of transnational fraud.

AML watchdog the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) warned in a new report that large physical scam compounds are a major driver of a global fraud economy estimated to be worth $500bn annually.

Often staffed by trafficked victims, 120,000 of whom are forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone, these operations are also supported by crypto and instant payment platforms, money mules, social media, messaging services and AI-enabled content, FATF said.

The trend is increasingly one of smaller and more mobile operations, with compounds created out of repurposed casinos, rented rooms, apartments, coffee shops and even moving vehicles, the report warned.

Read more on scam compounds: Scam Centers Expand Global Footprint with Trafficked Victims

The FATF report noted that countries are generally better at tackling scam compounds through downstream action such as asset tracing and targeting victim payments.

But it called on FATF member nations to combine these efforts with upstream disruption targeting things like fraudulent advertising, recruitment activity, malicious domains and suspicious phone numbers and telecom indicators,

“With criminals weaponizing AI and other technologies to intensify their scam operations, we need to urgently modernize and accelerate our response,” argued FATF president, Giles Thomson. “This means focusing on dismantling the criminal networks behind scam compounds, working proactively with technology, social media and communications sectors to prevent and disrupt more scams before they happen, and quicker intervention to freeze and seize the proceeds of scams once they’ve happened.”

Six Principles to Combat Illicit Money Flows

With this in mind, the FATF report promoted six pillars to its approach:

Shift the focus from physical compounds to criminal leaders, recruiters and traffickers, and other supporting players

Disrupt the infrastructure and services, including stopping, tracing, freezing and recovering victim payments

Share information between financial institutions, technology companies, telcos and authorities

Act at speed across borders, as the first 24-72 hours after a scam are critical for freezing funds and recovering assets

Ensure investigations put the protection of trafficked and scam victims front and center

Continuously update approaches as scam operations decentralize and adapt

Jonathan Frost, director of global advisory at BioCatch, welcomed the focus on compounds and the need for action by platform providers.

“Those platforms need to act on what they can already see. But when push comes to shove, banks are often the last and sometimes the only line of defense,” he added. “Funds can leave an account in minutes, and customers are often groomed into trusting the scammer over their bank. Banks must detect the manipulation itself, not just the transaction, and intervene before the money moves.”

A CybSafe report published last month found that over a fifth (22%) of Brits have received a scam call impersonating a familiar person’s voice or appearance. Over a third (36%) of these reports have led to their employer losing money or data.

articles.title: Taiwan-Based Hacker Used BOSSAI AI Agents to Steal Taipei Emergency Dispatch Records
articles.context: A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week
articles.full_text:
A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week.

The agents also found a Taipei fire department platform exposing patient data from 2018, including ECG readings and ambulance video footage, without a login.

The researchers are highly confident that the attacker is a single person based in Hualien City, Taiwan. He aimed the agents at hundreds of organizations in at least 11 countries, including emergency services, banks, universities and military systems. The agents collected data or accessed systems at about 10 of them in Taiwan, Mexico and Thailand.

The evidence comes from the attacker's own server, which initially appeared to be a misconfigured development system. It turned out to be his operational attack platform, containing more than 90,000 files, including the agents' conversations, his command history, hacking tools, credentials, and victims' data.

The agents did not communicate with each other, so the attacker manually pasted one agent's output into another. Commercial AI models mostly refused to help him attack. The attacking agents therefore ran almost entirely on "abliterated" models, meaning AI models run locally with their safety training removed.

What the Agents Reached

Taiwan was targeted far more heavily than any other country, according to the researchers' technical analysis. The most serious confirmed harm there involved emergency-services data.

The dispatch records came from a city's system for 119, Taiwan's emergency number for fire and ambulance services. The agents pulled them from the system's API, and they include incident times, response types, case status, and street-level locations. They are case records, not live ambulance tracking.

The researchers' summary says breaches at emergency services and universities led to the theft of medical and personal data. Their detailed account of the Taipei patient platform, however, says only that the records were exposed.

The agents also went after five other targets tied to Taiwan's emergency services:

Target

What the agents did

Result

Fire-dispatch technology vendor

Logged into its database admin panel with default root credentials. A web shell attempt through a known CVE failed.

Access to 18 or more database tables

Emergency management information system

Found a hardcoded AES-256 key in the site's front-end JavaScript that exposed session-cookie contents, including an administrator's identity

No confirmed compromise

National disaster-response center

A scanning tool reported a critical Apache remote code execution flaw

The flaw did not exist

National fire agency single sign-on portal

Tried to guess logins (brute force)

No confirmed access

Fire-department systems in five cities

Scanned them to identify the software they run

No confirmed compromise

The report does not say whether the affected organizations or Taiwan's authorities were told, or whether the exposed data can still be reached.

Outside emergency services, the agents pulled data from an account table at a Taiwanese lending firm through SQL injection. In Thailand, they collected data from three universities in the same way, after selecting 489 potential targets across 45 institutions.

In Mexico, they collected about 206,800 home phone records containing names and addresses, using government statistics, postal code lists, and telecom authority data.

About 15 more organizations were attacked without a confirmed break-in. In at least eight other countries, targets were only scanned or lined up for attacks that had not run by the time the researchers looked.

The researchers watched the operation for 12 days. One recorded exchange shows the attacker at work on July 25.

How the AI Was Used and Where It Failed

The setup, called BOSSAI, had 12 AI agents, with 9 in use. Some built and maintained the attacker's servers and tools, while others scanned targets and carried out attacks.

Commercial cloud models did most of the building, with Grok as the main builder. When the attacker directly asked them to attack, Grok and MiniMax M3 refused and requested written proof that the work was authorized. The researchers say it is unclear whether a fake authorization letter would have changed that.

Grok made one exception, repairing a broken proof-of-concept script that the attacker then handed to an attack agent. The attacker also redirected the coding agents Claude Code and Codex to an abliterated model, though they mostly did infrastructure work. Cursor, another coding agent, attacked a Taiwanese emergency-services site while running such a model.

The abliterated models were versions of DeepSeek, GLM, and Qwen.

The agents also got things wrong. One scanning tool invented CVEs, and more than half of its high and critical findings were false positives or wrongly classified. The main attack agent also reported results that had not happened.

Who Ran It

Acronis's attribution rests on mistakes the attacker made while hiding his identity, combined with publicly available information. He reused a single identity across his legitimate businesses and his attack servers, including a GitHub profile, a logo, an SSH key name, and an email address.

His home IP address appeared during an SSH session in one of his Grok conversations.

Why he did it is less clear. Some attacks on government, emergency, and military targets looked like the work of state-backed hacking groups, while others looked like ordinary cybercrime. The researchers think he probably wanted to make money, and it is unclear whether he works for anyone.

What Stopped the Agents

What the agents found was mostly data that was already poorly protected, according to the researchers: a medical data port left open since 2018, dispatch records on a public-facing API, a lender with 16 SQL injection points, and universities running unpatched Oracle databases.

The agents failed where logins were enforced, where paywalls required a valid session, and where endpoints were properly filtered. The AI made it cheap to find and reach many targets at once, but it did not get past defenses that held.

Nine IP addresses and nine domains from the attacker's setup appear in the indicator list at the end of the analysis. None is marked as active or inactive, and most come without a note on what they were used for.

articles.title: The code and the court: Why your email security thinks like Napoleon
articles.context: A codified system is only as current as its code
articles.full_text:
In 1804, Napoleon gave France a code that much of the world still runs on. The Code civil replaced a tangle of local customs with a single written statute: orderly and knowable. In that tradition, the judge’s job, in Montesquieu’s phrase, is to be the mouth of the law, nothing more. Certainty was the point.

Certainty has a cost. A codified system is only as current as its code. When the world produces something the code did not anticipate — a new technology, a new fraud — there is no statute to apply, and everyone waits for someone to write one.

Your email security works exactly this way. That is the problem.

Security by statute

A signature is a statute. Someone observes an attack, writes a rule that describes it, and from that moment you are protected against that attack and its close relatives. It is fast, certain, and blind to anything the code has not been written to see.

Signatures alone were never enough, so the industry made the code bigger. Anomaly detection and behavioral models are a thicker statute book, trained on what already happened and scoring how far a message deviates from it. More sophisticated than a signature, but not a different philosophy. A zero-day is a crime with no statute.

The strongest evidence against codified defense is not the attack that fails a check. It is the attack that passes every one. When a supplier’s mailbox is compromised, the message arrives from a real domain, with valid credentials and earned reputation. Every check comes back clean because the infrastructure is genuine. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that breaches involving a third party now account for 48% of the total, up 60% in a single year. Authentication did exactly what it measures: it confirmed the letter came from who it said, and had no rule for whether it should be believed. The code was consulted. The code said valid. The message was a theft in progress.

Attackers understand this. A codified defense is cheap to walk around. You do not break the code; you do something it was never written to cover. The FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report put business email compromise losses above $3 billion in a single year, much of it carried by messages that broke no rule because no rule described them.

The other tradition

The English-speaking world chose a different system. Common law does not always wait for the legislature. A judge facing a situation no statute anticipated can reason from principle and precedent to a verdict. It adapts case by case. It is not simply a code that has to be rewritten. It is a court that knows how to weigh a new set of facts.

That is the difference between detecting and reasoning. The fair objection is that a reasoning system also learns from the past. True. But there is a difference between matching a case to a stored pattern and applying a principle to a case you have never seen. A judge who has never encountered your particular dispute still knows how to weigh evidence.

None of this means throwing out the code. Most mail is open and shut and should be settled that way in milliseconds. You keep the fast rule for the easy calls and save a full hearing for the contested ones.

A court can also answer a question a code struggles with: why. A codified system can say “this matched” or “this deviated.” A verdict can cite its evidence: what the sender actually is, whether the relationship supports the request, what the message is asking for. You do not have to trust the reasoning. You check the evidence, because a ruling stands or falls on whether its facts hold up, not on the private thoughts of the judge. It is the opposite of a black box: a decision you can read, challenge, and overturn.

None of this retreats from zero trust. Zero trust governs access, who gets in and what they can touch, and assumes nothing. This is about the verdict, whether a message is what it claims to be, and there the posture is not to presume guilt or innocence but to let the evidence decide.

The court of last resort

For the highest stakes matters, a mature legal system does not let the machinery decide alone. In security, some decisions belong with the person whose money is about to move.

When a message asks for a wire, a change to vendor banking details or a payroll redirect, the right design does not render a silent verdict and hope. It escalates and asks the owner to approve the action itself. Reasoning handles the general docket. The human is the court of last resort, reserved for the decisions that deserve one. Match the process to the stakes.

No analogy is perfect. Real judges in both traditions do more than this, and civil-law systems evolve through their own doctrine.

The question worth ending on

For most of this industry’s history, there was no choice, because machines could apply a code but could not weigh evidence and reason for a judgment. That is no longer true.

There is a simple way to find out which system you are running. Ask your team how many attacks that reached a user came from infrastructure you already trust: a compromised vendor, a real account, a genuine DocuSign or Microsoft notification bent to a purpose it was never meant for. If that number is high, your defenses are not failing to enforce the code. They are enforcing it perfectly; against threats the code was never written to describe.

So, the question is not whether your defenses are up to date. A code is always, by definition, up to date with yesterday. The question is whether your security is a code or a court, and whether it can rule on the case it has never seen, because that is the only case that was ever going to hurt you.

articles.title: 7 tips for achieving defensive agility
articles.context: McGlasson points to the recent “Citrix meltdown,” a severe, ongoing security crisis affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, creating a mass wave of...
articles.full_text:
Defensive security agility reflects an organization’s potential to rapidly detect, adapt, and respond to evolving cyber threats and vulnerabilities without disrupting core operations. By abandoning static, rigid defense architectures, an agile defense plan emphasizes continuous iteration, automation, and cross-functional flexibility.

Defensive agility allows cybersecurity teams to rapidly adapt and respond to evolving threats while minimizing business disruption, says Anant Adya, an executive vice president at business and technology consulting firm Infosys. “As attack surfaces expand, organizations must prioritize risk quantification and identify vulnerabilities to strengthen their security posture and improve their ability to recover from attacks that are inevitable.”

Is your organization taking the steps needed to achieve a high degree of defensive agility? Read on to find out.

1. Establish a zero-trust baseline

Achieving defensive agility should begin with a zero-trust approach that continuously verifies access across users, devices, and applications, Adya advises. “An effective zero-trust strategy must be embedded into an organization’s technology framework and business lifecycle in order to build resilience and foster an organization-wide security mindset.”

As enterprises adopt AI, modernize applications, and operate across highly distributed environments, security must evolve from a protective afterthought into a business accelerant, Adya says. “By integrating zero trust into day-to-day operations and AI workflows, organizations can strengthen their ability to adapt to evolving threats while innovating faster, integrating acquisitions more securely, and scaling globally without accumulating architectural or operational debt.”

2. Modernize (and rationalize) your existing security infrastructure

Many large organizations are struggling to keep pace with emerging challenges because their systems are incredibly complex or filled with old software, custom code, and a mixture of disconnected security tools that can hinder containment speed, says Sharon Chand, cyber defense and resilience leader at Deloitte.

Chand advises CISOs to evaluate their existing infrastructure and technologies to consider how they’re currently responding to threats. Meanwhile, it’s important to streamline operations into a more integrated system. “Security organizations must also have access to AI-driven systems to detect and automate response to machine-speed attacks at the pace of adversaries,” she states.

3. Enlist AI where confidence is high and actions are reversible

Randy Gross, CISO at training and certification organization CompTIA, recommends deciding in advance which defensive actions are safe enough to happen without placing a human in the middle. “Locking an account, killing a session, or isolating a device should already be automated when confidence is high and the action is easy to reverse,” he says.

Review your strategy at least quarterly, but never equate a strategy review with operational governance, Gross warns. “In a medium-to-large enterprise, agents’ permissions and integrations may change frequently, so the guardrails around them must be continuous and automated,” he advises. “The CISO and team should also revisit their strategy when enough changes have been made to the point where risk has changed materially.”

Gross adds: “The strategy shouldn’t be just to put more AI in the SOC; it should be to reduce the latency between finding a threat and doing something useful about it.”

4. Forego higher walls in favor of dynamic, structural resilience

Defensive agility requires an enterprise system with the architectural capacity to absorb, isolate, and adapt to anomalous behavior without relying on human intervention, says Jatin Chopra, a senior software engineer at Microsoft. “It marks the transition from static perimeter defense — where you build higher walls — to dynamic, structural resilience where the environment itself constantly shifts to restrict threat propagation.”

Using an approach with sufficient capacity also detaches security from manual bottlenecking, Chopra says. “When defensive protocols are codified into the architecture rather than enforced by a review board, engineering teams can maintain high developer velocity while inherently restricting the attack surface.” It transforms security from a workflow tax into an automated platform capability, he states.

5. Beware bureaucracy that does not lead to decisive action

Stop treating your security strategy as an annual document process and begin viewing it as a loop that runs continuously utilizing data you trust, says Bob Maley, CISO at security-as-a-service provider Black Kite. Feed decisions to someone who actually has the authority to make rapid critical choices, he recommends.

Attackers are already highly vigilant, Maley warns. “When a new vulnerability opportunity lands on a Friday afternoon, nobody on a ransomware crew is waiting for a quarterly review to approve going after it,” he explains. “If your defense team needs a steering committee before it can react, the gap between their tempo and yours is where the breach lives.”

6. Embrace automation to free up human judgment

Most security teams I’ve worked with build static defenses, observes Timur Rakhmatullin, senior software engineer at Softline Solutions, a consulting and social media marketing services provider. “They set up rules, configure alerts, and write runbooks, but then something happens that doesn’t match the runbook and everyone freezes.”

Rakhmatullin believes that automation is essential. He runs automated security scans across 30-plus repositories using in-house tools. “The scans catch vulnerabilities, license issues, and other gaps,” Rakhmatullin explains. “But the key part is that any engineer can override a scan result, escalate it, or reclassify a finding in minutes.”

Still, automation does all the heavy lifting, Rakhmatullin says. “Humans make the judgment calls.”

7. Conduct regular ‘fire drills’

Rehearse ugly scenarios before they happen, suggests Chris McGlasson, founder of ClearStack Advisory, a fractional executive technology and AI strategy firm.

Know who patches, who tests, who talks to the business, and who has the authority to take something offline at 2 a.m., McGlasson says. “Write it down and run it twice a year,” he recommends. “The teams that do so treat incident response like a fire drill.” McGlasson adds that many CISOs risk disaster because they treat security like a research project instead of a fundamental initiative.

McGlasson points to the recent “Citrix meltdown,” a severe, ongoing security crisis affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, creating a mass wave of critical zero-day exploits. Citrix immediately warned IT administrators to patch their systems at once to address the issue.

As a result, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, gave federal agencies a three-day patch window, while other organizations were left to create their own timeline, McGlasson says. He notes that the shops that handled this challenging event well weren’t always the ones with the best tools. “They were the ones that already knew who patches, who tests, and who calls the shots before the advisory ever dropped.”

Agility is a muscle, McGlasson observes. “You build it through repetition.”

articles.title: Fake GitHub Security Tools Infect Over 2,000 PCs With Malware
articles.context: Cybersecurity firm Doctor Web has found malware hidden in GitHub projects that look like security tools
articles.full_text:
Fake GitHub security tools are spreading malware that disables defenses, steals sensitive data and infects over 2,000 PCs.

Cybersecurity firm Doctor Web has found malware hidden in GitHub projects that look like security tools. The campaign targets blockchain game fans and, more recently, information security professionals. The researchers discovered that more than 2,000 PCs were infected.

“The attackers behind these compromised development projects target blockchain game enthusiasts and (most intriguingly) …information security professionals.” reads the report. “At the time of Doctor Web’s research into this matter, more than 2,000 PCs were infected.”

The campaign started two years ago with Visual Studio projects related to blockchain games, game bots and cheats. The attackers targeted people who used crypto wallets. They hid malicious code in project files, including commands that ran before a project was built and PowerShell commands stored in configuration files. They even provided instructions on how to install Visual Studio and download the projects from GitHub, making it easy for people with limited technical knowledge to use them.

Now the attackers are targeting cybersecurity professionals. Their new GitHub projects claim to offer tools for automated scanning, security testing and log analysis. Doctor Web found one that pretends to analyze and clean results from the Fscan security scanner.

The attackers also hide malicious code in Python and Go files, using large blocks of blank spaces to make it harder to spot. Some of these fake security tools even remove the antivirus software installed on the victim’s computer.

Once a victim opens the project, a PowerShell script runs and contacts the attackers’ servers and legitimate platforms, including YouTube, Telegram, Google Docs, GitCode and Pastebin. An encrypted string it retrieves holds a link to an archive, which unpacks into a folder disguised as a Windows Photos component. Its main program is Microsoft.exe, a modular app built with the Electron framework.

It does most of the damage. The loader collects system information and sends it to a Telegram bot, keeps itself running, raises its privileges, and turns off Windows Defender, UAC, System Restore and shadow copies. It also adds its own Defender exclusions, injects code into legitimate processes, and removes McAfee, ESET and Malwarebytes antivirus products.

Its default mode, called Mode3, stacks several evasion tricks. It fakes its parent process, disables Smart App Control, removes security software hooks from ntdll.dll, makes direct system calls, and patches event tracing and antivirus script scanning in memory. If that fails, Mode2 takes over, adding Defender exclusions and injecting through PowerShell.

Three payloads follow. AsyncRAT, a remote access backdoor, runs as two identical copies on different ports, which probably lets two operators control one device. A clipper swaps crypto wallet addresses in the clipboard while taking screenshots, and a stealer takes browser data, FileZilla, MobaXterm and Total Commander configs, VPN settings, messenger files, game accounts and Discord tokens. Everything is zipped and sent through Telegram, and the malware edits the hosts file to block antivirus vendors’ domains.

The attackers are still developing the malware. Doctor Web found an unfinished component that could install itself as a system service, download Microsoft.exe again if someone deletes it, manage startup and install updates.

“Attackers are constantly updating the Trojans to introduce new features. For example, Doctor Web’s researchers discovered certain unused routines that facilitate downloading and decompressing yet another archive—Lodge.7z.” concludes the report. “It contains an Electron project that hasn’t been completed yet. The executable file’s name is WUDFHost.exe. Its code offers us a glimpse of some of the trojan’s future features.”

Doctor Web advises users to keep their antivirus software up to date and scan every file they download. The researchers warn that attackers are constantly improving the Trojans and adding new features.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Fake GitHub Security Tools)

articles.title: Former OpenAI Engineer Pleads Not Guilty to Planting Covert Device in Executive Meeting Room
articles.context: The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty
articles.full_text:
The OpenAI engineer who was arrested and charged last month for planting a covert audio recording device in the company's office has pleaded not guilty.

According to reports from Bloomberg and CNBC, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan made an appearance in San Francisco federal court on Friday, where he entered the plea. His next hearing is scheduled for November 17, 2026.

If proven guilty, the 35-year-old faces a maximum of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release. He has been held without bail since his arrest on October 9, 2026.

Late last month, a grand jury indicted Alfozan on a single count of interception of oral communications.

Prosecutors allege that the former OpenAI employee placed a "sophisticated recording device" in an executive OpenAI conference room in what has been described as an attempt to unlawfully record sensitive conversations.

He was arrested three days before he, along with his wife and son, were scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way ticket.

"His wife and son, however, immediately left the United States without him," U.S. prosecutors said. "Rather than wait until the October 12 flight as booked, they initially planned to fly to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on October 11 on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by the Saudi government."

"That flight was canceled, however, when a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for yet another one-way ticket for the defendant's wife and son, this one business class to Doha, Qatar, on October 10, 2026. They did make that flight, departing San Francisco about 36 hours after the defendant was arrested."

In a subsequent court filing, it was alleged that Alfozan was in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi Royal Family via WhatsApp. He was also deemed a flight risk, with court documents claiming that the defendant took great pains to create bespoke, encrypted recording devices to record sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives.

articles.title: The BBC has a plan for a Black Sky event, and it runs on FM radio
articles.context: ” The government’s Be Ready campaign warns that severe weather and cyberattacks could disrupt essential services, although it says there is no specific threat to the electricity...
articles.full_text:
The BBC plans to use emergency FM radio to keep the UK informed during prolonged blackouts, with a self-sufficient studio ready for 72 hours.

If electricity fails across the UK for days, the BBC says it has a plan to keep people informed. David Sillito, the BBC’s media and arts correspondent, explained the strategy in a BBC News report, starting with the 2015 Lancaster floods and ending with a simple lesson: when digital infrastructure fails, FM radio may be the most reliable way to reach the public.

On December 5, 2015, the River Lune flooded Lancaster, cutting electricity to 61,500 people. Roger Kemp, an engineering professor at Lancaster University specializing in safety and electrical systems, was watching television when the power went out. The following day, he described the scene to the BBC as almost resembling a zombie movie, with residents searching for phone reception and queuing at the only working telephone box.

Homes lost heating and lighting, while some water supplies stopped because their pumps depended on electricity. Railway stations, petrol stations and shops closed, cash machines stopped working, and traffic lights failed. Only two communication systems remained operational: copper landlines and FM radio. Local station The Bay continued broadcasting using an emergency generator and a single landline. Kemp’s subsequent report highlighted the irony: a society increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure had relied on technologies dating back decades to receive essential information.

The incident illustrated the risk of a wider catastrophe known as a Black Sky event, in which electricity, water, shops and communications fail simultaneously. At a recent UK resilience summit, discussions focused on maintaining essential services for at least 72 hours. One expression often heard in civil contingency circles, “nine meals from anarchy”, captures the concern that three days without food could turn an emergency into widespread disorder.

“We are nine meals from anarchy” is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.” BBC states.

“In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan.”

The government’s Be Ready campaign warns that severe weather and cyberattacks could disrupt essential services, although it says there is no specific threat to the electricity grid. According to government advice reported by the Express, households should maintain at least three days of food and drinking water and keep a battery-powered FM radio. Sillito also recommends a hand-cranked radio that can generate its own power.

The BBC’s contingency plan revolves around precisely this technology. Around 100 people would operate a dedicated emergency radio studio, equipped with secure communications independent of the internet, alongside enough fuel, water and food to survive at least three days without resupply. Reports published by French outlet Telesatellite and Open magazine on November 7 describe a self-contained studio, generators powering transmission facilities and FM radio as the fallback communication channel.

Only a small number of BBC staff know the complete details. The studio would broadcast pre-prepared government announcements, with scripts already published online. These include practical instructions on daily water consumption and disposing of toilet waste when flushing is impossible.

Additional reporting would come from satellite vehicles and journalists stationed at emergency centres across the UK. Transmission towers, disconnected from the internet, would use diesel generators and storage tanks ranging from 5 to 40,000 litres, providing approximately three days of power. Satellite phones would support communications between teams, with agreed meeting points and procedures if those systems also failed. FM radio remains central because it can reach almost everywhere, even during a major blackout or disruptive cyberattack.

The BBC’s planning assumptions have evolved. An insider told Sillito that the original scenario considered outages lasting five to seven days, while the latest advice from the National Energy System Operator suggests electricity could return within two to three days. The corporation’s contingency arrangements have surfaced before. In October 2022, media reports described leaked draft scripts for a national blackout, including half-hourly Radio 4 updates from an emergency broadcasting centre at an undisclosed rural location.

There is, however, a discrepancy in the Express report, which claims that only around 100 people worldwide know the full details. The BBC says approximately 100 people would operate the emergency studio, while only a small number have access to the complete plan.

Concerns about grid resilience are not new, but the massive blackout affecting Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 renewed attention to the issue. Lord Harris, chair of the National Preparedness Commission, argues that the consequences extend well beyond losing electricity. Water supplies could stop because pumping stations need power, while sewage systems could become blocked when water can no longer circulate. Governments across Europe increasingly advise citizens to maintain emergency supplies, and Harris believes the UK has been slow to prepare its population.

Some initiatives are already underway. ARIA, the government’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency, is investing £70 million in high-altitude aircraft designed to provide at least a week of emergency mobile and internet connectivity over the UK. Programme director Rico Chandra has warned that satellites alone have limitations when terrestrial networks fail.

Harris argues that decades of efficiency-driven decisions have gradually removed essential redundancies. One example is the migration of emergency services from dedicated radio systems to mobile network technology, potentially exposing their communications to the same outages affecting the public. The government maintains that the transition to 4G and 5G provides reliable and resilient communications.

“The UK has one of the most resilient electricity systems in the world, and there has never been a complete outage in the grid’s 75-year history.” The Cabinet Office states describing the UK electricity system.

Government efforts to improve resilience predate the current debate. In May 2024, then deputy prime minister Oliver Dowden launched the previous Conservative government’s disaster preparedness initiative.

During his investigation, Sillito also reconsidered the BBC’s isolated transmission infrastructure. What initially appeared outdated became a strength: independence from the internet could help keep broadcasting alive when digital networks collapse.

Yet the UK is preparing to switch off its copper landline network on January 31, 2027, while the future of FM radio is also under review. The government’s position is that copper landlines, although useful during power cuts, have become unreliable and increasingly difficult to maintain.

Kemp is less convinced that the country is moving in the right direction. Asked whether his report had improved national preparedness for a Black Sky event, he argued that the planned landline shutdown showed little consideration for how people would communicate during a prolonged power failure.

Sillito experienced a smaller reminder while preparing his report: a power cut in his own street, leaking torch batteries, missing candles and an emergency radio he could not find. His conclus: “If anything, we’ve gone backwards,” he said. “Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you’ve no longer got power.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, BBC)

articles.title: CISA Flags SonicWall SonicOS MFA Bypass Flaw Amid Reports of Possible Exploitation
articles.context: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a high-severity vulnerability impacting SonicWall SonicOS to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog,...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a high-severity vulnerability impacting SonicWall SonicOS to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports that it said may have been exploited in real-world attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-19868 (CVSS score: 7.1 / 7.5), has been described as an authentication reinforcement vulnerability via alternate authentication methods.

"An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSL-VPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls. Successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA)," SonicWall said in a Friday advisory.

The company also acknowledged that it "investigated a report indicating potential exploitation of this vulnerability," urging customers to update to the latest version as soon as possible. SonicWall did not disclose any additional specifics about the nature of the attack or who is behind the effort.

Also patched by SonicWall are a number of other high-severity flaws -

CVE-2026-107155 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A permissive cross-domain policy vulnerability in the SonicOS management interface that could potentially enable a remote unauthenticated attacker to perform unauthorized operations under specific conditions.

CVE-2026-107154 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A session validation vulnerability in the SonicOS management interface that could potentially enable a remote unauthenticated attacker to perform unauthorized operations under specific conditions.

CVE-2026-82308 (CVSS score: 7.5) - A pre-authentication heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the SonicOS SSL-VPN service that could potentially enable a remote unauthenticated attacker to cause an application level denial-of-service.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the patches by November 20, 2026, to secure their networks against the threat.

The development comes days after SonicWall detailed two unpatched vulnerabilities impacting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems (CVE-2026-109593 and CVE-2026-109594), urging customers to upgrade to Network Security Manager (NSM).

articles.title: Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked
articles.context: That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI
articles.full_text: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds. Writing in his weekly kernel update post, the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons. One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel. The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.” Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. “This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote. That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel. “I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn,” he added. “Don't hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we'll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.” If Torvalds is correct, that’s welcome news. The Linux kernel’s 40-million-plus lines of code makes it one of the world’s bigger software projects. If AI soon stops finding flaws in other parts of the kernel beyond eBPF, perhaps the deluge of fixes developers and users alike will need to handle has peaked. ®
