Introducing AWS account access manager: IAM role flexibility with centralized workforce access
articles.context: Account access manager launch partners Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into...
articles.full_text:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is introducing account access manager, a flexible new way to manage workforce access to your Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts. This combines the IAM role flexibility your teams already rely on, delivered through the centralized federation of AWS IAM Identity Center, with user-level visibility built-in.

Account access manager streamlines the assignment of your existing IAM roles from individual AWS accounts to your workforce users and groups in an organization instance of IAM Identity Center, giving you a clear path to centralized access management at scale. You can adopt account access manager on its own or alongside IAM Identity Center permission sets; both draw on the same users and groups you already synchronize from your corporate identity provider. That means you assign your existing IAM roles to those users and groups directly, without duplicating identities or managing per-account federation points.

Why use account access manager?

Enterprises scaling on AWS have long faced a difficult choice in workforce access: the flexibility of IAM roles or the central control of IAM Identity Center. Until now, granting workforce access to AWS accounts generally meant choosing one of two approaches, each with trade-offs to consider. Federating into each account separately with IAM roles gives you the full flexibility of IAM roles—custom trust policies, tags, and paths—but requires you to configure an identity provider and manage role assignments independently in each account, making it harder to assign a group across multiple accounts or maintain a unified view of who has access where. Federating once through IAM Identity Center with permission sets gives you a single federation point with centrally provisioned, uniform access, but permission sets can feel restrictive for teams whose roles vary from account to account, or that have difficulty generalizing their existing roles into uniform sets.

Account access manager removes the trade-offs. It’s built for customers who want the single federation point and identity-propagation benefits of IAM Identity Center together with the flexibility of IAM roles. Because it uses the IAM roles you already own, you keep the tailoring capabilities you rely on today:

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) – Use IAM role tags, or session tags populated from your identity provider as SAML claims, for fine-grained, attribute-driven authorization.

Precise trust policies – Restrict role assumption with network conditions or identity provider (IdP)-asserted claims, such as group membership, department, or cost center, as trust-policy conditions.

Role paths for organization at scale – Use IAM role paths to group roles and simplify administration as your environment grows.

Because roles are managed in the account you provision access to, account access manager scales with your account usage rather than relying on Identity Center specific quotas. Assignments are made to users and groups, reducing administrative overhead, and providing accountability and auditability to the specific user and role being used.

How it works

Access flows through IAM Identity Center and carries the user’s identity through trusted identity propagation. Even when multiple users assume a shared IAM role, each role session contains user context that attributes every action to the individual user. Access is granted and audited against the actual user, so you can see who assumed which role in which account. The result is user-level visibility across your organization, not just at the point of sign-in. You also maintain access to the full set of IAM role capabilities, such as role paths, tagging, naming conventions, and other IAM primitives.

Figure 1: Account access manager connects IAM Identity Center federated workforce users and groups to AWS accounts specific IAM roles

To grant a user access to a specific role in an account using account access manager, an administrator creates an entitlement. The user can then access that account from the new account access manager application portal or from their IAM Identity Center access portal, or retrieve credentials from the command line with aws login.

You can manage account access manager through the AWS Management Console for IAM and programmatically through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) (aws login and the account-access API namespace), AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, and HashiCorp Terraform and Pulumi, so you can enable it and manage role assignments the same way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. It exposes its own API namespace, account-access, separate from the IAM API, with its own permissions and AWS CloudTrail events.

How to enable account access manager

Here’s how to enable account access manager in your own environment, from prerequisites through your first role assignment.

Prerequisites

An organization instance of IAM Identity Center enabled.

Users or groups in IAM Identity Center that you want to entitle with IAM roles from individual AWS accounts. If users or groups don’t exist already then either:

Connect Identity Center to your external identity provider to automatically provision your corporate identities into Identity Center using SCIM.

Create users and groups in the Identity Center directory.

IAM roles in the individual AWS accounts that you want to assign to users and groups of IAM Identity Center. If the role you need doesn’t exist, create a role using custom trust policies first.

Appropriate permissions to enable account access manager and manage assignments (see the IAM policy examples later in this post).

Both the organization instance of IAM Identity Center and account access manager must be enabled in your organization’s management account.

For CLI access: Install or update to the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2.36.0 or newer.

Step 1: Enable account access manager

Before enabling account access manager, run the following command from the AWS organization management account to grant account access manager access to your organization:

aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal account-access.amazonaws.com

Next, use one of the following methods to enable account access manager:

Console:

Sign in to your organization’s management account.

In the AWS Management Console for IAM navigation pane, under Multi-account access, choose account access manager.

The console Region should be set to the primary Region of your IAM Identity Center instance.

If there is no organization instance of IAM Identity Center, you’ll be prompted to enable one before continuing. Otherwise, choose Enable account access manager.

Figure 2: Account access manager enablement from the IAM console

AWS CLI:

Fetch the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of your IAM Identity Center organization instance, confirm the Region code matches its primary Region, and run:

aws account-access create-application \ --region <Region> \ --identity-source '{ "identityCenter": { "instanceArn": "<IAM Identity Center Instance ARN>" } }'

As an output, the account access manager application ARN will be generated.

After you enable account access manager (through the console or AWS CLI), you will get the account access URL and the account access manager ARN along with other details on the capability.

Account access portal URL is the single sign-on entry point for your workforce. This is where your users will go to access AWS accounts. Its format is - https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws , found on the Settings tab of the account access manager console.

Account access manager ARN: the identifier for the application instance created when you enable account access manager. Note this ARN to use in your IAM role’s trust policies so that only your specific account access manager application can assume those roles, providing confused-deputy protection (see Step 3 for details) and pass it as --application-arn when creating entitlements using the AWS CLI so each assignment is tied to the correct application instance.

Figure 3: Account access manager settings after enablement

In the AWS CLI, run the command aws account-access list-applications to get the application ARN and tenant-ID of the enabled account access manager instance ARN.

Step 2: Update firewalls and gateways

If you filter access to specific AWS domains or URL endpoints with a next-generation firewall (NGFW) or Secure Web Gateway (SWG), allowlist the account access portal domains and endpoints in the following list. Account access manager has no IPv4-only endpoints; endpoints are dual-stack.

Account access portal URL – https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws

Portal APIs – [Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws/api/* and /auth/*

Control plane – account-access.[Region].api.aws

Runtime – account-access-runtime.[Region].api.aws

Console – console.aws.amazon.com/account-access

Step 3: Prepare your IAM roles

Before assigning IAM roles to users and groups, update the role’s trust policy to allow account access manager service to assume it.

Add the following statement to the role’s trust policy (or paste the entire policy that follows if you’re creating a new role). Replace <your-account-id>, <region> (your IAM Identity Center primary Region), and <application-id> (from the Settings page of the console).

Figure 4: Account access manager ARN details

IAM role trust policy:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AccountAccessManagerIAMRoleTrustPolicyStatement", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "account-access.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:SetContext", "sts:TagSession" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": "<your-account-id>", "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:account-access:<region>:<your-account-id>:application/<application-id>" } } } ] }

Define the Condition block to enforce confused-deputy protection. It helps ensure that the role can be assumed only by the specific account access manager application instance (defined using the application ARN) created when you enabled the service, and only when the request originates from your AWS account where that instance resides.

Best practice:

Propagate identity attributes with ABAC – The sts:TagSession action listed in the preceding IAM role trust policy allows upstream attributes from your identity provider (group memberships, department, cost center) to flow through as principal tags on the session. Without it, role assumption still succeeds; only session-tag propagation is suppressed. Add it when downstream IAM policies use aws:PrincipalTag/<key> and the tag is populated from your IdP SAML claims; leave it out otherwise.

Automate the trust-policy update – We recommend updating your IAM role-creation workflows to add this trust-policy statement automatically wherever it’s needed, so new roles are assignable from day one. You can use this sample-aam-migration tool as a reference.

Step 4: Assign access to users and groups

Like IAM Identity Center role entitlements, an entitlement in account access manager requires three components: a user or group ID, an account ID, and an IAM role ARN (instead of a permission set ARN). You can create assignments from the Accounts, Users, or Groups tabs in the console, or using the API or AWS CLI. For assignments where the same role needs to be assigned to multiple users, you must create each assignment individually. You can automate it using the account access API, the AWS SDK, or AWS CLI.

Assign from the console:

Choose the Users tab and search by username or display name.

Select the user, then choose Assign new access.

Figure 5: Assign new access in account access manager

On the Assign account access page, enter the workforce user or group, account ID, and IAM role name, then choose Assign access.

Assign a user using AWS CLI:

aws account-access create-entitlement \ --region <Region> \ --application-arn "<Account_access_manager_ARN>" \ --entitlement '{ "principalRole": { "principal": { "identityCenter": { "userId": "<Identity_Center_User_ID>" } }, "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/<ROLE_NAME>" } }'

To assign a group, replace the userId block with "groupId": "<IDC_GROUP_ID>". To remove access, use aws account-access delete-entitlement with the entitlement ID.

Note:

The console can search users, groups, and accounts, but it can’t detect IAM roles because they can come from different AWS accounts in your organization; you must know the role name beforehand.

Only IAM roles whose trust policy grants account access manager as an allowed service principal are eligible for assignment.

IAM role sessions assigned by account access manager use the maximum session duration configured on the underlying IAM role in each AWS account, up to 12 hours.

Step 5: How workforce users can sign in

Workforce users can federate to AWS accounts using IAM roles assigned through account access manager in any of the following ways:

Directly through the account access portal URL – Navigate to the portal URL (for example, https://aa-xxxxxxxxx.account-access.us-east-2.app.aws, or a vanity URL) and sign in.

Through the AWS access portal – Go to the Applications tab, select the Account Access application, and you’ll be redirected to the account access portal, where your assigned accounts and their respective roles are listed.

Tip: We recommend that users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal for faster navigation. In addition, if you use a supported IdP, such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity, you can add the account access portal as a bookmark app in the IdP’s dashboard, giving users authenticated, single-click access to the portal directly from the tools they already sign in to each day.

Access through a web browser

Use the following steps to use account access manager through a web browser.

Navigate to the account access portal URL and sign in with your credentials.

On the portal, find the AWS account you need. Search by account name or ID to filter the list of accounts you’re assigned to.

Expand the account to see the roles you can assume.

Select a role (for example, Developer). A new tab opens, signed into that account with the selected role.

Access through the AWS CLI

Account access manager works with the aws login command. To get started:

Install the latest AWS CLI (v2.36.0 or newer).

Sign in through your default browser – Sign in to your account access portal and into the target AWS account using one of your assigned roles.

On the AWS CLI, run:

aws login

Set a default Region if prompted – If you haven’t set one, the AWS CLI will prompt you for a Region (for example, us-east-2).

Select your session – The AWS CLI opens a browser page; select the tile for the session you initiated.

Confirm and return to the CLI – The page confirms that your credentials were shared successfully. Close the tab and keep working in the AWS CLI for the duration of your session.

The temporary credentials are automatically rotated by the AWS CLI, AWS Tools for PowerShell, and AWS SDKs, and remain valid for the default session duration of an IAM role. After the session expires, you’re prompted to sign in again on the browser.

Note: IAM Identity Center–specific commands, such as aws sso configure, don’t work with account access manager assignments; use aws login instead. If you want to continue to use aws sso login, refer to AWS CLI Integration for IAM Account access manager.

Create shortcut links to specific console destinations

The portal also lets you create a shortcut link that opens a specific console destination for a given account and role. Shortcut links work only with accounts and roles already assigned to the user—they can’t grant new access—and URL parameters must be URL-encoded. Because shortcut links are Regional and expose the account ID and role name in plain text, review your organization’s sharing policies before experimenting with them.

Customer managed key considerations

If your IAM Identity Center instance is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, which is required when you replicate IAM Identity Center to additional Regions, check the key policy before you enable account access manager. We recommend implementing the current baseline KMS key policy to ensure account access manager can read user, group, and instance data from IAM Identity Center.

Best practices summary

Enable in the right place – Enable account access manager in your organization’s management account and in the same Region as your IAM Identity Center instance and confirm your organization instance is in place before you begin.

Automate trust-policy updates – Build the account access manager trust-policy statement into your role-creation pipelines so every new role is assignable from day one, with no manual intervention.

Add sts:TagSession only when you need it – Include it only where downstream policies consume principal tags; otherwise leave it off to keep sessions lean and least-privilege.

Assign roles to groups, not individual users – Granting access at the group level reduces administrative overhead and strengthens the auditability of user-level access.

Scope administrator permissions tightly – Separate managing the feature from managing assignments, and enable delegating administration to keep day-to-day operations out of the management account.

Allowlist the portal domains before rollout – Add the account access portal domains and endpoints to your next-generation firewall or Secure Web Gateway ahead of launch to avoid access disruptions.

Prepare your workforce users – Have users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal and communicate the aws login flow clearly to your developers.

Account access manager launch partners

Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into their existing solutions, making it available to our joint customers from day one. Leading identity providers Okta, PingIdentity and Cisco Duo extend account access manager so customers can manage human workforce access to AWS accounts directly from the identity platforms they already use. Alongside them, access-governance and privileged-access partners Apono, BeyondTrust, Britive, Sonrai Security, C1.ai and Lumos added capabilities to govern, provision, and audit that access through the tooling our customers already rely on.

Account access manager also integrates with leading infrastructure-as-code (IaC) partners, so teams can define and manage access assignments declaratively alongside the rest of their AWS infrastructure. Pulumi enables customers to codify account access manager role assignments as part of their existing provisioning workflows, bringing repeatable, version-controlled automation to workforce access at scale.

Conclusion

Account access manager combines the flexibility of the IAM roles your teams already own with the single, centralized federation point of IAM Identity Center, adding user-level visibility into what users or roles have done across your organization. You assign existing IAM roles to users and groups centrally, scale with your account usage rather than a fixed quota, and give developers a fast, secure command-line experience with aws login. It’s available at no additional cost, enabled by default in Commercial Regions (excluding opt-in Commercial Regions, GovCloud (US), China, and other non-commercial Regions).

To see account access manager in action, watch the enablement video, which walks through enabling the service, preparing your IAM roles, and assigning access to your workforce end to end. You can also extend account access manager through our launch partners; leading identity, access-governance, and IaC providers who have integrated the service into their platforms, so you can govern, provision, and automate workforce access to AWS using the tooling you already rely on. Review the preceding partner integrations to find the ones that fit your environment.

To learn more and get started, visit the AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide. We encourage you to enable account access manager in a test organization, assign your first entitlement, and explore how centralized, user-attributed access can simplify your AWS environment.

Moumita Saha

Moumita is a Sr. Identity Specialist Solutions Architect, currently driving identity innovation, she builds customer solutions, shapes product direction, and advances access management practices across industries. With over 14 years of security expertise, she has delivered high-impact security innovations for Fortune 500 enterprises and Global Systems Integrator partners.

Omar Zoma

Omar is a Principal Security Solutions Architect with AWS Industries. With 15 years of security experience spanning multiple industries, his goal is to help customers understand and improve their security and compliance posture in a scalable way. He tackles global security challenges through content creation, teaching, knowledge sharing, and contributing to global standards and organizational bodies.

Blake Franzen

Blake is a Sr. Security Solutions Architect at AWS Industries. He works with large enterprises across industries like Media & Entertainment and Healthcare and Life Sciences to help secure their most critical workloads and find new ways to innovate securely. He is based out of Seattle with over 7 years of experience.

articles.title: Get root on a musl Linux system by slamming it with an overly long password
articles.context: The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions
articles.full_text: On certain Linux systems, an attacker could gain root access by entering a password longer than 256 bytes. The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions. The flaw affects certain Linux systems using musl libc instead of the traditional GNU C library, and even then only those running OpenSSH's secure shell daemon without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) and with password authentication enabled. If those conditions are met, and at least one other account has a valid password hash, accounts that shouldn't accept passwords, such as root, key-only deployment users, and LDAP users, may be accessed by supplying a password between 257 and 1,024 characters. The targeted accounts must have an asterisk (*) in their password field, and direct root login remains subject to OpenSSH's configuration. That might seem niche, but sorry: It’s not. Musl libc is common in embedded Linux systems due to its low footprint. More critically than that, it's also the standard C library for Alpine Linux, which provides official cloud images for both AWS and Azure. Some Alpine systems running in those environments may therefore be vulnerable, depending on their configuration. Dawn of the *sshole The vulnerability in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux systems dates back to 2016, but Kültekin explains that its roots go back much further – to the BSD Unix era, actually. In 1980, Sun Microsystems cofounder and BSD Unix heavyweight Bill Joy was involved in the development of BSD Unix, whose password file contained a single asterisk in the /etc/passwd entry for the daemon user. The asterisk wasn't a password hash and effectively disabled password authentication for that account. Nowadays, password hashes typically live in /etc/shadow and contain hashed information that the system uses to verify a plaintext password entered by a user. Asterisks are still present for accounts that aren't supposed to accept password logins, but as Kültekin explains in his writeup, that isn't exactly a foolproof way to keep people out. The crypt() function, which generates password hashes for comparison with stored values, can return NULL if it can't compute a hash. Applications that fail to check that result may crash. Musl libc's developers instead chose to return a single character for certain failures, and they picked the asterisk. Musl also added SHA-512-based password hashing around the same time, which Kültekin notes gets slower the longer a password is, potentially leading to denial of service if someone floods a server with a super-long password. Musl capped passwords at 256 bytes, and you can likely see where this is going. In 2016, OpenSSH introduced a workaround to prevent attackers from enumerating valid account names through SSH. Before the change, sshd could reject authentication attempts for nonexistent users more quickly than those for valid accounts. Attempts against valid accounts took longer because the server had to hash the supplied password before rejecting it. The solution was to have sshd perform dummy password hashing for invalid users, using an appropriate hashing algorithm and salt to reduce differences in response times. On affected musl-based Linux systems, accounts marked with an asterisk instead of a password hash could be busted open by supplying a password longer than 256 bytes – a flaw dating back to 2016. Any musl-based Linux system running a vulnerable OpenSSH configuration without PAM, with password authentication enabled, at least one account marked with an asterisk, and another account with a valid password hash could be vulnerable to a *sshole attack. Luckily, OpenSSH acted fast to fix this issue, and any OpenSSH build 10.6p2 (released Thursday) or newer is protected. Alternatively, if you can’t update your OpenSSH implementation on an affected system, just disable password authentication and restart the SSH daemon and you should be all set. There’s no indication that vulnerable systems have been exploited, but if you want to check, Kültekin has included a simple CLI command in his writeup that can be used to check if any no-password accounts on a sensitive machine recently took a password. ®

articles.title: October crypto-tracker hack: Access cracked, law enforcement tokens packed
articles.context: In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of...
articles.full_text: Blockchain analysis outfit Chainalysis has confirmed that when attackers broke into its systems in October, they managed to grab usernames, password hashes, and live tokens. In an update written late Wednesday evening, the company, a leader in blockchain analysis which has some very high-profile global customers and partners, confirmed the impact of the attack for the first time. In previous updates, which Chainalysis has issued regularly since it detected the intrusion on October 30, it confirmed that user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels were exposed. The news of password hashes and live tokens also being accessed reflects a worsening picture for the company. Chainalysis did not confirm the type of hashing algorithm it used to encrypt users' passwords, which makes it difficult to draw conclusions about the offline crackability of users' hashed credentials. Some users received emails instructing them to change their passwords, but Chainalysis said in its latest update that the password reset functionality is currently down. Nevertheless, users were also encouraged to change their passwords on any site where they reuse credentials. In addition to the exposed data, Chainalysis also detected "abnormal activity" on its transaction screening products, and has taken services down while "our team completes critical work." These include, but are not limited to, the Reactor blockchain investigation platform used by international law enforcement customers, the Data Solutions threat intelligence platform, and the KYT (know your transaction) anti-money laundering solution's user interface and login page. Regarding Reactor and the associated investigation data, Chainalysis said: "At this time, we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated." The company plans to reinstate KYT and the risk-intelligence Address Screening tool at some point today (Thursday November 5). Customers will have to provide the company’s support team or their account manager with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can begin resetting their passwords. "We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary. "We know how business-critical these services are to our customers, and we are working expeditiously alongside our outside experts to restore them securely." Chainalysis has not yet commented on who was behind the attack, but implied that the culprits used an AI agent, and likened the attack to others that have hit "many other tech platforms in recent weeks." "This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," it told customers in its initial disclosure on October 30. "Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems." In Wednesday's updates, it referred to the intrusion as an "ongoing multifront cyberattack," and later, an "on-path attack," otherwise known as an attacker-in-the-middle (AitM) attack, without elaborating further about what it entailed. Per its own company description, Chainalysis counts government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, financial institutions, and cybersecurity companies among its customer base. It is one of the world's foremost blockchain analysis companies and is routinely engaged to assist in cyber-related law enforcement investigations. Recent cases the company was asked to support include the takedowns of crypto-laundering network AudiA6 and bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine, both of which were known facilitators of ransomware crews. It also played a role in bringing down the infamous LockBit ransomware operation, among other engagements in the interim. ®

Researchers Bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode to Exfiltrate Chats Without User Interaction
articles.context: " Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt,...
articles.full_text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability that could be exploited to bypass Lockdown Mode protections in OpenAI ChatGPT.

Lockdown Mode was introduced by the artificial intelligence (AI) company in June 2026 as an optional setting to minimize data exfiltration risks arising from prompt injections.

"The flaw could enable silent chat data theft, phishing, and malware delivery, including zero-click data exfiltration in the ChatGPT desktop application," Eli Smadja, head of research at Check Point, said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The problem stems from HTML page previews inside ChatGPT code blocks, which allow HTML content to be rendered directly within the application. Given that executing user-supplied HTML and JavaScript can introduce security risks of its own, the content is placed inside a sandbox so that it cannot access data from the app, such as cookies and local storage.

The sandbox also prevents the rendered content from communicating with external resources without user consent. Lockdown Mode acts as a security barrier, mitigating data exfiltration risk by limiting outbound network requests that could be used to transfer sensitive information to an attacker-controlled infrastructure.

However, Check Point found a loophole in the manner popup windows are handled during HTML previews that made it possible to escape the confines of the sandbox and bypass Lockdown Mode.

"The HTML preview used nested sandboxed frames, and while ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying sandbox permissions still allowed popups and permitted them to escape the sandbox," Smadja explained.

"By creating another nested frame within the rendered page, it was possible to access an unmodified popup function and bypass the restrictions placed on the original HTML preview. Content opened through this route was no longer subject to the same sandbox restrictions, providing a way to circumvent the protections of Lockdown Mode."

Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat.

What's more, as the attacker is in complete control of the content displayed in the popup window, it could be used to render convincing social-engineering lures, such as a fake ChatGPT update, and trick the victim into downloading malware by persuading them to click on a link.

That said, the underlying issue is not limited to the Electron-based desktop environment, highlighting how weakness outside of the scope of the AI model can undermine AI security controls. Following responsible disclosure, the vulnerability was addressed by OpenAI on September 18, 2026.

"Lockdown Mode was specifically intended to reduce the possibility of data leaving a conversation through potentially malicious outbound requests, yet a weakness in another application feature provided an alternative path around that security boundary," Smadja said.

"The finding raises a broader enterprise security issue: AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them."

The disclosure comes a week after Parameter Labs detailed a way to bypass ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy (CSP) and take over anyone's account simply by sending an attacker-controlled public ChatGPT share link and prompting them to click the HTML preview once. If the HTML block is marked as previewable, it's opened automatically.

"An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," security researcher Mukul Goyal said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt[.]com with access to the victim's authenticated web session."

Earlier this September, Check Point also demonstrated a covert cross-account command channel through which an attacker could use a victim's ChatGPT session to run hidden tasks with the tools, data, and connected apps available to that session, alongside the visible conversation.

"The victim could receive a normal answer to their visible request while the attacker's task was processed separately and its result returned across accounts," Check Point said. "The channel operated through code-execution environments belonging to different ChatGPT accounts."

"The hidden instruction could be delivered through a malicious prompt, a shared ChatGPT conversation, or a custom GPT. Once it was present in the victim's conversation context, an ordinary message could trigger the attacker-controlled task without revealing it in the visible response."

The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of security shortcomings in various AI-driven tools and services over the past few months to trick them into spilling secrets or carrying out unauthorized actions -

An attack called SkillJacking that hijacks dependencies used by skills (repositories, packages, domains, or cloud apps) to compromise every agent installing them.

A set of vulnerabilities in built-in browsers associated with five AI coding assistants, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, and Anthropic Claude Desktop that could be exploited to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof web browser address bars. The issues have been codenamed Embrace, short for EMbedded BRowser - Arbitrary Code Execution, Arbitrary Content Exfiltration, and Arbitrary Context Emulation.

A technique called Repeat-After-Me that targets LangChain LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft AutoGen, Google Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS Strands Agents, and CrewAI and tricks them into running tool calls by means of a "seemingly benign text-repetition request."

A vulnerability called AgentCorruption that could allow an attacker to interact with an exposed AI agent running on AWS Bedrock AgentCore and leverage prompt injection techniques to influence that agent and extract its IMDS credentials, and then use them to access other agents, read private conversations, steal connected-tool credentials, and manipulate agent behavior.

A vulnerability in SpaceXSI Grok and GitHub Copilot CLI called Cryptographic Context Injection that could be exploited to read a developer's local files and send them to an external server from a single web page via an indirect prompt injection, which hides malicious instructions inside AES-encrypted text.

A zero-click vulnerability called SalesBleed that could be exploited to extract sensitive account data out of Salesforce Agentforce by leveraging the Web-to-Lead form to plant an indirect prompt injection payload.

A proof-of-concept (PoC) attack called not-a-mused that allows an unprivileged local attacker (or process) to redirect Meta Muse's dictation traffic and abuse the permissions granted to the AI assistant to perform arbitrary actions.

A zero-click vulnerability called Plugin4Shell that could be exploited to conduct an AI supply chain attack by silently swapping a trusted plugin with a malicious one while bypassing SHA pinning. "The agent checks out the exact commit the marketplace pinned but never verifies it landed there, so an attacker who controls the plugin's repo makes the checkout resolve to malicious code while the pin still looks honored," Air Security said. "The result is zero-click remote code execution across Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI."

An attack called BragJack that can be exploited to hijack the AI agents built into browsers like Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, and Anthropic Claude in Chrome by using an already installed malicious browser extension in conjunction with prompt forcing.

A behavioral effect called sampling drift demonstrates how adding an invisible watermark to a large language model's (LLM) output can unintentionally change how the model behaves, including the tools an AI agent invokes, and likely weaken safety refusals. "Watermarking changes refusal behavior on bare harmful requests, but the effect is more pronounced when the same requests are paired with the prompt-injection technique," Lasso Security said. "On several models, watermarking then makes the model more likely to answer harmful requests that it would otherwise refuse."

A set of attacks that exploit customer support AI agents to compose and send phishing emails, invoke tool calls, and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) protections.

A prompt-crafting technique called PuzzleMask that bypasses quick LLM-based policy checks carried out by a lightweight gatekeeper model by planting the malicious instruction in a specially crafted prose wrapper, after which the payload is processed by a more powerful target model to trigger malicious actions.

A technique called Workflow Identity Hijacking allows an attacker to bypass standard controls by sending normal, benign requests through an unauthenticated entry point, causing the enterprise AI pipeline to process the request and execute the action as designed. "The core failure is that the requester had no authority to make that request," Noma Security said. "When an AI workflow performs downstream actions, it executes using high-privilege service accounts or developer API keys rather than enforcing the permissions of the external user. As a result, AI workflows become unauthenticated proxies for privileged actions and silent data exfiltration."

A zero-click vulnerability class called PleaseFix that could be exploited to hijack AI agents embedded in agentic browsers by placing malicious instructions inside emails, calendar invitations, or web pages, and exploit a technique referred to as intent collision to cause the agent to "act on the attacker's behalf using the user's own identity, permissions and access."

A set of vulnerabilities impacting AI coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that could be exploited to trick them into handing over a victim's secrets, achieving persistent instruction poisoning by modifying the AGENTS.md file, and compromising software releases through prompt injections placed inside untrusted user inputs, like GitHub issues.

"Agents are becoming the default infrastructure across CI/CD, messaging, triage, incident response, and support," Novee Security said. "The more autonomous they get, the more the harness decides what's safe on your behalf, and the more untrusted input reaches real execution."

articles.title: Tobacco company got smoked by leaving secret recipes on a file share
articles.context: He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential
articles.full_text: Welcome once again to PWNED, where all of the security victims are self-owned. Today, we celebrate a company that makes a supremely unhealthy product having a supremely unhealthy security posture. Our tale of terrible data management, once again, comes courtesy of professional pen tester and red teamer Dahvid Schloss. Assigned to find flaws in the network of a tobacco company, Schloss stumbled onto some very poorly protected trade secrets. Schloss started by probing the network with tools like Metasploit, a popular open-source pen testing app. Surprisingly, the company’s Trend Micro antivirus did not issue an alert even as he was scanning the network for vulnerabilities. He compared the process to shooting a machine gun and having no one hear it. "I'm running through this environment, and I'm basically just using the loudest toys and tools you can imagine," he told The Register. It seemed as if the client simply didn't care much. "I'm feeling like there's not a whole lot of value that I'm providing here." Schloss then asked his boss what else he could do to make his findings more useful and compelling to the client. "My senior manager turns to me and goes 'Think about what is important to this organization. If it got leaked, how detrimental would it be to their business?'" Schloss said. "I’m thinking it’s a products company. Maybe their recipes." Schloss began searching for network file shares that allowed unauthenticated or anonymous access. After discovering an open share, he scanned it using the network mapping tool Nmap. The scan revealed that ports 139 and 445 were open, indicating that the system was running the Windows SMB file sharing protocol. Despite hosting sensitive IT and HR records, this specific file share had no access restrictions and was completely exposed to every employee in the company. He clicked through the directories and found a folder named “confidential." He found files in there which were named recipe, the product name, the sub product name, and the date. He opened one file and discovered that it had information about how that tobacco product was made, including the weight and volume and what percentage of each chemical it had inside. The file was marked with red letters at the top that said "Confidential" and another set at the bottom that said "Do not share." “I think we found a smoking gun here. This is pretty bad,” Schloss said. He noted that anyone on the network could simply use Windows Explorer to find the file. Schloss downloaded the file, thinking he'd be able to show it to the company to prove that the data could be exfiltrated. But his manager asked him to delete the downloaded file, because it was such sensitive information that he shouldn't retain a copy. This would later harm his ability to show that it had ever existed at all. He then told the security team at the tobacco company what he had found, expecting them to lock down all the recipe files. But when he returned to the site the next morning, he got a big surprise: His contact came by and told him that the recipes he found were not real. He denied the files had ever existed and that there was a security problem at all. "And we're just kind of baffled because we're like, what? What are you talking about? This is clearly a recipe you guys have," Schloss said. "It's in the right department. It's in the right folder structure, it's named the right way. Anybody who saw this would consider this a recipe." He listed the recipe files in his security report, but the security people at the tobacco company vehemently denied that the files were real or that he had seen a real recipe. They continued arguing about it for a year and Schloss could not show them the recipe file he had downloaded because he had been forced to erase it. "The funny thing is, I went back and checked towards the end of the engagement to see if those files are still in that folder. And no, they were gone, they were deleted or moved, or something," he said. "So there was obviously some truth behind it, but they wanted to deny the finding." ®

articles.title: Vulnerability Scans for Older Cisco IOS Vulnerability / Opt-Out Headers, (Thu, Nov 5th)
articles.context: Instead, I first ran into some GeoServer exploits, but found them to be too boring to write up
articles.full_text:
This morning, I was browsing our honeypot data for any new and existing PHP exploit attempts. Instead, I first ran into some GeoServer exploits, but found them to be too boring to write up. This Cisco IOS exploit attempt was a bit more interesting. Still nothing new. I suspect this is for CVE-2023-20198.

POST /%77ebui_wsma_https HTTP/1.1 Host: [redacted]:8000 User-Agent: RootEvidence/1.0 Content-Length: 720 Connection: close Content-Type: text/xml; charset=UTF-8 Opt-Out-Email: re-abuse@rootevidence.com Opt-Out-Url: https://www.rootevidence.com/scanners Accept-Encoding: gzip

<?xml version="1.0"?> <SOAP:Envelope xmlns:SOAP="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" xmlns:SOAP-ENC="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/encoding/" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"> <SOAP:Header> <wsse:Security xmlns:wsse="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/ws/2002/04/secext"> <wsse:UsernameToken SOAP:mustUnderstand="false"> <wsse:Username>admin</wsse:Username><wsse:Password>*****</wsse:Password></wsse:UsernameToken></wsse:Security></SOAP:Header><SOAP:Body><request correlator="exec1" xmlns="urn:cisco:wsma-exec"> <execCLI xsd="false"><cmd>uname -a</cmd><dialogue><expect></expect><reply></reply></dialogue></execCLI></request></SOAP:Body></SOAP:Envelope>

I highlighted the actual command (uname -a) above. But also interesting is the use of a "Opt-Out-Email" and "Opt-Out-Url" header. Rootevidence is yet another exposure/vulnerability management Platform. I couldn't find a standard that suggests them, and I think it is the first time I've seen them. Rootevidence has been using them since December last year, but this is the first time I noticed them.

Oh, and they are doing URL encoding for the "w" in the URL. I bet there are some stupid WAFs that fall for that.

-- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter|

articles.title: Zyxel Switch Patch Missed Flaw Behind Wave of Attacks
articles.context: A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks...
articles.full_text:
A flaw in Zyxel GS1900 switch firmware has been found to survive a June security update, raising questions about whether that patch fixed the vulnerability exploited in attacks on 996 switches in 48 countries.

Firmware security company Binarly detailed the finding in research published on November 3, linking it to an exploit that threat intelligence firm GreyNoise had described in September. The vulnerability now carries a new identifier, CVE-2026-107441. It is an out-of-bounds write flaw in the switches' web management program that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to run operating system (OS) commands with root privileges.

The attacks had originally been tied to CVE-2026-7273, which Zyxel fixed on June 16 and described as a stack-based buffer overflow in the same program, rated 8.8. On September 21, GreyNoise reported that an attacker had exploited that flaw against 996 Zyxel GS1900 switches in 48 countries, taking switch configurations, hashed root credentials and networking information.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog the same day.

Read more on network device zero-days: Critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Zero-Day Under Active Exploitation

June Fix Left Vulnerable Code in Place

Binarly analyzed an obfuscated Python exploit that matched the one GreyNoise described. On September 28, the researchers confirmed that all 10 firmware releases shipped as the June fix remained vulnerable to it.

Binarly said the June change added a check, but the check ran only after the unsafe copy had already occurred. The researchers wrote that the change "does not address the vulnerability."

The firm offered two explanations. Either the June patch, its description and its Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score were incorrect, or the attacks used a different flaw and CISA's link to CVE-2026-7273 would be wrong.

Either way, Binarly said, all 10 releases advertised as fixes contain the vulnerable code.

Severity Disputed as Zyxel Ships New Firmware

Zyxel rates CVE-2026-107441 at 8.8 and says an attacker must be on the local network to exploit the vulnerability, while Binarly rates it 9.8 and says exploitation requires only network access to the switch's management service.

Binarly said it notified Zyxel on September 29. Zyxel confirmed the flaw on October 11, released a fix on October 22 and published its advisory on November 3.

The flaw affects ten GS1900 models. On the GS1900-8, for example, firmware 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and earlier is affected and 2.90(AAHH.3)C0 contains the fix.

Zyxel told users to install the updates "for optimal protection." Its advisory lists the June releases among the affected versions, so switches last updated in June still need the new firmware.

articles.title: GitHub to Block pull_request_target Workflows by Default Starting December 2
articles.context: A malicious contributor can exploit those mistakes to execute commands with access to credentials and other resources intended only for trusted automation
articles.full_text:
GitHub will begin blocking GitHub Actions workflows triggered by pull_request_target in public repositories on December 2, 2026, expanding its protections against a class of CI/CD vulnerabilities that has repeatedly enabled attackers to steal credentials and compromise open source software releases.

The restriction, originally announced in September, will prevent affected workflows from running unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. GitHub had initially scheduled enforcement for November 2 but confirmed the postponed December 2 deadline in a new update this week, giving maintainers additional time to review their automation and configure exceptions.

The new restriction goes beyond protections introduced in June, when GitHub updated actions/checkout to prevent common attempts to check out untrusted pull request code inside privileged workflows. This time, GitHub is blocking the pull_request_target trigger itself by default, including for workflows that use it safely.

pull_request_target Is Now a Common Attack Vector Vector #

GitHub introduced pull_request_target in 2020 to help maintainers automate tasks involving pull requests from external contributors. Unlike the standard pull_request event, which restricts access to secrets and provides a read-only token for contributions from forks, pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository with access to its configured secrets and token permissions.

That elevated access makes the trigger useful for legitimate maintenance tasks such as assigning reviewers, labeling pull requests, and posting authenticated comments. The workflow definition runs from the repository's trusted default branch, rather than the contributor's proposed changes.

The security risk emerges when that privileged workflow checks out and executes code from an untrusted fork or passes attacker-controlled pull request data into shell commands. A malicious contributor can exploit those mistakes to execute commands with access to credentials and other resources intended only for trusted automation.

Researchers have warned about these vulnerabilities, commonly called "pwn requests," since at least 2021. Variations of this attack pattern contributed to major supply chain incidents involving Nx, PostHog, and TanStack.

GitHub's June changes addressed a common source of these vulnerabilities by making actions/checkout reject unsafe fork checkouts in privileged workflows unless explicitly overridden. The December policy takes a broader approach, preventing the event from triggering a workflow at all unless administrators have authorized it through an applicable policy.

Two Test Windows Before December Enforcement #

GitHub's default restriction currently operates in evaluation mode, allowing affected workflows to continue running before enforcement begins.

The company has scheduled two temporary enforcement periods, known as brownouts, to expose configurations that will stop working under the new policy:

November 9, 16:00–18:00 UTC

November 16, 16:00–18:00 UTC

During those windows, blocked pull_request_target attempts will generate failed workflow runs with an error annotation instead of executing. The default policy will return to evaluation mode after each test.

On December 2, the restriction becomes permanent for affected public repositories without an applicable policy allowing the event. The change applies to public repositories on GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise Cloud, but excludes private and internal repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server.

Maintainers who still require pull_request_target can create an Actions event policy that explicitly permits it. GitHub supports targeting individual workflow files, allowing administrators to preserve specific automation without enabling the trigger across an entire repository. Existing applicable event policies are not replaced by the new default.

Some Open Source Maintainers Face a Complicated Transition #

The broader restriction introduces complications for open source projects that have relied on pull_request_target for legitimate automation, sometimes across dozens of repositories.

A carefully configured workflow that only labels pull requests or manages project metadata may pose little of the risk GitHub is addressing, but it will still be subject to the new restriction. Maintainers must either allow these workflows explicitly or move them to another trigger where appropriate.

There are also differences in the administrative tools available across GitHub's pricing tiers.

GitHub's documentation for workflow execution protections describes policy configuration at the repository, organization, and enterprise levels for public repositories, including those on free plans. However, the ability to create policies in evaluation mode is reserved for Enterprise Cloud, where administrators can examine policy insights before turning on enforcement.

That disparity had already prompted questions following GitHub's September announcement of the new defaults.

In a GitHub Community discussion, open source maintainer George Joseph questioned how smaller organizations were expected to assess the impact without Enterprise policy insights.

"How would us mere mortals who run open-source organizations see what workflows would be affected?" he asked.

A community response suggested manually searching repositories for workflows using pull_request_target, inspecting existing workflow runs, and testing explicit allowlisting policies. These approaches can identify affected configurations, but require additional work from maintainers managing multiple repositories.

The December deadline gives projects several more weeks to prepare, while the scheduled brownouts offer a preview of what enforcement will look like. GitHub's decision also represents a significant shift for a feature originally created to make external contributions easier to manage: privileged pull request automation will now require an explicit exception to continue running under the new default.

articles.context: 5 Million Fraud Network Busted Investment Fraud Scheme Dismantled in Europe Authorities have arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed...
articles.full_text:
$4.5 Million Fraud Network Busted

Investment Fraud Scheme Dismantled in Europe

Authorities have arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed potential victims in more than 50 countries, according to Europol. The operation caused estimated losses of at least $4.5 million. The "crime-as-a-service" offering was run by a company from Cyprus and Israel, and allegedly provided cybercrime groups with an assortment of trading websites and fraudulent call centers tasked with tricking victims into transferring their savings. These call centers operated from Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia. "More than 100 servers were seized and seven suspects arrested during coordinated action on 3 November 2026," Europol said. "Authorities searched 17 locations and seized servers, other evidence and assets." Like other fraudulent investment schemes, the operation leveraged deceptive advertisements to funnel people towards fraudulent investment platforms, promising them substantial, quick returns from cryptocurrency trading and foreign currencies. Although victims were encouraged to transfer a small amount, they displayed illusory gains to push them into transferring increasingly large sums. The operators resorted to delaying tactics to block payments when they attempted to withdraw their funds. "Behind seemingly legitimate platforms, supposed brokers used fictitious profits and sustained psychological pressure to persuade victims to invest more," Europol said. "Personal data collected through this process was sold to criminal groups operating call centers. Operators then contacted potential victims with supposed investment opportunities, turning their initial interest into repeated demands for money."

articles.title: India Warns of New AI-Driven Cyber-Attacks Targeting Financial and Crypto Businesses
articles.context: Financial companies are being targeted in successive attacks by a newly identified cyber threat actor known as ‘Crafty Falcon’ using AI and agentic AI tools, including some...
articles.full_text:
Financial companies are being targeted in successive attacks by a newly identified cyber threat actor known as ‘Crafty Falcon’ using AI and agentic AI tools, including some previously attributed to Chinese hacking groups.

In a new security advisory published on November 4, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned that non-banking financial companies, including digital lending platforms, fintech firms, payment aggregators, payment services providers and cryptocurrency exchanges, have reported falling victim to repeated cyber-attacks.

Some of them received a restricted-distribution advisory in early October warning them of cyber threat actors exploiting application programmable interfaces (APIs) traditionally used for payment and disbursement transactions to make unauthorized transfers.

Despite undertaking remediation after receiving this previous warning, these financial organizations were attacked again, with CERT-In noting “incomplete remediation” on their part.

Attacks were typically observed during holiday periods, on weekends and “other low-monitoring windows” to delay detection and response, CERT-In added.

Crafty Falcon’s Attack Lifecycle

According to CERT-In’s Finance branch (CERT-Fin), Crafty Falcon is a previously undocumented threat actor that uses a range of AI and agentic AI penetration testing tools to breach the systems of its victims.

Typically, Crafty Falcon gains initial access through internet-exposed non-production environments, such as user acceptance testing (UAT), staging and testing environments.

Once inside, the threat actor moves from non-production environments into production systems by exploiting shared credentials, authentication tokens or network paths between the environments.

The actor reverse-engineers the organization's application codebases to develop tailored exploits. They then use altered or modified application packages to initiate unauthorized API calls, bypassing security controls that assume only the legitimate client application will communicate with the APIs.

The actor also bypasses IP allow-listing restrictions by routing traffic through whitelisted third-party fetcher IP pools, such as content-acceleration services and app-store review fetchers. These shared services can be instructed by any internet user to fetch arbitrary URLs, allowing the actor to originate traffic from IP addresses already trusted by the organization.

Another Crafty Falcon characteristic move is to target the victim’s cloud infrastructure, including compute, serverless and management services. Cloud management services, such as AWS Systems Manager and Lambda, are abused to execute commands and deploy malicious files, allowing malicious activity to blend into legitimate cloud management operations.

Before executing large-value transfers, the actor performs micro-value test transactions, such as transactions of Rs. 1, to validate that unauthorized fund flows are possible. They exploit or abuse merchant settlement APIs belonging to payment aggregators to move funds.

The actor targets cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual digital asset service providers, stealing wallet keys and siphoning funds from cryptocurrency wallets.

CERT-In noted that Crafty Flacon also exploits newly published vulnerabilities as soon as they become publicly available. These include file-upload and deserialization exploit chains, leading to the deployment of web shells in PHP and Node.js applications.

Throughout these activities, Crafty Falcon creates large numbers of custom, tailored scripts on the fly. Functionally identical variants are refined in rapid succession, a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development.

Notably, CERT-In and CERT-Fin observed the use – and combination – of several AI-powered offensive security tools against affected entities. These include:

Penetration testing tool ARTEX, based on PentAGI, an autonomous, multi-agent framework that can be plugged to large language models (LLMs)

Penetration testing framework CyberStrikeAI

Attack search engine Cairn

These tools allow attackers to “execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession and adapt their payloads based on target responses,” CERT-IN indicated.

While these tools are publicly available and could be used by many threat actors, most previous malicious campaigns where they were deployed were linked to China-based actors.

Read now: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants

CERT-In Provides Crafty Falcon Threat Mitigation Recommendations

In its latest advisory, CERT-In provided a long list of recommended security measures organizations can take to mitigate the threat. These include:

Maintaining heightened 24/7 security monitoring, increased staffing and lower alert thresholds during holidays, weekends and periods of reduced monitoring

Centralizing real-time monitoring of cloud audit logs and alert on high-risk events, including remote command execution, serverless function code updates and creation of roles, users or access keys

Restricting cloud management and serverless execution to approved principals and accounts

Implementing instance metadata service protections, least-privilege roles, restrictions on wildcard egress and default-deny internet egress for serverless functions

Separating UAT, staging and testing environments from production, ensuring no shared credentials, tokens, API keys, databases or direct network paths

Making application deployment directories read-only for application runtime users and implement file-integrity monitoring to detect web shells

Treating client applications and packages as untrusted and enforcing server-side transaction validation, API request signing using nonces and timestamps, application attestation and certificate pinning

Establish rapid patching SLAs for Internet-facing applications, prioritizing file-upload and deserialization vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js. Use WAF virtual patching as an interim measure

Extending real-time transaction monitoring to identify small-value test transactions to new beneficiaries followed by high-value transfers. Treat these as strong indicators of potentially unauthorized fund transfers and hold or review such transactions

Storing cryptocurrency wallet keys in hardware security modules or cold custody

Prohibiting unauthorized security and attack tools, including publicly available AI-driven offensive frameworks, on corporate infrastructure

Monitoring and governing LLM API usage and keys. LLM API traffic originating from servers or non-development hosts may indicate an attack infrastructure or planted operator console

Adjusting SIEM correlation to identify machine-speed, multi-technique attacks, parallel attack threads, adaptive payload changes and continuous activity outside business hours. Implement automated SOAR-based containment

Adopting zero-trust principles, micro-segmentation, identity-based access controls for every user and service and inspection of east-west traffic

The agency also urged organizations to report any suspicious activity that could be related to Crafty Falcon to incident@cert-in.org.in with all relevant logs and to contact the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C) and its Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS).

Read now: AI-Powered Cybercrime Tools Surge on Dark Web

articles.title: Is Your Exposure Management Platform Leaving You Exposed? Five Tests to Find Out
articles.context: Threat activity: Whether attackers are targeting the vulnerability or technology
articles.full_text:
A critical finding can move through several security tools and still leave the organization exposed.

The vulnerability has a severity score, and a ticket has reached the queue. Progress then depends on information the finding may lack: who owns the system, whether attackers can reach it, what protection exists, and how a change could affect the business.

Each missing detail creates another investigation, another handoff, and another delay.

An exposure management platform should connect discovery with a clear priority, an appropriate response, and evidence that protection has improved.

Continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) connects this work through scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation, and mobilization. These five tests establish whether a platform can support that process across infrastructure, identities, sensitive data, and external threats.

Security teams often have several records of the same asset. A cloud platform identifies an instance, an endpoint tool records its hostname, and an inventory lists an owner who has changed roles.

Cyber asset attack surface management (CAASM) connects those records, helping reveal stale information, missing ownership, and protection gaps.

The resulting view needs enough detail to support action: the asset’s owner, business purpose, assessment history, and security coverage. A system with no reported vulnerabilities should be distinguishable from one never assessed.

Disagreements between sources also need to remain visible. If an endpoint tool reports an active server while the inventory marks it retired, source records and update times help teams resolve the conflict.

Figure 1. CAASM connects source records with asset ownership, security coverage, and exposure context.

External discovery adds another perspective. External attack surface management (EASM) helps uncover what assets make accessible from the outside, including shadow IT, forgotten subdomains, and exposed services that internal tools never see.

EASM and CAASM work best together: CAASM maps what you know you own, while EASM validates that picture from the attacker’s point of view and surfaces what’s missing. Every unmanaged asset EASM finds can be fed back into CAASM, closing coverage gaps and giving each asset an owner. EASM also covers brand exposure, extending discovery to phishing sites, fraudulent profiles, and brand impersonation, so the same external view that finds your unknown assets also finds the lookalikes attackers build to target your customers and employees.

Read CAASM Was Never Meant to Stand Alone to see how asset intelligence supports the decisions and actions that follow discovery.

2. Explain Which Exposures Require Action First

Prioritization depends on understanding what an exposure actually puts at risk. A customer-facing application may carry the same severity score as an isolated development system while presenting very different business risk.

Prioritization should connect:

Reachability and exploitability: Whether attackers have a usable path to exploit the weakness.

Threat activity: Whether attackers are targeting the vulnerability or technology.

Business impact: What the system supports and what compromise could affect.

Existing protection: Whether relevant controls cover the system and are enforced.

Those conditions change. New exploitation activity may accelerate a response, while a disabled protection may invalidate an earlier assessment.

External threats need similarly specific reasoning. A fraudulent support account approaching customers may require rapid disruption; an abandoned company profile may first need ownership review.

See what the 2026 Exposure Gap Report reveals about prioritization and remediation performance.

3. Validate the Exposure and the Proposed Response

A clear priority can still stall when the system owner lacks confidence in the proposed change.

Validation needs to establish what the exposure allows and how the response could affect operations.

Identifying vulnerable software, confirming reachability, and demonstrating exploitability establish different things. A platform should distinguish observed evidence from analysis and untested assumptions. Attack-path relationships also need supporting evidence and clear limitations.

The proposed response requires separate assessment. A patch may depend on application testing and a maintenance window. An intrusion prevention system protection may require observation in Detect mode before enforcement.

Evidence should address the action’s scope, dependencies, false positives, performance impact, and recovery options. Following a proposed change through this assessment reveals what the platform establishes and what teams must investigate themselves.

4. Carry Safe Remediation Through Existing Workflows

Knowing what to fix first is great, but only if the fix happens quickly. The permanent patch often waits on testing, approval, and a maintenance window, and the exposure stays open the whole time. That’s true whether the weakness is on an internet-facing server or a phishing site targeting your customers.

Speed comes from confidence. Teams hesitate when they can’t say what an action will touch. When the platform already knows the asset, its owner, the active threat, and the controls in place, that hesitation disappears. Many Check Point Exposure Management customers remediate safely within one hour, because the context is complete and the safety checks are built in.

To test this, take one real finding and follow it from priority to protection:

Owner: Is the right person assigned automatically?

Safety: Is the action validated before it runs, including its impact and a way back?

Execution: Does it run through the controls you already have, whether a virtual patch, a configuration change, or a takedown?

Confirmation: Is the result verified, with the permanent fix still tracked?

Interim protection buys time, but it shouldn’t replace the long term fix.

Figure 2. Safe remediation connects observation, validation, action, and confirmation.

Speed holds up at scale. Between January 1 and October 26, 2026, an airline group completed more than 1,500 takedowns of profiles impersonating its airlines and support teams, combining analyst review with automated remediation.

And when an action fails, the exposure should stay visible with a clear next step.

Read Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production to see how validation, execution, and confirmation work together.

5. Show What Changed and What Remains

A completed action needs evidence of the resulting state.

A patch may miss unavailable systems. A policy update may exclude an intended asset. A takedown request may be accepted before the account disappears.

Verification should establish whether the vulnerability remains, protection is enforced, or malicious content has been removed. Monitoring should identify recurrence.

Reporting must distinguish removed vulnerabilities, interim mitigations, completed takedowns, and accepted risk. Each leaves different responsibilities outstanding.

Mean time to remediate (MTTR) requires agreed starting points, completion criteria, and treatment of temporary protection.

Tracking assignment, approval, execution, and verification separately reveals delays.

Recurring findings, failed actions, and aging mitigations can expose operational problems another scan will not resolve.

Apply the Tests Across Vendors

Platforms approach these requirements from different foundations. The five tests provide a consistent basis for evaluating coverage, evidence, and action.

Check Point Exposure Management combines internal asset intelligence, external discovery, threat intelligence, and brand protection with prioritization, exploitability validation, and safe remediation. It spans infrastructure weaknesses, phishing, and brand impersonation, supporting action through existing controls and takedown workflows.

Bring Intelligence Through to Safe Action

The five tests follow an exposure from discovery to a confirmed response. Each stage should give the next team enough reliable information to act while keeping unresolved work visible.

That connection helps organizations strengthen protection while accounting for production constraints and building on existing investments. It creates a traceable path from an identified exposure to an evaluated, implemented, and confirmed response.
