articles.full_text: As the news from last week has settled down, it would seem this headline was pretty spot on. The foretold apocalypse didn't eventuate, and there were no internet-destroying outages. In fact, it took days before I could find a single story of PHP2Shell being reliably attributed back to a breach. And I don't think we can say the relatively benign outcome was only achieved because we did take it so seriously either; there's a massive trove of sites out there that have been left to rot and would have every opportunity to be pwned by a bug of this magnitude that was readily exploitable, yet here we are. Which is good 🙂

articles.title: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines
articles.context: With all the different types of deduplication, we get this final picture: Again, looking at just the actionable vulnerability reports (likely the best measure), we see an...
articles.full_text:
Summary

Project Zero compared two automated tools used by Google to find vulnerabilities in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, on a regular basis. Fuzzilli is a generative JavaScript engine fuzzer and BigSleep is an LLM-based bug finding system. In the past six months, BigSleep found more vulnerabilities than Fuzzilli (45 versus 37) with a 25% overlap in the specific bugs reported. Since this comparison methodology has a tendency to underestimate overlap, we also performed dedicated experiments to test theoretical overlap in vulnerabilities reported since 2023. These experiments estimated overlap at roughly 60%. Regardless of which value is accurate, a substantial portion of vulnerabilities were discoverable by only LLMs or only fuzzing. While it is extremely promising that LLMs have become able to find so many vulnerabilities so quickly, fuzzing and LLMs are still complementary approaches. We recommend vendors perform both fuzzing and agentic analysis of their code to maximize the number of vulnerabilities that get reported before they impact users.

Introduction

Fuzzing has long been successfully applied to software projects such as Chrome or V8 (Chrome’s JavaScript engine) to detect bugs. Recently, the arrival of powerful LLMs able to read, reason about, and write code is causing a transformative change to software development and software security. With hundreds, sometimes thousands of new bugs and vulnerabilities having been discovered in well-fuzzed targets, a natural question arises: how do new LLMs compare to “traditional” fuzzers? Are they starting to replace them or do the two approaches complement each other? To help answer this, we look at three key questions:

How many bugs does each approach find in the real world?

What is the overlap between the two approaches?

What is the “shape” of bugs discovered by one system but not the other?

For this blog post, we will limit ourselves to two concrete systems: Fuzzilli, a JavaScript engine fuzzer, and BigSleep, an agentic bug finding system. Both of these systems run in production and automatically look for bugs in newly added code, which makes them fairly directly comparable. Specifically, Fuzzilli runs continuously across many instances, with the first ones usually picking up new changes within a few hours, while BigSleep currently runs once per day and is prompted to review new commits and write proof-of-concept testcases for any bugs it discovers. Both systems report bugs through Clusterfuzz, which will do basic crash triaging, then file bug reports in Chrome’s issue tracker.

We also limit ourselves to V8 as a target, a high-performance JavaScript and WebAssembly engine with a sophisticated and mature testing and fuzzing setup. In particular, Fuzzilli is a special-purpose fuzzing tool designed to find bugs in these engines. The usually complicated nature of these bugs makes for an interesting “playground” to compare the two approaches’ ability to find deep and complex bugs in well-tested software. We leave it to future work to perform similar analysis on a broader set of targets, fuzzers, and agentic bug finding systems.

We will now look into each of the three main questions in a dedicated section. Each section will first summarize the general approach, then describe the methodology in detail (often as bullet points, so you can skip those blocks if you don’t care too much about the details) before exploring the results. We conclude with an attempt at interpreting the results to get a picture of the current state of fuzzing vs. AI.

Part 1: Production Statistics

This is the simplest part to analyze, although with some caveats we’ll see in a bit. The basic idea is to query issues from Chromium’s bugtracker (where V8 bugs are tracked) and extract various statistics from there. This is especially easy since there’s a dedicated hotlist for each of the two systems. We limit our analysis to the six months from April to September 2026 as the automatic BigSleep pipeline only became active in April this year. As such, our raw data comes from the following two bug tracker queries:

Fuzzilli: hotlistid:5433121 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30

BigSleep: hotlistid:8067258 created:2026-04-01..2026-09-30

From there, the raw numbers of bug reports are:

Fuzzilli: 316

BigSleep: 441

Small win for BigSleep. However, this includes all types of bugs, and BigSleep initially also found a lot of configuration and integration issues in V8, for example crbug.com/503869331 where the unsafe flag blocking mechanism didn’t work properly yet. These are legitimate issues, but less relevant for our comparison since there’s little real-world security impact. One easy way to get rid of these is to look specifically at vulnerabilities by limiting the results to type:vulnerability:

Fuzzilli: 178

BigSleep: 95

Suddenly a clear win for the fuzzers? Not quite. There are still some problems with this data, notably duplicates and unactionable reports (e.g. bugs closed as WAI). At first, this seems like a simple thing to fix: just include another constraint such as status:(fixed | verified). Unfortunately, things are a bit more complicated. Take for example Fuzzilli bug crbug.com/511935486. The events on this bug are basically:

The bug is filed by Clusterfuzz on May 11 and assigned to an engineer

The bug is closed by Clusterfuzz as the testcase no longer reproduces later that same day

As such, this bug received zero developer interactions. Most likely what happened here is that this bug was a duplicate of another bug, crbug.com/511210507, but Clusterfuzz didn’t realize it as the crash signature (derived from the stack trace) was slightly different. When the other bug received a fix, the testcase stopped reproducing on Clusterfuzz, which closed the issue.

Maybe the best thing we can do is to look at “actionable” bugs, defined as those that are not marked as duplicates or WAI and that received at least one fix commit referencing them. Then, looking at only Type-Vuln bugs filters out a lot of the less-relevant BigSleep bugs, even though these were “actionable”. With that, the final picture looks like this:

So in terms of vulnerabilities, it’s roughly a tie (small advantage BigSleep) at the moment: 45 vs. 37.

This naturally raises the question of cost: how expensive is each of the two approaches and what does that mean in terms of cost-per-bug? Unfortunately, it’s challenging to make a comparison at this stage in the research. While some effort has been dedicated to making Clusterfuzz more efficient, similar effort has not been expended for Big Sleep and neither system is particularly calibrated for an optimal cost-per-bug ratio.

Part 2: Overlap

The next question is how much these approaches overlap each other. For this, our approach is twofold: we first attempt to find an answer in the bugtracker, by trying to identify bugs discovered by both systems. Next, we run a dedicated experiment in which we let BigSleep try to rediscover old Fuzzilli bugs.

Bugtracker Overlap

The basic idea is to see which bugs were found by both systems, so we’re effectively looking for duplicate bug reports. Similar to part 1, there are a few steps we need to take to ensure we get a somewhat accurate picture:

First, we look for bugs filed by one system that get deduplicated into a bug filed by the other. For example crbug.com/522410841 which is a duplicate of crbug.com/522860268. This is a clear overlap.

Next, we need to take into account that many “unactionable” reports (those with zero associated fixes) are often duplicates. For those reports, we need to find the commit that fixed them, then look at the bug associated with that commit, and treat these two bugs as duplicates. This can be a multi-prong relationship: both bug X found by BigSleep and bug Y found by Fuzzilli might be a duplicate of bug Z reported by someone/something else. In that case, that bug still counts as overlap.

Then, we need to realize that many duplicates never receive a bugtracker entry since they are already deduplicated at the Clusterfuzz level (since both Fuzzilli and BigSleep rely on Clusterfuzz for basic triage and bug filing). As such, we need to query Clusterfuzz’s underlying database to find more duplicates.

Finally, we need to decide what to do with separate bugs that get fixed by the same CL, for example the four bugs fixed by crrev.com/c/7965120. While this can legitimately happen for distinct bugs, it’s probably more likely for the bugs to be duplicates (such as in this case), and so we count them as such.

With all the different types of deduplication, we get this final picture:

Again, looking at just the actionable vulnerability reports (likely the best measure), we see an overlap of roughly 25% (20 out of a total of 81), with a slight majority of these found first by Fuzzilli and later by BigSleep.

Overlap Experiment

The second way to measure the overlap is to run a dedicated experiment in which we try to re-discover bugs found by one system in the past using the other. Specifically, here we try to re-discover old Fuzzilli bugs using a BigSleep setup that’s as close to the production configuration as possible. For each bug we collect the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, and ask the agent to review those changes just as in the production CI environment. Note that the other direction, trying to rediscover past BigSleep bugs with Fuzzilli is more difficult to set up, since fuzzers cannot easily be given a similar “starting point”. Moreover, for many of these bugs we already know the outcome of such an experiment: the majority of “historic” BigSleep bugs (e.g. those from 2025) were found after fuzzers like Fuzzilli had already been fuzzing vulnerable builds for months, sometimes years. So they would most likely also not rediscover them in an experiment (except perhaps in a few cases where Fuzzilli was since updated to support new language features). Similarly, in production, BigSleep only reports crashes with a delay of 1-2 days (as there’s currently only one run per day). As such, fuzzers also get a head-start there.

In more detail, here is how the experiment is set up:

We start with a list of historic Fuzzilli bugs (from early 2023 until mid-2026) by querying the bug tracker hotlist. This gives us around 1150 raw bugs.

We restrict this to only type:vulnerability as these are the types of bugs we care most about and will remove some “noise” as above. We are left with roughly 600 vulnerabilities.

Next, we filter this list down to bugs that reproduce in the environment used by the agent. This involves two parts:

Bugs that reproduce on an x64 debug+asan build of the d8 shell as provided by Chrome’s public build infrastructure. This is important because many bugs only reproduce in special builds, for example because they are architecture-specific or need certain compile-time features.

Bugs that can be reproduced without special flags. The problem here is that fuzzers often set custom flags, either to enable in-development features (e.g. --experimental-wasm-jspi in crbug.com/361123483) or to turn on different fuzzing modes that make certain types of bugs easier to discover (e.g. --deopt-every-n-times in crbug.com/362784006). However, we can’t let the agent set arbitrary flags on historic V8 builds as these didn’t have a “safe-flags only” mode (leading to many false-positive crashes), and we also don’t want to tell the agent which flags it should use for a given challenge as that would be a hint. As such, for simplicity we limit ourselves to bugs that can reproduce with a standard set of flags (--fuzzing, --jit-fuzzing, --expose-gc) and only allow the agent to set those.

We end up with 132 historic bugs.

We now perform some deduplication similar to what we did above to identify implicit duplicates, which we remove. This leaves us with a final number of 112 bugs.

For a realistic comparison, we then convert these bugs into “code review challenges” similar to the ones used by the production BigSleep pipeline. For that, we try to identify the commit that (likely) introduced the bug, for example based on bisection. We note that this skews the comparison against BigSleep for two reasons:

We likely sometimes identify the wrong commit that is unrelated to the bug in question, making the task harder or even impossible.

We only have one commit per bug, while in the real world, the agent might discover the bug from another, subsequent commit that touches a similar part of the codebase.

We now run the agent for 25 attempts on each commit. The agent is asked to find bugs related to the commit and prove their existence by writing a testcase that crashes the vulnerable build. The attempt is terminated once a crash is found, so each attempt can report at most one bug. We use essentially the same configuration that was used in production BigSleep at that time, including the same underlying model: Gemini 3.6 flash.

Finally, we run some post-processing on the results to check if the agent found the “right” bug or an unrelated one. For that, we check that the testcase crashes the pre-fix revision but not the post-fix revision. This is imperfect but fairly easy to implement.

Here are the results from the experiment:

Starting from just the commits that (likely) introduced the bugs, BigSleep was able to re-discover ~62% of the original bugs, while finding a different (but by now fixed) bug for another ~12% of commits. On around 26% of the commits it failed to find any bugs.

Memorization

One thing to worry about with experiments such as this one is memorization: the LLM remembering specific bugs from its (pre-)training data and as such having an easier time “re-discovering” them during evaluation. We can try to get some idea of the effect of this by looking at the success rates for bugs from different time spans, e.g. every half-year period for which we have bugs in the data set. If there was memorization, we’d expect higher success rates (both for a single attempt and for the combined run) on bugs prior to the learning data cutoff of the model. Here are the results for our experiment:

For the model used in this experiment (Gemini 3.6 flash), the knowledge cutoff date is March 2026. Combining that with the fact that in early 2026, Chrome bugs would only become publicly visible after ~3 months, the effective knowledge cutoff for Fuzzilli bugs should be around Jan 2026. Looking at the data, there seems to be no statistically significant amount of memorization pre-2026. We note, however, that this may be different for other models or future model generations and as such recommend that this be re-evaluated for similar experiments in the future.

Difficulty

A follow-up question we might ask is how the overlap compares with “difficulty”. For example, in the best case a system like BigSleep would easily find issues that fuzzers struggle with and vice versa. In that case, budget that was previously spent on long fuzzing sessions may now be re-allocated and put to different uses. Here are the results of analysing this, where “bug difficulty” is measured by the time it took Fuzzilli to discover the bug:

While we do get a statistically significant result here (although not of particularly great magnitude), it actually points in the other direction! Bugs that are hard to find for a fuzzer are likely also hard to find for an AI agent. As such, those fuzzers should probably be kept running for now.

Components

Another thing we can look at is a per-component breakdown of the bugs and their rediscovery rates:

Interestingly, the overlap is significantly smaller for compiler bugs. This is the area where Fuzzilli probably specializes most in, which may explain the results. Later on (in part 3), we’ll also develop another hypothesis for why (some) bugs in the compilers may be more difficult to rediscover for BigSleep.

Prompting

A final question is how much the specific prompting played a role in the performance of the AI agent. For that, we run two quick follow-up experiments, only on the bugs that weren’t previously re-discovered and with different prompts:

Instead of starting from commits, we start from the vulnerable file or function. This may be an easier starting point but is still a fairly realistic setup since both can for example be obtained by extracting modified files and functions from a given commit.

Instead of asking the agent to find memory corruption vulnerabilities (what we care most about), we specifically tell it that assertion failures and similar crashes are also desirable.

Running these two experiments with only 5 attempts per bug (instead of the 25 used in the main experiment), the agent re-discovered 10 additional bugs in total: 8 from the different starting points and 7 with the rephrased prompt (with 5 found in both runs).

In total, combining these results with our original experiment, we get the following picture:

So the share of “correct” bugs found climbs to ~70%, and we find some kind of bug for ~84% of starting points. However, for fairness it should be noted that equivalent tweaks to a fuzzer could likely also result in higher discovery rates for certain bugs, so the results of this follow-up experiment should be treated with some caution.

Summary

The main results from our two angles are:

In production, the overlap is noticeable but not substantial at around 25%.

In our experiment, overlap was around 60% of historic Fuzzilli bugs (70% with additional runs that used different prompts).

The overlap is not uniformly distributed:

Bugs that are difficult for a fuzzer to find are more likely to also be difficult to find for an agent, so there’s more overlap on “easy” bugs.

The overlap seems to be smaller in the JIT Compilers and higher in the rest of the engine.

From just the experiment, we might expect a higher overlap in production. However, there are probably a few factors that prevent(ed) this:

There’s a limited time window for overlaps: once a bug reported by either system is fixed, the other system no longer has a chance to rediscover it (as the bug won’t reproduce on Clusterfuzz and will therefore be discarded).

Our experiment only looked at a subset of Fuzzilli bugs that reproduce on a standard x64 d8 fuzzer build and without special flags. In production, each system has access to slightly different and specialized builds, as well as different runtime flag constraints, and there the overlap is potentially smaller.

Pipeline hiccups such as overloaded servers or bugs in the automation likely prevented a number of commits from being reviewed by BigSleep in the last months, so bugs introduced by them may have been missed.

Since its introduction in April, the model underlying the BigSleep pipeline has been upgraded multiple times. Earlier models likely performed worse, and we expect future models to perform better.

Part 3: Shape of Bugs

In this section, we will first look at three case studies of bugs found by one system but not the other, then attempt to draw conclusions from these and other bugs.

BigSleep: Chrome Bug 449760249 (October 2025)

This bug is a nice example of BigSleep benefiting from the underlying model’s reasoning capabilities to discover a variant that was (likely) too complex to trigger by a fuzzer in a reasonable amount of time. It’s also a good example to show the general working of an agentic bug finding system.

Background: TDZ and Hole Check Elision

Before diving into the bug specifics, we first need to look at some JavaScript internals, specifically variable initialization. In JavaScript, variables declared with the let or const keywords cannot be used before they are initialized, and attempting to do so will lead to an exception (”ReferenceError: Cannot access 'foobar' before initialization”). In V8’s terminology, these variables reside in a “temporal dead zone” (TDZ) until they are initialized. Internally, V8 sets variables in the TDZ to a special sentinel value, the_hole, and then checks for this value when accessing the variable’s content.

To limit the performance impact of these hole-checks, V8’s bytecode compiler implements an optimization (behind the default-enabled --ignition-elide-redundant-tdz-checks flag) to identify redundant checks and subsequently remove them. The idea here is to identify “dominating” checks where it can then be guaranteed that a hole-check has already been performed for a given variable on all possible paths leading to the current position.

This is a security-relevant optimization as an incorrectly removed hole-check would result in the internal the_hole value leaking to JavaScript code, a condition that has historically been exploitable (although new mitigations for this bug class have since shipped).

The Original Vulnerability

The original bug (issue 40071027 - discovered two years earlier by Fuzzilli!) involved do-while loops containing a break statement. In a do-while loop, the loop condition evaluates after the body. If the condition contains an assignment to a variable, the bytecode compiler will mark the variable as initialized. However, if a break statement executes in the loop body in the first iteration, then the condition will never execute. The bytecode compiler originally failed to account for this, leading to an incorrectly omitted hole check and subsequent leak of the_hole value.

To fix this, the implementation of BytecodeGenerator::VisitDoWhileStatement was modified in the following way:

- VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + if (!loop_builder.break_labels()->empty()) { + HoleCheckElisionScope elider(this); + VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + } else { + VisitForTest(stmt->cond(), ...); + }

Specifically, the patch works by creating a HoleCheckElisionScope for processing the condition code in case the loop contains break statements. This means that any updates to the TDZ state of variables will be discarded once the scope object is destroyed. As such, code after the loop will see the previous TDZ state (which is the correct behavior in this case).

Discovery of the Variant

The BigSleep agent began its analysis by examining the patch to VisitDoWhileStatement, realizing that the fix relied on loop_builder.break_labels()->empty() to decide if a protective HoleCheckElisionScope was required. It then began creating and testing various hypotheses for scenarios in which no break statement was registered with a given loop but the condition would still be skipped at runtime. For example, it hypothesized that a try-catch in combination with a throw inside the loop might confuse the hole-check elision logic. It then investigated how try-catch was implemented in the bytecode compiler and concluded that this was handled correctly.

Eventually, the agent started investigating labeled breaks, which allow directly breaking out of inner loops. It hypothesized that these might not be handled correctly and continued to investigate how these were being processed, for example by studying the logic in BytecodeGenerator::VisitBreakStatement. This time, it seemed to have identified a real flaw: in the case of nested breaks, the inner loop was apparently not being informed of the existence of a break statement! It therefore formulated the following vulnerability hypothesis:

If a labeled break inside a do-while loop targets an outer scope, the inner do-while loop’s LoopBuilder is not notified.

Consequently, loop_builder.break_labels()->empty() remains true.

Therefore, when generating the code for the loop condition, the HoleCheckElisionScope introduced by the patch is not used.

The condition is bypassed at runtime, but the bytecode compiler erroneously removed a later hole-check, leading to a leak of the_hole to JavaScript.

The agent then began writing a testcase to prove the existence of this bug. The initial attempt with simply two nested loops and a label failed, however, as the bytecode compiler would add another protective scope object for the labeled block. To work around this, the agent decided to use a switch statement. When handling a switch statement, the bytecode compiler uses a HoleCheckElisionMergeScope to compute the intersection of initialization states across all branches. By ensuring that the variable was initialized in a default case, the merge logic then concluded that the variable was correctly initialized on all paths.

Proof of Concept

With that, the agent had everything in place to produce a testcase to demonstrate the vulnerability. Below is the agent’s PoC:

// Flags: --ignition-elide-redundant-tdz-checks function trigger(cond) { { target: switch(1) { case 1: do { // Labeled break targeting the switch. The do-while LoopBuilder remains unaware. if (cond) break target; } while((x=1) && false); // Condition performs a check/assignment on x. break; default: x=1; // Ensure x is considered initialized across all switch branches for merging. } // Generator incorrectly believes x is checked/initialized. Elides TDZ check. x + 1; let x; } } trigger(true);

Here is how this testcase works:

trigger(true) executes, entering case 1 of the switch.

The do-while loop executes break target.

Control flow jumps to the end of the switch, bypassing the do-while condition where x is assigned.

At runtime, x remains uninitialized (holding the_hole).

Because the TDZ check was elided at compile time, the engine leaks the internal the_hole value to JavaScript code in the x + 1 expression, leading to a potentially exploitable condition.

We can see how this bug would be difficult for a fuzzer to find since the testcase is quite complex. While a coverage-guided fuzzer would have received rewards for triggering individual code paths (such as the handling of labeled break, the switch statement, the do-while loop, etc. in the parser), there is no additional reward for putting these together “in the right way” and so ending up with a testcase like this is quite difficult.

BigSleep: Chrome Bug 443765373 (September 2025)

This bug is an example of a relatively simple bug type that is challenging to discover with standard fuzzing approaches.

Background: Exception handling in V8

To understand this bug, it is necessary to briefly look into exception handling in V8. Take the following example JavaScript code:

function simple() { try { throw 42; } catch (e) { return e; } }

Here, we have a function consisting of a try-catch block in which an exception is raised. Running this in d8 with --print-bytecode, we can see the internal bytecode that the engine generates to execute the JavaScript code:

[generated bytecode for function: simple] 0x2ad5001000e4 @ 0 : 1b ff f9 Mov <context>, r0 0x2ad5001000e7 @ 3 : 0d 2a LdaSmi [42] 0x2ad5001000e9 @ 5 : b5 Throw 0x2ad5001000ea @ 6 : d1 Star1 0x2ad5001000eb @ 7 : 8d f8 00 CreateCatchContext r1, [0] 0x2ad5001000ee @ 10 : d2 ... ... 0x2ad5001000f7 @ 19 : b7 Return Handler Table (size = 16) from to hdlr (prediction, data) ( 3, 6) -> 6 (prediction=1, data=0)

For the purpose of this bug, the relevant part is mostly the last line of the output. Here, the bytecode essentially says “if there is an exception while the PC is between offset 3 and 6 in this bytecode, then execution should continue at offset 6 (the start of the exception handler)”.

The Bug

The agent spotted the bug while looking at the following function, responsible for writing the handler table data structure in memory:

void HandlerTable::SetRangeHandler(int index, int handler_offset, CatchPrediction prediction) { int value = HandlerOffsetField::encode(handler_offset) | HandlerWasUsedField::encode(false) | HandlerPredictionField::encode(prediction); int offset = index * kRangeEntrySize + kRangeHandlerIndex; Memory<int32_t>(raw_encoded_data_ + offset * sizeof(int32_t)) = value; }

Here, the int offset is being combined with a few other bits of data into a new int value. As such, the handler_offset cannot have the full integer range in the new field, possibly leading to integer truncation issues. The agent then investigated the specific bounds of these values and realized that the HandlerOffsetField had only 28 bits (allowing for 256MB) while the maximum bytecode size was 512MB! From there it was relatively simple to craft a testcase that crashes, simply by creating a huge function (resulting in >256MB of bytecode) with an exception handler at the end, then triggering an exception inside of it. The result is a jump to a wrong bytecode offset, a primitive that’s easily exploited. Here is the relevant part of the testcase:

// yield statements turn into a large chunk of bytecode let kNumYields = 500000; let body = ` if ("foo" === "bar") { ${"yield* 42;".repeat(kNumYields)} } try { throw 42; } catch (e) { // Will never get here } `;

Such a testcase would again be difficult to craft by a fuzzer as the fuzzer isn’t rewarded for creating large code (at least not with generic coverage feedback). In fact, the fuzzer is likely even actively discouraged from finding this bug since generating and executing large bytecode takes some time (in debug builds, the testcase generated by the agent needs a few seconds to trigger) and would therefore probably have led to timeouts during fuzzing.

Fuzzilli: Chrome Bug 40076141 (November 2023)

This bug is a good example of a type of bug that is likely difficult to find just by looking at (one part) of the source code. It was originally discovered by Fuzzilli and not rediscovered by any of the experiments from part 2.

Background: Value Representation in V8

Consider the following piece of JavaScript code:

let i = 42; let f = 13.37; let s = "foobar" i = s;

Here we create multiple variables holding values of different types. Note, however, that we never declare the type of a variable, and that variables can hold values of different types throughout their lifetime (i first contains an integer, later a string). What we see here is that JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, and so variables (and also object fields, etc.) have no fixed type. However, the actual runtime values still need to have a type: the engine somehow needs to know that foobar is a string value and that certain operations (e.g. substring search) can therefore be performed on it. Conceptually, this is possible by representing runtime values with a struct such as

enum JSType { JS_TYPE_INT, JS_TYPE_FLOAT, JS_TYPE_STRING, ... }; struct JSValue { JSType type; // Either the raw value or a pointer to another object, e.g a JSString. uintptr_t value; };

However, this is somewhat inefficient since we now need something like 16 bytes to represent a simple 4-byte integer at runtime. As such, modern JS engines use clever tagging schemas, which rely on unused pointer bits to encode type information. Specifically, in V8 the JSValue type is a tagged pointer (or just tagged for short) which stores one bit of type information in the least-significant bit:

If the bit is one, then the value minus 1 is a pointer to another object. This works because objects are aligned and so cannot start at an uneven address.

If the bit is zero, then the next 31 bits contain a raw integer value (also called a small integer - Smi)

As such, to figure out the type of a value at runtime, the engine first looks at the least-significant bit. If that is zero, the value can be “untagged” to obtain the integer value by right-shifting by one. On the other hand, if the bit is one, the value is a valid pointer to an object that contains further type information. For more details on V8’s pointer tagging scheme see also this blog post.

The Testcase

Let’s start by looking at the testcase produced by the fuzzer, which isn’t overly long:

function f0() { let v2 = 1; for (let i3 = v2; i3 >= v2; i3 += v2) { v2 = v2 && i3; } } f0();

The bug is caused during optimization of the loop by the Maglev compiler, specifically due to a conflict between two stages of the compiler pipeline: the initial graph builder and the later MaglevPhiRepresentationSelector.

The Graph Builder

The graph builder is responsible for building the initial Maglev intermediate representation (IR) of the code. For that, it consumes both the input code (in the form of V8 bytecode) as well as runtime feedback that was collected while the code executed in lower tiers such as the interpreter. When processing the loop in this testcase, the following happens:

Both i3 and v2 are modified during the loop. Since the IR uses static single-assignment (SSA) form, these turn into Phi nodes, which make the code look like every variable only has a single assignment :)

For the i3 >= v2 comparison, the runtime feedback states that i3 was so far always a Smi and therefore speculates that this will be the case in the future. It guards this assumption by emitting a CheckedSmiUntag, which will extract the raw int from the tagged value and will bail out to the interpreter if the input is ever not a Smi.

For the following operations on v2, the compiler can then rely on the existing check and emit UnsafeSmiUntag nodes, which avoid the runtime checks but are only safe to use if the input is guaranteed to be a Smi.

The resulting code for the loop now looks roughly like this (in Maglev pseudocode):

loop: i3 <- Phi(1, i3_next) // loop variable, tagged v2 <- Phi(1, v2_next) // loop variable, tagged i3_int <- CheckedSmiUntag(i3) // deopt if i3 is not a Smi v2_int <- CheckedSmiUntag(v2) // deopt if v2 is not a Smi if i3_int < v2_int: break v2_next <- Phi(i3, v2) // result of `v2 && i3`: "known Smi" v2_next_int <- UnsafeSmiUntag(v2_next) // no (re-)check needed i3_next_int = i3_int + v2_next_int i3_next <- Int32ToNumber(i3_next_int) // tag the int32 result for the phi

The MaglevPhiRepresentationSelector

The purpose of this optimizer is to identify Phi nodes where all inputs have the same raw representation (e.g. int32), and if so convert the Phi to that representation to avoid future untagging operations. For the code above, the code sees that both inputs to i3 are int32 and therefore decides to convert the Phi to int32 representation. Following CheckedSmiUntag operations then become a no-op and can be removed, while consumers that need a tagged value now require a conversion step. With that, the final code now looks like this:

loop: i3 <- Phi(1, i3_next) // all inputs int32, so i3 becomes a raw int32 v2 <- Phi(1, v2_next) // stays tagged v2_int <- CheckedSmiUntag(v2) if i3 < v2_int: break // CheckedSmiUntag(i3) removed as a no-op i3_tagged = Int32ToNumber(i3) // HeapNumber if i3 >= 2^30! v2_next <- Phi(i3_tagged, v2) // stays tagged, needs tagged inputs v2_next_int <- UnsafeSmiUntag(v2_next) // HeapNumber pointer treated as a Smi i3_next <- i3 + v2_next_int // tagging no longer needed here

The Conflict

The bug now occurs because of two optimizations interacting badly with each other:

The graph builder uses UnsafeSmiUntag as it believes that the value must be a Smi at this point

The representation selector removes a CheckedSmiUntag as it believes it is no longer required

Specifically, what can happen now is that eventually, i3 becomes larger than the maximum Smi value. At that point, Int32ToNumber can no longer fit the integer into a Smi and instead allocates a HeapNumber object (a container holding a larger number, basically). At this point, however, the UnsafeSmiUntag is no longer safe as the input is now a pointer. This leads to a corrupted pointer value being extracted and subsequently to memory corruption. Note that in the original code, this could not have happened as the HeapNumber would’ve been rejected by the CheckedSmiUntag(i3).

What may have made this bug difficult to find for BigSleep is the fact that both optimizations are correct in isolation. As such, looking at just one of them would’ve made it difficult to spot the issue. The agent would somehow have needed to hypothesize about the other optimization or stumbled upon the relevant code by chance (or exhaustive search).

Overview

Looking at the examples above as well as other bugs found by LLMs, we can see a few clear examples of bugs where an LLM has the advantage:

Bugs that require complex logic to trigger but can be found through progressive logical reasoning and experimentation with the target program, such as crbug.com/449760249 discussed above. This is likely the strongest advantage.

Bugs that require specific “magic” values (e.g. edge-case integers, specific strings, etc.), such as crbug.com/443765373 discussed above.

Bugs that require new (or less common) features that a fuzzer may not be aware of. Examples include crbug.com/436181695, where the fuzzer didn’t support the new await using syntax yet, and in fact also crbug.com/449760249 above where Fuzzilli lacked support for labeled breaks at the time.

Bugs that require a non-standard harness, custom flags, or special helper tools/functions that a fuzzer is not configured to use (e.g. crbug.com/516833326 which required --expose-fast-api and the d8.test.FastCAPI API).

On the other hand, here are some advantages that fuzzers enjoy (for now):

They can find “non-local” bugs reasonably well if not too many individual pieces are required. crbug.com/40076141 discussed above is an example for such a bug.

They can find bugs that are hard to spot by reasoning about the source code alone. One clear example would be bugs caused by (incorrect) C++ compiler optimizations such as crbug.com/500771385. Another potential example is bugs such as crbug.com/414840455, which are related to handling dead code in V8’s compilers. This is likely an unusual state and therefore may be hard to reason about. BigSleep missed a few of these in our experiments.

They are immune to certain biases affecting the agentic approaches, such as the choice of starting point (e.g. commits), the exact prompt phrasing, or the bug types seen (and not seen) during training. They do suffer from other types of biases though (e.g. the weights of individual mutators and generators).

They don’t get distracted by “shallow” bugs, whereas BigSleep missed a few bugs because it found easier ones instead. This is probably somewhat self-correcting though as the shallow bugs would eventually get fixed, giving the agent another chance to discover the deeper bug.

There is probably also a category of bugs that are hard to find for both approaches: bugs that are very non-local (bad for the agent) and require complex testcases (bad for the fuzzer) to trigger. In this case, a fuzzer would probably discover the individual pieces of the testcase (through coverage feedback) but won’t be able to find the right combination to trigger the bug (as in our first example). A code-reviewing agent, on the other hand, may struggle with the large search space of code fragments that may interact badly with each other (as in our last example). This is only a hypothesis, however, and would require further experiments and data to validate.

Part 4: Conclusion

In this blog post, we’ve compared coverage-guided fuzzers with vulnerability-discovery agents that read and reason about the source code. Specifically, we’ve looked at Fuzzilli and BigSleep, which both run as automated pipelines on V8 to discover newly introduced bugs. Looking at the data from those pipelines, we saw a roughly equal share of vulnerabilities found in the last 6 months (around 40 each), and a moderate overlap in discovered bugs of around 25%. However, in a dedicated experiment, overlap was closer to 60%. For now, this means that the two approaches remain complementary, and specialized fuzzing continues to provide value by finding bugs quickly and identifying certain kinds of issues that are otherwise hard to spot. At the same time, LLMs only very recently became capable of finding bugs in software like V8 at all, and have made tremendous progress since. The model used for our experiment is by now already outdated and outperformed by newer generations. Looking to the future, we expect further model improvements, potentially coupled with better prompting and more flexible harnesses (that e.g. allow the model to build, improve, and run fuzzers itself instead of being limited to pure code auditing), to lead to a growing share of bugs being discovered by agentic systems.

articles.title: Locked and Loaded: Phishing through Fake Bids and Protected Documents
articles.context: Password protection lends the file an air of legitimacy, mimicking a practice companies use every day, while providing threat actors with a critical advantage - most email...
articles.full_text:
By Don Santos, Cofense Phishing Defence Centre

In the sales process, few emails carry as much weight as an invitation to bid. It opens the conversation that can eventually lead to revenue, and professionals are conditioned to treat it with urgency and care. Threat actors understand this, and they have learned to pair that urgency with a simple tactic: the password-protected document. Password protection lends the file an air of legitimacy, mimicking a practice companies use every day, while providing threat actors with a critical advantage - most email security tools cannot inspect the contents of an encrypted file. In this walkthrough, we break down how an important sales invitation and a "secured" document combine to set up a tricky and deceptive credential phishing campaign.

Figure 1: Invite to Bid Email Body

The campaign starts with an email titled "Project Bid Invitation - Proposal Due August 35, 2026" as shown above in Figure 1. The subject and opening message immediately signal good news: an invitation to bid for a new project. The prospect of new business has a way of lowering an employee's guard because it often encourages a sense of urgency, not scepticism. The message says more details are in the password protected PDF attachment. This is another factor that makes the campaign tricky, as it’s a simple yet remarkably effective tactic for evading suspicion. It builds a false sense of trust with the recipient, and more importantly, it allows suspicious URLs or payloads to evade detection from automated email security tools. These tools typically work by scanning a file’s contents for suspicious patterns, but encryption keeps that content unreadable until a password is manually entered, letting the payload bypass detection entirely. Invitations to bid and password-protected files are also used in legitimate business processes, imitating these makes it difficult for untrained employees to spot suspicious emails, as shown in Figure 1. Adding to the difficulty is the fact that the sender's email address itself may belong to a legitimate, previously compromised account rather than an obviously spoofed or unfamiliar domain. This adds another layer of trust, removing one of the most apparent red flags before the recipient even opens the message.

Figure 2: Inside the Password Protected PDF

If the recipient does proceed with opening the attached PDF and unlocking it, the file reveals content as shown in Figure 2: a single button styled to resemble a OneDrive document preview, prompting them to "View" or "Download" the project files. With only one possible action, there is no room for ambiguity, and the familiar OneDrive branding makes the next click feel valid and legitimate. Hovering over the button reveals the underlying URL, [hXXps://slotpastimaxwin50jt[.]online/autoproject@autoproject[.]com/index[.]php], a clear red flag, as this is not a OneDrive domain, but a redirecting URL designed to carry the recipient further into the campaign.

Figure 3: Fake Bid Document Drive

Clicking the View/Download button leads to a page that resembles a shared document drive, complete with a list of files that appear to be related to a real contract, as shown above in Figure 3. This displays an effort to be consistent with the "invitation to bid" narrative, keeping the intended target hooked and committed to see the process through. Just like a legitimate shared document page, the intended target can choose which files to download via checkbox, then click "Download Selected", continuing the illusion of a normal bid process.

Figure 4: Email Input Required

Once the "Download Selected" button is clicked, a pop-up window appears asking for an email address, as seen in Figure 4. This again mimics the behaviour of real shared document platforms, which often request a login email to confirm that only the intended recipient can access the file. Entering an email to continue redirects to the fake Microsoft login, closely resembling the real Microsoft sign-in, first asking for an email, then a password, as shown in Figure 5. Looking at the address bar reveals the URL [hXXps://mm-lasertechnik[.]lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/1Dmw9/?key=NKsIDYXvtY], a clear indication that the victim is not on a real Microsoft sign-in page. If the victim proceeds to enter their email and password here, the credentials are sent directly to the attacker's server [hXXps://nbpn[.]lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/nasa[.]php], completing the phish.

Figure 5: Fake Microsoft Login Page

This campaign shows how threat actors continue to weaponize everyday business processes such as invitations to bid, password-protected files, and shared document platforms, turning them into effective phishing campaigns. The best defence is a habit of caution at every stage: Was this bid expected? Does the sender's domain check out? Does the URL of the login page match the platform it claims to be? When something feels off, contact your IT or security team before entering any credentials, as a moment of caution costs far less than a compromised account. Cofense combines phishing-specific AI trained on expert-validated, real-world intelligence with campaign-level remediation. Once a threat is confirmed, analyst-controlled quarantine can extend across the related campaign, with explainable decisions and a full audit trail. Schedule a demonstration to see how Cofense helps stop trusted-brand credential phishing after it gets through.

Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on...
articles.full_text:
A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic. The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs. AI developers get a crash course in key management. A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges. Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers. Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes. Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals. Patching what matters…matters. Monday business briefing. Tim Starks from CyberScoop is discussing targeted ads as a security risk. Championship rings come with a catch.

Today is Monday October 26th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A cybersecurity startup claims to have accessed sensitive internal documents at Anthropic.

Cybersecurity startup Cathedral says its researchers used AI agents to gain access to sensitive internal systems at Anthropic in less than twelve hours. According to The Washington Post, the researchers exploited vulnerabilities in third-party business software, accessing systems containing meeting transcripts, salary information, and internal Slack messages.

Anthropic confirmed the intrusion but said access was limited to certain sales, human resources, and IT systems. Customer conversations, proprietary code, and AI model weights were not exposed. The company says its monitoring detected some suspicious activity, and it disabled the affected systems and worked with vendors to address the vulnerabilities.

Cathedral, founded by former DOGE employees, conducted the research through Anthropic’s security testing program. Anthropic disputes the startup’s characterization of the national security implications and says researchers violated some program rules.

The findings highlight a familiar security problem with potentially higher stakes: even cutting-edge AI companies depend on ordinary enterprise software, with all its ordinary vulnerabilities.

The Pentagon spins up covert technology programs.

The Pentagon has quietly established a new agency dedicated to disrupting foreign military technology programs through covert operations.

According to POLITICO, the Technology Support Office, established in April, consolidates two classified intelligence programs and aims to expand capabilities including cyberattacks, supply-chain sabotage, and deception operations.

The agency reportedly employs engineers, intelligence officers, and special operations personnel to develop tools that could delay adversaries’ technological advances, particularly in artificial intelligence and advanced weapons systems.

Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg spearheaded the initiative, which has attracted opposition from Cyber Command and Special Operations Command over competing responsibilities and resources.

Supporters argue the effort is necessary to preserve America’s military advantage. Critics worry its secrecy could enable questionable operations and undermine congressional oversight.

The Pentagon disputes POLITICO’s reporting, calling its underlying claims inaccurate.

AI developers get a crash course in key management.

A supply-chain attack affecting tens of thousands of AI developers began with a security mistake made months earlier.

LiteLLM says it accidentally published a configuration file containing a master key in May. Although the file was removed, the key was never revoked. An attacker subsequently used it to gain control of LiteLLM’s GitHub repositories and distribute credential-stealing malware through a compromised software update.

Security firm Wiz says the malicious package was downloaded roughly 49,000 times. Within hours, attackers were testing stolen AWS credentials for access to AI models, suggesting a possible LLMjacking operation.

LiteLLM warns anyone who installed version 1.107.0 to assume their credentials were stolen and rotate them.

No organization has publicly confirmed a resulting breach. It’s LiteLLM’s second supply-chain compromise this year.

A ransomware recovery executive faces federal fraud charges.

A Florida businessman faces federal fraud charges for allegedly charging ransomware victims millions of dollars to recover their data while secretly paying the hackers responsible.

Prosecutors say Zohar Pinhasi, who operated the data recovery firm MonsterCloud, claimed he could decrypt files without paying ransoms. Instead, investigators allege he collected more than $19 million from clients while paying hackers over $8 million. In one case, an $8,200 ransom payment reportedly became a $150,000 customer bill.

The indictment follows a 2019 ProPublica investigation exposing the alleged scheme. MonsterCloud’s clients included law enforcement agencies that believed they were avoiding payments to criminals.

Pinhasi has pleaded not guilty and faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

For victims already paying one extortionist, prosecutors allege MonsterCloud effectively added another.

Two men are accused of using AI generated phone calls to scam bank customers.

Dutch police have arrested two men accused of using AI-generated phone calls to steal more than $425,000 from 170 bank customers.

The scheme began with automated calls warning of suspicious account activity. Victims who pressed a button were connected to a fake bank employee, who instructed them to download an app and scan their debit cards.

The app captured contactless payment data, which accomplices used to withdraw cash from ATMs.

The suspects, ages 23 and 25, were arrested October 6. Police also seized servers, phones, and laptops.

Both remain in custody as the investigation continues.

Stadia RAT rises from the StealC ashes.

Four months after European law enforcement disrupted the StealC malware operation, its seller is back with a new product.

Researchers at Varonis say Stadia RAT builds on StealC’s credential-stealing capabilities, adding remote desktop control, command execution, file management, and the ability to deploy additional malware.

The Windows malware targets browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and messaging applications. It also avoids systems configured for several Eastern European and Central Asian languages, establishes persistence through scheduled tasks, and can disable portions of Microsoft Defender’s protection.

Subscriptions range from $300 to $900 a month, with former StealC customers offered a free trial.

Researchers confirmed that Stadia reuses code from StealC, illustrating a familiar limitation of law enforcement takedowns: dismantling criminal infrastructure doesn’t necessarily put its operators out of business.

Researchers extract sensitive information using USB power-management signals.

Researchers at Korea University have demonstrated a technique for extracting sensitive information from air-gapped computers using USB power-management signals.

Called SPECTER, the method allows malware with administrator privileges to encode data through changes in USB device states, without conventional network connections or USB data transfers.

Researchers demonstrated three ways to receive the signals: monitoring smartphone charging indicators, observing changes in USB peripherals, and detecting electromagnetic emissions from USB cables.

Transmission speeds were extremely slow, topping out at one bit per second, making the technique more suitable for stealing passwords or cryptographic keys than large files.

The attack also requires hardware or firmware modifications, and some configurations produced no usable signals.

Researchers suggest monitoring unusual USB power-management activity, although the effectiveness of that approach remains untested.

Patching what matters…matters.

Security teams are patching more vulnerabilities than ever, but new research suggests all that effort isn’t necessarily making organizations safer.

According to Qualys, vulnerability closures increased sixfold between 2022 and 2025, reaching 473 million. Yet the percentage of critical vulnerabilities remaining unpatched after seven days actually increased.

The problem? Prioritization.

Researchers say fewer than one percent of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, but organizations continue allocating resources based largely on severity scores rather than evidence of real-world attacks.

Meanwhile, attackers are moving faster. Across the most critical exploited vulnerabilities, manual remediation failed to keep pace 88 percent of the time.

Qualys recommends shifting toward intelligence-driven, automated remediation that prioritizes actual exploitation and business impact.

The takeaway: Security isn’t necessarily about patching more. It’s about patching what matters.

Monday business briefing.

Investment and acquisition activity remains brisk across cybersecurity, with AI security attracting particular attention.

San Francisco-based Reach Security raised $50 million in Series B funding to expand its exposure management platform. AI agent security startup Opsin secured $21 million, while Asymptote Labs raised $5.5 million for its AI runtime security technology. AI penetration testing firm ManticoreAI also announced an undisclosed seed round.

On the acquisition front, Proofpoint agreed to buy data and AI security company Varonis for $6.3 billion, potentially creating a combined business serving more than 16,000 enterprises.

Anthropic acquired confidential AI data specialist OPAQUE, while Canadian AI company Cohere agreed to purchase Czech vulnerability management provider AISLE.

Elsewhere, legal technology firm Lineal acquired Swiss digital forensics company Forentec, and Britain’s Bytes Technology Group purchased Microsoft security specialist CyberOne.

The common thread across these deals is growing investment in AI security, data protection, and automated vulnerability management.

Championship rings come with a catch.

The New York Knicks celebrated their first NBA championship in more than half a century by offering employees free championship rings. Unfortunately, the offer was fake, and the real prize was mandatory cybersecurity training.

According to The New York Times, Madison Square Garden sent employees a simulated phishing email inviting them to choose between two ring designs. Anyone who clicked the link earned a trip to cybersecurity class instead.

The exercise followed a real security incident in which attackers reportedly used phished employee credentials to hack and extort the organization.

MSG acknowledged that using championship rings as bait was an unfortunate mistake. The company says it’s distributing more than 275 actual rings and pieces of jewelry worth over $3.7 million.

For employees who fell for the phishing test, the championship celebration apparently came with a refresher course in disappointment.

articles.title: Gheist Attackers Stumble in Attempt to Abuse GitHub Tokens
articles.context: A recent campaign targeting GitHub repositories has been disrupted after attackers were found planting secret-stealing workflows across more than 13,500 branches across...
articles.full_text:
A recent campaign targeting GitHub repositories has been disrupted after attackers were found planting secret-stealing workflows across more than 13,500 branches across repositories using stolen access tokens.

In research published October 25, Wiz said it had tracked the campaign, dubbed Gheist, since September 15 and recovered the branches from more than 850 compromised accounts. The operation targeted every repository the stolen tokens could reach, from personal projects to private enterprise repositories.

Wiz identified infostealer logs and earlier supply chain compromises, such as the March compromise of the Trivy security scanner, as sources of the stolen tokens. Some of the accounts were also being used for malware distribution and cryptomining.

Workflow Trick Meets GitHub Approval Hold

The attackers used the tokens to create branches and commit a GitHub Actions workflow that printed repository secrets into its own log. They then downloaded the log through GitHub's application programming interface (API) and deleted the run seconds later, so the campaign needed no external command-and-control (C2) server.

The campaign's main obstacle has been a GitHub control introduced July 28 that places potentially malicious workflow runs in public repositories on hold until a collaborator approves them. Wiz said every public Gheist run it examined, across all variants, remained in an action_required state, preventing the malicious workflows from executing.

The protection does not extend to private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server. In those environments, Wiz observed workflows completing on attacker-created branches before the runs were removed.

Read more on stolen supply chain secrets: TeamPCP Explores Ways to Exploit Stolen Supply Chain Secrets

Private Repositories Remain Exposed

In enterprise organizations, Wiz observed the attackers cycling through user and automation account tokens and cloning private repositories. Hours later, cloud credentials from the same organizations were used to enumerate Amazon Web Services' Secrets Manager.

Two variants of the tool ran in parallel. One added support for deployment environments, exposing environment-scoped secrets that are often production credentials. It later gained a job that searched self-hosted runners for credentials and other sensitive files, though Wiz described the job as "buggy."

As of October 24, roughly two-thirds of implicated accounts were no longer available on GitHub, which Wiz said likely reflected response activity after it reported the campaign to GitHub. However, the researchers said Gheist remained ongoing and continued to evolve.

The campaign demonstrates how stolen GitHub tokens can turn legitimate automation features into a credential theft mechanism, while newer platform controls can disrupt some abuse without eliminating the underlying risk from compromised credentials.

articles.title: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A working exploit for a Linux kernel flaw has been made public before the bug received a CVE identifier or a merged upstream fix.

Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent that report and five others to maintainers and public mailing lists on October 20 and 21, according to analysis published by the Sysdig Threat Research Team on October 24.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported when Sysdig published its analysis, but several flaws still had no fix in any released kernel.

Public Disclosure Creates Patch Gap

ZDI-CAN-33367, the flaw with the public exploit, is a local privilege escalation (LPE) bug in the Linux networking stack that ZDI gave a CVSS score of 7.8. It can allow an unprivileged user to alter the in-memory contents of files they can only read.

It sits in a code path the kernel's fix for the earlier Dirty Frag page-cache flaws missed. Linux support provider TuxCare reproduced a root shell with the public proof of concept (PoC) on AlmaLinux 8 through 10, CloudLinux 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Sysdig said.

Two of the other five, ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, are the highest rated, at 9.0, and affect ksmbd, the kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) server. The first is a remote, pre-authentication flaw that can leak kernel memory and crash systems, while the second requires SMB Direct, a Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) interface and a writable share.

Read more: Rushed Patches Follow Broken Embargo on New Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

Exposure Varies Across Linux Systems

Of the remaining three, ZDI-CAN-34068 is an LPE rated 8.8 in the kernel's VMware graphics driver. Sysdig said there was no patch and only the report's title was public.

The last two are ZDI-CAN-34076, an information leak in the kernel's Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target, and ZDI-CAN-32005, a userspace stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager.

Sysdig said defenders should prioritize by the components they run rather than CVSS scores. It advised unloading ksmbd where it is not needed, restricting port 445 to trusted networks where it must stay and watching for a vmwgfx patch on VMware guests.

For ZDI-CAN-33367, Sysdig said restricting unprivileged user namespaces should block the public PoC, though TuxCare had not validated this, and noted that rootless containers depend on them. AlmaLinux had patched kernels in testing, but not production, by October 23.

The disclosure leaves a fragmented patching picture, but the public root exploit makes ZDI-CAN-33367 the most immediate concern of the six.

articles.title: Microsoft Issues Emergency Patch Update for Critical .NET Buffer Overflow Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has released out-of-bound (OOB) security updates for its .NET developer platform, which includes a fix for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability.

The tech giant published the updates for .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 Release Candidate 3 on October 25. Platform users have been urged to apply the updates as soon as possible to reduce the risk of compromise.

They contain patches for two newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as well as two flaws that were not fully addressed in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday rollout.

Single updates are available for each of the affected .NET versions and .NET 11 RC2 users should update to RC3 to receive these fixes.

.NET is a free, open-source framework that developers can use to build apps and cloud services. It is managed by Microsoft and is supported on Windows, Linux and macOS operating systems.

Updates Address Critical Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

One of the new vulnerabilities addressed is CVE-2026-111497, which affects .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 across all operating systems.

The vulnerability is contained in the Brotli decompression algorithm, which is used by .NET. It can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory, leading to information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege.

Microsoft said that applications may be affected if they process Brotli-compressed data through ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient automatic response decompression or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs.

The flaw has a critical CVSS Score of 9.2. Users of Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 also need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries to the latest available version.

Brotli was designed by two engineers at Google in 2015 to allow developers to speed up algorithm compression for developers.

Microsoft’s OOB update also addresses CVE-2026-114148, which can allow an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally by exploiting unsafe ownership metadata in affected .NET tarballs.

CVE-2026-114148 affects .NET versions 7-11, but only for Linux systems. For .NET 10 and .NET 11, CVE-2026-114148 affects source-build tarballs only. For .NET 8 and .NET 9, it also affects ASP.NET Core distributions obtained through ASP.NET Core tarballs, including users who do not build .NET from source, the advisory noted.

It has not been assigned a CVSS score at the time of writing but has been reserved by a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA).

In addition, Microsoft has re-issued fixes for two vulnerabilities disclosed in its October 13 Patch Tuesday rollout. These are for CVE-2026-70197, a memory corruption flaw affecting .NET versions 8-11, and CVE-2026-102870, a code injection vulnerability affecting .NET 10 and 11.

Remediation Guidance for Developers

Microsoft issued advice for .NET users on how to update their applications and build environments in light of the updates. These include:

Install the updated runtime for the .NET version for your framework-dependent application, then restart the application

Rebuild and republish self-contained applications with the updated runtime

Rebuild and redeploy containers using updated .NET container images

Obtain the updated source-build artifacts for your .NET version and rebuild your packages to incorporate the tarball ownership fix

For ASP.NET Core tarball users on .NET 8 and 9, update your installation using the refreshed ASP.NET Core Runtime tarball for your .NET version

Image credit: II.studio / Shutterstock.com

articles.title: Blue Initiative Offers Maritime Sector Dedicated Vulnerability Database
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

articles.title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.
