articles.title: Head of AI Security Roles Surge in Large Organizations
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
A head of AI security role has been established in 65% of large organizations with an annual revenue of $10bn plus, according to new data.

The research, conducted by IANS and Artico Search, found that large businesses are taking steps to update their security organizational structure to enhance accountability and board level oversight for enterprise AI governance.

Around a fifth (18%) of all $10bn+ firms have made the head of AI security a dedicated position, while 47% combined it with another leadership role, making it “one of the fastest emerging functional roles,” according to the researchers.

Head of AI security was observed to be less common in medium and small companies, with the position established in 9% of organizations with a revenue of $1-$10bn, and 6% in firms with under $1bn in revenue.

Steve Martano, IANS Faculty and partner at Artico Search’s cyber practice, commented: “The growth of AI is creating a premium for leaders who can bridge technical security, risk and compliance while still understanding how the business wants to use the technology.”

AI Governance Rarely Falls Under the CISO Remit

The IANS report, published on October 20, found that despite the growth of dedicated head of AI security roles in large organizations, overall accountability for enterprise AI governance remains unsettled.

CISOs hold primary accountability in 26% of small businesses, in 11% of medium firms and just 7% of large organizations. The position that most often is held accountable for AI governance in large businesses are chief AI officers, at 22%.

Read now: AI Agent Adoption Creates Risk as Oversight Struggles to Keep Pace, Splunk Finds

Across all three tiers, 14-19% of organizations reported that no single executive is accountable.

In addition, most organizations have not yet fully implemented a board committee dedicated to AI ethics or responsible AI, with 43-48% across all three tiers stating that they have no such committee planned.

Martano said organizations must restructure security teams to ensure that their governance strategies keep pace with rapid AI adoption.

“Companies need to strategically think about what they need from the function and whether they can develop that expertise internally before going to an increasingly competitive external market,” he noted.

Experience the Biggest Dictator of Security Pros’ Pay

The report assessed experience level as the single biggest driver of compensation differences in the same role – more significant than factors such as company size and geographic location.

In $10bn+ businesses, security professionals with eight to 15 years’ experience earn about $35,000 more than those with fewer than eight years’ experience.

The gap grows to around $50,000 between early-career staff and professionals with more than 16 years’ experience.

In large businesses, the average salary for Deputy CISOs was $350,000 per annum.

BISOs earnt a similar amount on average, at $342,000.

Data around average compensation levels for CISOs was not included in the report.

articles.title: Researchers Warn OpenCode Quietly Patched Critical RCE Flaw, Leaving Users At Risk
articles.context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
articles.full_text:
The Pillar Security team reported the vulnerability privately via GitHub Security Advisory with full reproduction material at the end of August 2026.

A month later, Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, confirmed it had received the report, but said malicious MCP servers are “outside their threat model.”

Pillar Security researchers said Anomaly patched the vulnerability on September 28 in version 1.18.33 – without a CVE or security advisory. “As a result, conventional vulnerability scanners and dependency alerts will not identify affected installations, potentially leaving enterprises unaware that they need to upgrade,” Pillar Security researchers warned.

URL Validation Falls Short of Preventing OpenCode RCE Attacks

Pillar Security researchers claimed that the standard fix isn’t enough to fully remediate this vulnerability, which they assessed should be allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.8.

According to the researchers, URL scheme validation alone cannot prevent the attack because the malicious payload can be embedded in a seemingly legitimate HTTPS URL.

On Windows, the vulnerable open dependency passed the URL to PowerShell without properly escaping it, allowing the shell to interpret part of the URL as a command.

Although OpenCode added URL scheme checks in version 1.18.33, the researchers said the crucial fix was to update the dependency to a version that correctly quotes the URL, preventing PowerShell from interpreting the payload as executable code.

They recommend that developers avoid passing untrusted URLs through shell commands altogether, instead using argument-based process execution to reduce the risk of command injection.

OpenCode RCE Flaw Unrelated to Recent Console Security Breach

This vulnerability report comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Pillar Security’s Cohen stressed that this newly disclosed vulnerability was not related to the Console breach.

“The breach hit a legacy system behind a hosted key proxy, and exposed provider keys users had stored there. The vulnerability we reported runs the other way: a malicious remote MCP server executing code on a developer's own machine during the OAuth handshake. Different target and attacker position,” he explained.

Nevertheless, Cohen highlighted that both incidents come down to the same thing, “Who you let hand credentials and inputs to an AI coding tool, and what that tool does with them.”

articles.title: Introducing a new AI chapter in the NCSC research problem book
articles.context: Concepts such as vulnerability management, incident response and risk management will need to evolve to account for both AI-enabled systems and AI-enabled attackers
articles.full_text:
The latest frontier AI capabilities are re-writing what is possible for both cyber attackers and defenders, with recent publications from the NCSC highlighting the opportunities and risks presented by AI.

The Five Eyes cyber security agencies have warned that AI is accelerating the pace and scale of cyber threats, while the NCSC’s Cyber Shield initiative sets out an ambitious vision for harnessing AI to strengthen cyber defence.

Turning this vision into reality will require more than advances in AI capability alone; it will require answers to difficult questions around system design, assurance, security and trust.

To help focus innovation across this new AI-enabled world, we’ve re-written our NCSC research problem book to include an entirely new chapter 'AI in cyber security problems’.

For years, AI and machine learning have helped defenders analyse data, identify threats and automate routine tasks. The new generation of AI systems (particularly generative AI and agentic AI) can plan, reason, use tools, and take actions with increasing autonomy. This is game-changing, making some things much easier to automate but in the process, creating new problems to overcome.

Many of the assumptions that underpin today’s cyber security best practice were developed before this kind of AI existed. Concepts such as vulnerability management, incident response and risk management will need to evolve to account for both AI-enabled systems and AI-enabled attackers. This evolution may require a re-design of processes from the ground up to fully leverage the potential benefits to defenders.

Our new problem book chapter on ‘AI in cyber security’ identifies seven areas spanning three broad themes:

the use of AI to strengthen cyber defence

the security and assurance of AI systems themselves

the use of data-driven methods to improve cyber resilience at scale

A common thread runs throughout them all: human-AI collaboration. As AI systems become more capable, we need to understand where autonomy can provide genuine value, where human judgement remains essential, and how meaningful oversight can be maintained without losing the benefits of machine-speed operations.

AI has the potential to fundamentally reshape cyber security. Whether that future is secure, resilient and trustworthy will depend on the choices we make today and the research we undertake tomorrow. The new problem book should focus attention on some of the most important challenges ahead.

Addressing these challenges will require a collective effort across the cyber security and AI communities. We welcome feedback on the challenges identified in the problem book, suggestions for additional research questions, and examples of ongoing or planned research that could help address them. Insights from across academia, industry and government will help ensure that future cyber security approaches remain effective, resilient and trustworthy in an AI-enabled world.

If you would like to contribute to the discussion, please complete our feedback form.

Paul J, Technical Director for Cyber AI Research, NCSC

Brad A, Principal Data Science & AI Researcher, Industry 100 Secondee & Alan Turing Institute Visiting Collaborator

articles.title: The New Release Metric: Less Cleanup Per Release
articles.context: A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project,...
articles.full_text:
AI makes it easier to create code. That does not automatically make software easier to ship.

A team can move from an idea to a pull request in minutes, then lose those gains to a failed build, a dependency conflict, a late finding, or an upgrade that was not worth making. The code arrived faster. But the release did not.

That gap matters when engineering leaders evaluate the effectiveness of AI-assisted development. Code output shows how much activity a tool generates. It does not show how much production-ready software reaches users, or how much unplanned work teams take on along the way.

A more useful question is: How much avoidable cleanup does each release require? The answer reveals how much of AI's speed advantage survives the trip from pull request to production.

Code Volume Is the Wrong Scoreboard

Code volume is the wrong scoreboard because it measures how much code a team produces, not how much production-ready software it ships. In AI-assisted development, that matters even more.

More generated code means more tests to review, more dependencies to validate, more pull requests to untangle, and more changes that may need to be rolled back. Agents can add, replace, and update components quickly, but each dependency decision can affect compatibility, maintainability, licensing, and security.

The result can look like progress: more code, more pull requests, more activity. Yet releases may still take longer because teams have to resolve the downstream work those changes create.

If AI-assisted delivery is improving, teams should see less avoidable cleanup, such as:

Dependency-related build failures and rework.

Late findings that require teams to replace components and retest.

Rollbacks and emergency fixes tied to dependency changes.

Unnecessary upgrades and version changes.

Time spent investigating components that entered the workflow.

Planned engineering work displaced by urgent remediation.

These signals matter alongside delivery speed and reliability. Fewer cleanup tasks do not represent progress if teams are shipping less or accepting more production risk.

Cleanup Is Where AI Gains Disappear

AI-assisted development delivers less value when teams spend the time saved during coding to resolve issues that surface later.

A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project, reruns tests, and determines whether a release is affected.

If the issue reaches a build or release, the work can extend to:

Identifying where the component was used and what it could access.

Replacing the dependency and validating affected builds.

Assessing whether credentials, systems, or releases may have been exposed.

That work appears as release churn, missed delivery dates, and engineers pulled away from planned work. It is easy to miss in an AI adoption dashboard, especially if the dashboard focuses on code generated or pull requests completed.

Not every build failure or dependency issue can be prevented at the point of intake. But known malicious packages are one avoidable source of downstream work. Blocking them before they are served through the repository path can keep them out of developer and build workflows in the first place.

Measure the Work Behind Each Release

Measure cleanup per release by tracking the dependency issues that trigger unplanned work and the time teams spend resolving them.

Start with a baseline and follow the trend across comparable releases.

Useful signals include:

Dependency-related build failures: How often do dependency issues cause failed builds, retries, or rework?

Late-stage findings: How many component issues surface after development has started or a release is in motion?

Dependency-related rollbacks and emergency fixes: How often do component changes contribute to release instability?

Remediation time: How long does it take to investigate a dependency issue and land a validated fix?

Engineering time redirected: How much planned work is displaced by dependency cleanup and release interruptions?

While tracking cleanup work is critical to understand the effort involved to ship production-ready code, tracking preventative measures like blocked malicious packages is equally as important. A blocked request is not a cleanup task, but it shows that a known malicious component was stopped before it could become one.

The point is not to create another vanity metric. It's to give engineering leaders a clearer view of where release effort goes, what causes avoidable rework, and whether teams are getting more useful work through to production.

Make the Trusted Path Easy to Use

Developers and agents should be able to request components through the repository they already use, with security checks applied in that path. Developers should not have to recognize every suspicious package name or track every attack campaign, and teams need a way to evaluate agent requests even when people are not reviewing each choice in real time.

Adding a ticket or manual approval to every dependency choice would move the bottleneck, not eliminate it. Consistent controls belong in the path developers, pipelines, and agents already use.

Sonatype Nexus Repository provides a one trusted place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs teams rely on. Sonatype introduced Pro+ and Enterprise editions to help address a growing source of release cleanup: dependency decisions that outpace manual review. Both editions add malicious package protection and configurable policies to Nexus Repository, so teams can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds.

This does not prevent every dependency conflict, late vulnerability finding, or release issue. Teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. Repository protection addresses one specific problem earlier: known malicious packages entering through the managed repository path.

Sonatype Guide extends that trusted path into dependency selection and remediation. It helps developers and AI agents evaluate components in context, choose safer versions, and address risk in the codebase with guided fixes. Together, Nexus Repository and Guide help teams make better dependency choices up front and spend less time correcting them later.

Measure the Release, Not the Output

AI increases activity across the software development life cycle: more code, more pull requests, and more dependency changes. The better test is if teams can turn that activity into reliable releases with less unplanned work.

Track dependency-related build failures, late fixes, and remediation time across comparable releases. If those costs fall while delivery remains reliable, teams are getting more from faster code generation.

This is why Nexus Repository now offers Pro+ and Enterprise to help teams keep the speed of AI assisted development from becoming more dependency cleanup and release time. Both editions can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds, giving developers and agents a trusted route to software inputs while teams focus on getting releases out the door.

Less cleanup per release. More engineering time for planned work.

articles.title: Police arrest Qilin ransomware suspect on holiday, as links made to Synnovis hack that contributed to patient’s death
articles.context: A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed
articles.full_text:
A 28-year-old Russian man has been arrested by German police, suspected of being a key member of the Qilin ransomware gang. As BBC News reports, detectives have linked the man to the 2024 attack against blood-testing firm Synnovis, that disrupted London hospitals, and resulted in the death of a patient.

The suspect, who has been named by German media only as "Vladimir K" was originally detained in May in Japan, after he travelled there on holiday. According to German officials, the man's vacation plans were intercepted and Japanese police were waiting for him on arrival. Earlier this month he was extradited to Germany.

Germany's interest in "Vladimir K" is related to a cyber attack in September 2024, which saw around US $160,000 worth of cryptocurrency extorted from a logistics firm. According to the BBC, German detectives have now included in their investigation possible links to the June 2024 attack which saw the Qilin ransomware group disrupting pathology services at various London hospitals, and resulted in the cancellation of operations and outpatient appointments.

The incident is said to have crippled Synnovis’s IT systems, and caused a critical shortage of O-type blood in hospitals. A subsequent probe into the attack by King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed that a patient died in part due to blood test results being delayed.

As a consequence, British police are reportedly examining whether their own inquiry could lead to a charge of unlawful killing.

No ransom was paid by Synnovis, a decision the firm made jointly with the NHS trusts to which it provides services.

Ransomware gangs have been accused of causing deaths in the past. For instance, in 2020 a different gang disrupted systems at a Düsseldorf hospital and caused a seriously-ill woman to be diverted to another health facility 30 km away.

According to reports, as a result of the attack doctors were not able to start treating the patient for an hour and she died.

The Qilin ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group has been operating since at least 2022, and has reportedly hacked more than 4000 organisations, and extorted over US $140 million. High profile victims include Japanese beer-maker Asahi, potentially exposing the data of more than 1.5 million customers and around 275,000 current and former employees and their families.

articles.title: 181: Ricky
articles.context: Alright, so they somehow discovered your IP and then they attacked your IP, and that was enough to knock you offline and lose the game. He discovers a whole world of ddossers and booters and punters and griefers who use malware to attack other players in the game to make them lose so you can win.
articles.full_text: JACK: I think that when I was a kid I was a good liar. Don't ask me where it stemmed from; probably because I was always getting in trouble, and that — I learned that if I was a good enough liar that I could sometimes lie my way out of trouble. But I was reading this post on Reddit the other day, and so many memories came back to me. [Music] There was this post. Some dad was complaining about his son being a ding-dong. He’s like, my son, who’s fifteen, wanted to get some ice cream, so we gave him a few bucks and sent him to the store. It happened to be a buy-one-get-one-free sale, and we all knew that, too. So, he went, he bought some ice cream on his own, and he came back with just one tub of ice cream. The knucklehead didn't get the free one. He just paid full price for a single tub of ice cream. The store clerk even told him, hey, there’s a sale. You know you can get a second one free. But my boy just said, well, I only want one, and refused the second one. His dad on Reddit was all miffed about how his son could be so daft and ignore free ice cream. He even said, I know that as soon as the boy finishes his ice cream he’s gonna want another, so why didn't he just get two? He knows that we all love ice cream, so why didn't he get one for his mom or his dad? Why did he get just one ice cream and not the second free one? It was free ice cream. This Reddit post blew up. Everyone was piling on about how dumb this kid was, saying stuff like, in my state you could disown your child for far less. Someone else said this is probably because the kid doesn't go buy things very often and doesn't know how to handle money very well or deals. The dad wrote in the post that he was starting to feel worried because people were saying some real mean things about his son, but nobody was saying what I was thinking. I feel like I know exactly what happened here, because I was in the exact same situation when I was a teenager. If you would have talked to my mom then, she would have been just like this worried dad. She would have told you that I’m the worst shopper in the world. Because I’m almost certain that what happened is he ate a full tub of ice cream on his way home and then lied and said he only bought one. I mean, it all adds up. The boy was hungry for ice cream before even leaving the house. There’s no way he’s gonna wait until he gets home to have his first bite. Grab a spoon at the store and start on your way home. Also imagine the look on his face when the clerk told him, you know you can get a second one for free, right? No way. Dang, this is my lucky day. So, he must have gotten two, and on his way home he started thinking, shoot, mom and dad don't know I got two. They only gave me enough money to get one. So, if I come back with one, they won't even know there was a second. So, if I could scarf this second tub down before I even get home, it would be glorious. No rules. No regulations. No speed bumps. Just eat a whole tub of ice cream as fast as I can. Challenge accepted. I’ll tell you, teenage boys can crush a whole tub of ice cream real easy. They can make a dozen cookies vanish instantly. They have the power to inhale desserts like no one else can. The real tell here is that the dad on the Reddit post even said, we would never let him eat a whole tub in one sitting. That’s the thing; the boy had an unregulated container of ice cream, and he thought no one is gonna know. No one is gonna stop him from eating all this in one sitting. Let’s do it. So, he saw this as his big stroke of luck and secretly slurped it down, and then tried to lie about it when he got home by saying, no, no, I only got one, I swear. But little did he know the entirety of Reddit was gonna believe that lie. He’s probably okay with them calling him names and stuff, because being misunderstood isn't as bad as being caught in your lies. But I see you, kid. I’ve been in that same situation before. I’ve been in that situation many times. Two cupcakes I bought at the bake sale became one. Two chocolate bars from the fundraiser became one. Yeah, of course two ice creams from the ice cream truck became one, too. My mom could never understand why I would sometimes pay extra for a single cupcake. Intro: [Intro music] These are true stories from the dark side of the internet. I’m Jack Rhysider. This is Darknet Diaries. JACK: Imagine going to a high school baseball game in New Port Richey, which is near Tampa, Florida. You see one kid, a center-fielder, who’s absolutely tearing it up out there. He’s catching anything that comes his way. He’s got an arm like a rocket. He could hit anything thrown at him. He’s built like a tank but runs like the wind, and it just looks like he’s in a different league than the rest of those high school players on the baseball field. He’s eating them up. It’s like all the other kids are in a lower league than him, and they're just all playing in slow motion compared to him. You can tell this kid is the star. That is Ricky Handschumacher. RICKY: So, I played center field, but initially I was really known for getting on base, getting hits, and then stealing bases. JACK: Stealing bases. RICKY: Yeah. JACK: Is this where all this starts? This is where all of it starts, stealing bases. RICKY: Coincidentally, yeah. JACK: But were computers interesting to you or not at all? RICKY: No, I was your gamer, you know? Like I said, I wasn't your average nerdy kinda guy who’s antisocial or anything. I was always out with my friends. I was always out on the streets playing sports; you know, football, baseball, basketball with all my friends. Like, Friday night and Saturday night I would go roller skating. So, I was never like, home, but I did have a passion for actual gaming. JACK: Alright. So, let’s talk about gaming. What was your game of choice? RICKY: Halo 3 was my primary game. JACK: [Halo sound effects] In 2010, fifteen-year-old Ricky is up late on a school night. His headphones are tuned in as he plays Halo 3 on his Xbox that’s humming away. Ricky doesn't want to disturb his mom, who’s sleeping in the other room. On his glowing TV screen he’s trying to escape what looks like a war zone. He’s destroying all the other players in the game. RICKY: I was good. So, I was always playing MLG and Team Slayer and all the ranked playlists against the pros and everything like that. Then, of course, naturally once you get to that level, there’s people who cheat on there and stuff. I was a high rank, but cheaters get high ranks, too, naturally because they're just cheating. So, it kept happening to me. JACK: People would go up against Ricky and see that they can't beat him, so they decided to cheat to win. He didn't know what was happening at first. RICKY: [Music] My screen would just go blank and then they would stop the attack when the game was over, which means they’d just win by default pretty much, 'cause we can't even move. Or if they hit you hard enough, we actually — our whole internet would just go out. I was with my mom. She’s like, why is the internet out? So, I had to play stupid. Like, I have no idea. I don't know what's happening. JACK: I’ve been in a similar situation. I remember the days when we had a family computer, and I downloaded a lot of random stuff and installed it on there. Time and time again I would break our computer. I didn't want to get in trouble, so I would try real hard to fix it before anyone noticed. Because of that, I got really good at detecting viruses and malware and fixing it on the family PC. But for Ricky, he was on an Xbox, and when he’d play, the internet would go down in the whole house, and it was just him and his mom living there. His dad left the picture a long time ago. But strangely, this pattern kept happening. When he would play Halo 3 against other players, the internet would go out. The game would disconnect, and then when he would finally get back on, he would see that he lost the match. RICKY: It happened to me again and again, and I’m like, alright. Then through the — through word of mouth I was like, oh, if they're DDoSing us, like, okay. So, I’m like, what the hell is that? I was getting DDoSed attacked over and over and over. JACK: Alright, so they somehow discovered your IP and then they attacked your IP, and that was enough to knock you offline and lose the game. RICKY: Yeah, and that’s kinda where it all started. Then curiosity — I was like, okay, how are they doing this? JACK: Remember, outside of gaming Ricky is not a computer guy. He doesn't know what's going on at all. So, he just turns his Xbox off and jumps on the family PC and starts trying to look for answers. RICKY: I started browsing some forums, and I was like, okay, it’s called DDoSing attacks. So, I started looking that up. I’m like, hm, okay, seems pretty simple. There’s a bunch of different kind of booters, like an IRC booter or a putty booter. You could just — or you could just go online to a website and use that booter, which was less powerful, but it would get the job done. I browsed the forums, found out what it was, downloaded the programs myself. So, I was like, okay, well, if they do it to me, I’m gonna do it back to them. JACK: Eventually he gets to the bottom of it. He discovers a whole world of ddossers and booters and punters and griefers who use malware to attack other players in the game to make them lose so you can win. Ricky decided, well, hey, I want to win, too. I want to try. [Music] So, he downloads a tool. He says it was Cain & Abel, and decides to try to use it to attack other players. He started a match, ran the tool to disconnect another player, then bingo; he sees they just freeze in the game and he can easily kill them, and he wins the match with almost zero effort. This was way easier than actually playing by the rules. RICKY: That’s kinda where I got introduced to that world. JACK: Yeah, so, at that point you were really competitive in baseball, you were really competitive at Halo. I just wonder, 'cause you had a sense of pride, of ranking up on your own and being competitive in sports — and where’d that sense of pride go with cheating? RICKY: I don't know. I just let it take over, pretty much. I was like, well, this is easier than actually trying. JACK: Yeah, but that’s not the sportsmanlike way. RICKY: Yeah. I don't know. I just took the easy way out and got the advantage. JACK: Were you cheating in sports at all? RICKY: No, that I was not cheating in. JACK: Alright. RICKY: No, I was naturally good. JACK: Yeah, well, you were naturally good at Halo, too. You were in MLG and all that stuff. RICKY: Yeah, I don't know. JACK: [Music] Who would have thought that this innocent little victory in Halo was going to lead Ricky down a long, dark path? From here he tried more Halo cheats like wall glitches, fast travel, reduced hitbox, and more. It was fun. This was the new game, not to compete competitively in Halo but to get around the game rules, to do things you weren’t supposed to, to be a god in the game. It gave him a sense of power. He saw the game differently now. He stopped seeing things on the screen like Covenant and Banshees and Needlers. Now he was seeing bytes and ones and zeros and the data behind the game, which gave him an incredible win streak. You know, the type of win streaks that you just have to take a screenshot of so that you can look back at from time to time and remember those matches. But even being a god can get boring after a while, and even though he was the winner in those screenshots of his, he would notice that some people seemed to be even cooler than him somehow. Everyone looks the same in Halo 3. You're all the same player, Master Chief. It’s just, everyone has a slightly different color. But there’s one thing that sets you apart from everyone else; your name, specifically your gamer tag. These are special, actually. They're unique. There’s only one person in the world with your gamer tag. Some people call themselves cool things like Shadow Strike or Nebula Storm or Blade of Odin. Fine, but what about that guy that’s just called Wolf? How did he get that name, Wolf? Now that is fricking cool. Well, it’s a first-come, first-serve kinda thing. So, Wolf must have made that gamer tag a long time ago when Xbox Live was first created, when gamer tags first came out. They probably made the name in the first week or maybe even the first day, which makes them OG, right? But instead of Original Gangster, they're the Original Gamer. Ricky wanted one of these short, cool gamer tags. That would really set him apart from the other normies playing in the game by the rules, but all the good names were taken. So, he goes back online into the hack forums and starts looking to see, how do you get one of these? It turns out there’s a whole underground marketplace of people buying and selling Xbox gamer tags, but not in the way you might think. See, a typical online market, you'll see people selling things that they've had for a long time or something that they've bought from someone else or something they made, right? But this was an underground hack forums marketplace. It operates differently. These gamer tags weren't ones that sellers were sitting on for a while. No, all these gamer tags were stolen. When Ricky found that out, he leaned in closer. How do you steal a gamer tag? Well, there are a few ways, but the easiest is just to get someone’s password and username and take over their account, change their password, and now that gamer tag is yours. But getting someone’s password is tricky. Maybe an easier way to get it is to trick Microsoft that you're the actual owner of the account and you just lost the password. Ricky saw some people were doing that and decided to try it himself. RICKY: There was a company called Zune, which is like Microsoft’s music app. Come to find out what you could do is you could call up Zune, and then halfway through the call you just tell them your gamer tag that you're targeting, and you say, okay, hey, my gamer tag is Jack. Then you just stop the conversation and be like, I have to go real fast. I’ll call back. JACK: Before hanging up, though, Zune support would give Ricky a reference number for the case that they were working on. Then he’d hang up and call a different number, Xbox Support this time, and they'd say, how can I help you? He’d say, oh, well, I was on a call but it dropped. I have a reference number if you want to pull the case details up. RICKY: Correct, yeah. You'd just simply say, yo, I have a reference number. Can you pull up my case? Then they would just give you the information right then and there. There was no questions asked. JACK: Ah, interesting. So, it’s almost like a bypass of a verbal authentication. So, then when you call Xbox and say, I have this reference number, then they give you the e-mail address. RICKY: Yep. JACK: Then you say, can you reset the password? RICKY: You would just be like, hey, yeah, here's my reference number — validate the account. Then just — you could just literally ask them, hey, what's the e-mail that I have on file? They'd read it off to you. JACK: How do you get the password? RICKY: Okay, so, back in the day AOL and Yahoo were your most popular domains. What's their proof of ownership of an account of an e-mail, was literally — AOL was like, your billing zip code would verify the account, and then they would be able to reset the password for you. Same with Yahoo. I think Yahoo was security questions, which back in the day was terrible because people would — a lot of the time chicken or pizza would be your favorite food that people would put, and stuff like that. So, they were pretty much takeable. JACK: See, that’s the thing that amazes me about these teenage hackers. They see the world differently than us, kinda like when you see motorcycles lane-splitting. You ever get stuck on a highway and there’s bumper-to-bumper traffic and you're standing still in your car and a motorcycle comes zooming past you right in-between the two lanes? You're like, come on. The motorcycle rider just looks back at you like you're a chump waiting in traffic like everyone else. They just whiz by like there’s no cars on the highway at all. These teenage hackers find ways through roadblocks that we just don't see. Like, you don't need someone’s password when the password reset question is ‘What's your favorite food?’ and you put ‘pizza’ up there. Now anyone can just write ‘pizza’ on there, and they could reset your password for you. It’s like, come on, what's the point of passwords if they could just be bypassed so easy? Sometimes it would try to validate it’s really you by asking for your zip code. Well, if you have their e-mail address, it’s not too hard to use some kind of people search tool online to look to see what someone’s zip code is. You and I don't think like that, though, but Ricky does. He’s the kind of guy that looks at us like we’re chumps for choosing an easy password recovery question. This was all happening in 2012, and Ricky was sixteen years old when he stole his first gamer tag. [Music] He found the one he wanted, Wolverine. Yeah, that sounds cool. He wasn't an X-Men fan; he just liked the sound of it. So, he called up Zune support, which is a Microsoft product, and is like, I have a problem with my account. They ask him for his e-mail address associated with the account. He says, well, I don't know. Can you just look up my Xbox gamer tag? They said, you know what? That works. What's your gamer tag? Ricky says, Wolverine. Zune support says, ah, yes, I see your account, sir. What can I help you with? Ricky says, okay, well, the problem is that when — you know what? Actually hold on; something just came up. Can I call you right back? Zune support says, yeah, sure. Do you want a reference number for when you call back? It’ll be easier for us to find your details. Ricky says, yes, yes, I do want that. He hangs up, and then he calls Xbox Support this time, and tells them, I was on with support but I got disconnected. Can you look up my case if I give you a reference number? They said, yeah, go ahead. He reads the number to them, and they see his details. Xbox Support’s mode of operation then was that if someone had a reference number, they must have already verified they are the account holder. So, they ask him, what's the problem? How can I help you? Ricky says, I just forgot what e-mail address I used for this account. He makes up some story about why he can't remember. He happened to be a good liar. Maybe it was that he got a new computer and didn't have those details on his new one. Xbox Support thinks, you know what? This is a harmless request. Sure. Your e-mail address is blahblahblah@aol.com. Great, he says. That’s all I wanted, and he hangs up. Now he has an e-mail address associated with that gamer tag. All he needs now is the password. Trying to get the password for an Xbox account is tricky, though. So, he has a better solution; try to reset the password on aol.com’s e-mail address. Once in there, he can reset the Xbox account and get control of that gamer tag. This is where he uses different tricks to get into an AOL account, by telling the website, I forgot my password, and it asking for his favorite food or zip code to verify it’s him. From there, bingo. He can now access the e-mail account and reset the password for that Microsoft gamer tag and get into it. This is how he became Wolverine. RICKY: Yeah, I thought it was cool, like a cool alias to have, and that was the first one I ever took. So, I was like, you know what? That’s what it is. JACK: So, Wolverine. RICKY: Yeah. So, that’s my alias. JACK: Ricky didn't have steel claws like Wolverine did. His weapons were his keyboard and telephone. Once Ricky got his first taste of stealing a gamer tag, he wanted more. He went back to that marketplace on hack forums where people were selling gamer tags. People were selling things like Gang or Spirit or Booty or Boss for a few hundred bucks each. Ricky started stealing gamer tags and then selling them for money on the site, for Bitcoin specifically. He started making some money off this, not bad money, either. A couple good gamer tags might sell for around $1,000. But many were just a few hundred bucks. He’d play with them, too, just to dunk on people. He’d log in with a stolen gamer tag, totally pwn some other players in Halo 3 by knocking them offline with some DDoS attack, and then just laugh at it all. But sometimes people would report him for abuse, and this would bring the party to a screeching halt. RICKY: I thought it was funny just to hit them offline and stuff like that. But eventually you just get banned. Like, back then Xbox was big on just banning your accounts and stuff for DDoS attacks. So, I would just get banned over and over, which then led to my consoles being banned. So, I was always at GameStop and whatnot just trading in consoles for new consoles and selling my banned consoles and stuff like that. JACK: He told me this happened over a dozen times, and he would just keep selling banned Xboxes at the same GameStop, and then go to another one across town and buy another. I just can't believe that they didn't catch on to him for constantly selling them banned Xboxes. RICKY: They would plug it in to make sure it turned on, which was fine with me, but they never checked like — connected to Xbox Live and stuff like that. JACK: He would do this again and again. RICKY: So, I would typically trade it in at one store and then go to a different GameStop and then buy the new console. I’ve probably went through at least ten, maybe closer to twenty. JACK: You would think after a while that Ricky would be like, alright, alright, enough of this getting banned. I’ll stop attacking people. But for some reason he was just so addicted to it that he would not stop attacking people and just kept getting reported for abuse again and again and again. You would think after five times, it’s like, okay, I’m tired of going down to get a new Xbox, but not Ricky. He would just keep doing it. Now, eventually he graduated to stealing something even more malleable. It wasn't just gamer tags anymore. [Music] His attention turned to Instagram handles. RICKY: I was always the old-school Halo guy, like Xbox guy. Like, I didn't want to transition into Instagram. I just stuck to what I know. Then just one day, a couple of my people were like, yo, why are you not doing Instagram? It’s a new wave. So, they kinda persuaded me. They were like, listen, here's an AOL e-mail address. It’s for the Instagram @bro, just like B-R-O. Nobody can take it. I’m like, dude, it’s an AOL. What do you mean nobody can take it? JACK: At the time, Ricky felt like he could steal any Xbox gamer tag he wanted. So, what do you mean you can't steal this Instagram name @bro? It’s tied to an AOL address account. Those are easy to get into. But this idea sparked something in Ricky. If he could get any gamer tag he wanted, then how different would it be to get Instagram names? It’s the same social engineering techniques that he figured out how to recover someone’s password, but there’s just way more money in it. RICKY: With the Instagram @bro, how nobody could get it that was trying to get it, it’s because it was linked — it was an adult account on AOL, but it had — it was like the parent account, and under the parent account it had other accounts. It was one of those e-mails under the parent account. That’s why nobody could get it. I was able to realize that. I realized it. Once I reset the main e-mail, and I was like, yo, this isn't my e-mail — like, you have other accounts under that e-mail. So, once I was able to match everything up, I was like, yo, it’s that specific one. I don't remember the exact e-mail. But I was like, it’s that one. I reset it, and the Instagram was right there. Funny story, though; the security question on it — I remember this conversation. Probably forever I’ll remember this. The lady was like, the security question is your favorite mythical creature. I was like, you know, I put something random. I apologize. I don't remember what it was. She’s like, okay, well, it’s big and hairy. As you can guess, I guessed Bigfoot. She started laughing and she goes, no, it’s another word for Bigfoot. I said, sasquatch. She goes, yeah, that’s right. Gave me the password reset. JACK: Man, I absolutely hate how easy this is for him. That customer service person really failed at keeping our accounts safe. I hope they got fired for giving Ricky this Instagram account @bro, because that’s ridiculous, and that’s how he got it. The way he’d steal an Instagram account is that he would get access to it, and he would log into it, and then he would have a second browser open with a brand-new, fresh Instagram account that he just made. He would change the username of the stolen one to something else, and then he would quickly switch to his fresh account and change its username to the stolen username.
